p1.en: As stated or reported by someone or something
p1.example: According to research, body language is more powerful than words.
p1.ex1: According to the interviewer, confident eye contact is essential.
p1.ex2: According to experts, facial expressions frequently replace spoken words.

p1.en: Used to say something is true despite what was said or expected before
p1.example: After all, body language is a major form of communication.
p1.ex1: She remained calm after all — her voice was clear and confident.
p1.ex2: After all, a single gesture can express a powerful emotion.

p1.en: A feeling of worry and nervousness about something uncertain
p1.example: Her anxiety before the interview was clear from her body language.
p1.ex1: He expressed his anxiety by avoiding eye contact with the interviewer.
p1.ex2: Anxiety can be reduced by maintaining a confident posture.

p1.en: Feeling worried or nervous about something that may happen
p1.example: She felt anxious during the presentation and frequently looked away.
p1.ex1: He was anxious because he was not well qualified for the role.
p1.ex2: An anxious person often slumps their shoulders and frowns.

p1.en: Except for something; or in addition to something
p1.example: Apart from eye contact, body language includes facial expressions.
p1.ex1: Apart from the voice, gestures are a major communication signal.
p1.ex2: Apart from being anxious, she remained confident throughout.

p1.en: To know about or notice something that is happening
p1.example: She was aware of how powerful her body language appeared.
p1.ex1: He was aware of the interviewer's facial expression and adjusted his posture.
p1.ex2: Being aware of your gestures helps you respond more suitably.

p1.en: To act in a particular way towards other people
p1.example: She behaved confidently despite feeling anxious inside.
p1.ex1: He was told to behave suitably during the important presentation.
p1.ex2: The purpose of body language is to show how someone behaves emotionally.

p1.en: To be the property of someone; or to be a member of a group
p1.example: This signal belongs to a major category of facial expressions.
p1.ex1: She felt she belonged to a group that valued confident communication.
p1.ex2: The gesture belongs to a particular culture and has a specific meaning.

p1.en: The way you communicate feelings through posture and gestures
p1.example: Her body language clearly showed she was anxious and not confident.
p1.ex1: He maintained strong body language throughout the entire interview.
p1.ex2: Body language can replace words and express powerful emotions.

p1.en: In a way that is easy to see, hear or understand
p1.example: She clearly expressed her emotions through confident body language.
p1.ex1: He clearly nodded to signal his agreement with the interviewer.
p1.ex2: Her anxiety was clearly visible from her slumped posture.

p1.en: Feeling or showing certainty about your own abilities
p1.example: She appeared confident despite her anxiety before the presentation.
p1.ex1: He maintained confident eye contact throughout the entire interview.
p1.ex2: A confident voice and suitable posture make a powerful impression.

p1.en: Always or all of the time, without stopping
p1.example: She constantly looked away, which made a negative impression.
p1.ex1: He was constantly aware of the interviewer's facial expressions.
p1.ex2: Anxiety makes some people constantly fidget and frown.

p1.en: A strong feeling such as happiness, anger or anxiety
p1.example: Her facial expression clearly expressed the emotion she was feeling.
p1.ex1: Body language can signal emotions more powerfully than voice alone.
p1.ex2: He relied on gestures to express his emotions during the presentation.

p1.en: To show thoughts or feelings through words, actions or expressions
p1.example: She expressed her confidence through strong eye contact and posture.
p1.ex1: He struggled to express his emotions clearly in the interview.
p1.ex2: Facial expressions frequently express emotions without any words.

p1.en: Looking directly into another person's eyes during communication
p1.example: She maintained confident eye contact throughout the presentation.
p1.ex1: He frequently looked away and avoided proper eye contact.
p1.ex2: Eye contact is a major signal that shows confidence and purpose.

p1.en: The way your face shows what you are thinking or feeling
p1.example: Her facial expression clearly showed she was anxious and confused.
p1.ex1: He relied on facial expressions to express emotions without speaking.
p1.ex2: A single facial expression can replace an entire spoken response.

p1.en: Happening many times at short intervals; regularly
p1.example: She frequently looked away during the interview, showing anxiety.
p1.ex1: He frequently nodded to signal his agreement with the interviewer.
p1.ex2: Facial expressions are frequently more powerful than spoken words.

p1.en: To make a serious or worried expression by bringing your brows together
p1.example: She frowned when she heard the interviewer's confusing question.
p1.ex1: He frowned constantly, making a negative and anxious impression.
p1.ex2: Frowning is a major facial expression that signals confusion or anger.

p1.en: A movement of the body used to express meaning or emotion
p1.example: She used a confident gesture to emphasise her point clearly.
p1.ex1: His gesture clearly matched the emotion he was trying to express.
p1.ex2: A single gesture can replace words and signal powerful meaning.

p1.en: A person who asks questions in a formal interview
p1.example: The interviewer clearly noticed her anxious body language.
p1.ex1: She maintained confident eye contact with the interviewer throughout.
p1.ex2: A skilled interviewer can read body language to understand emotions.

p1.en: To turn your eyes away from someone or something
p1.example: She frequently looked away, making a negative impression.
p1.ex1: He looked away when the interviewer asked a major question.
p1.ex2: Looking away during eye contact signals anxiety or lack of confidence.

p1.en: To keep something at the same level or continue doing it
p1.example: She maintained confident eye contact throughout the presentation.
p1.ex1: He maintained a suitable posture to make a powerful impression.
p1.ex2: Maintaining strong body language constantly is a major communication skill.

p1.en: Very important; large in size or extent
p1.example: Body language is a major form of nonverbal communication.
p1.ex1: She made a major impression by maintaining confident eye contact.
p1.ex2: Anxiety is a major signal that affects body language constantly.

p1.en: To correspond to something; to go well together
p1.example: Her facial expression did not match the emotion in her voice.
p1.ex1: He tried to match his gestures with the meaning of his words.
p1.ex2: A confident voice should match suitable and powerful body language.

p1.en: What something is intended to communicate or represent
p1.example: The gesture had a clear meaning that replaced spoken words.
p1.ex1: She remained aware of the meaning behind every facial expression.
p1.ex2: Body language frequently carries meaning beyond the voice alone.

p1.en: The act of moving the body or part of the body
p1.example: Her nervous movement clearly signalled anxiety to the interviewer.
p1.ex1: He relied on confident movement to express his emotions clearly.
p1.ex2: Every movement of the face is a major form of body language.

p1.en: To move your head up and down to show agreement or understanding
p1.example: She nodded to signal her agreement with the interviewer's point.
p1.ex1: He constantly nodded during the presentation to appear confident.
p1.ex2: Nodding is a single but powerful gesture that can replace words.

p1.en: Especially; to a greater degree than usual
p1.example: She was particularly anxious about maintaining eye contact.
p1.ex1: He was particularly aware of his body language during the interview.
p1.ex2: Facial expressions are particularly powerful signals of emotion.

p1.en: Having a strong effect or great influence on others
p1.example: A confident posture sends a powerful signal to the interviewer.
p1.ex1: Her voice remained powerful and clear despite her anxiety.
p1.ex2: Eye contact is a particularly powerful form of body language.

p1.en: The reason for which something is done or made
p1.example: The purpose of eye contact is to signal confidence and attention.
p1.ex1: She remained unclear about the purpose of the gesture.
p1.ex2: Every movement of the body has a major communication purpose.

p1.en: Having all the knowledge and skills needed for a job or role
p1.example: She was well qualified but remained anxious before the interview.
p1.ex1: He appeared confident and well qualified throughout the interview.
p1.ex2: A well qualified candidate uses suitable body language constantly.

p1.en: To depend on or trust something or someone for support
p1.example: She relied on confident gestures to express herself clearly.
p1.ex1: He relied on nodding to signal agreement without speaking.
p1.ex2: You cannot rely on voice alone — body language is equally major.

p1.en: To stay in the same condition, place or situation
p1.example: She remained confident despite her anxiety before the interview.
p1.ex1: He remained aware of his body language throughout the presentation.
p1.ex2: Remaining calm is a major signal of confidence to the interviewer.

p1.en: To take the place of something or someone
p1.example: A nod can replace a spoken response in certain situations.
p1.ex1: She replaced a verbal response with a confident gesture.
p1.ex2: Body language frequently replaces words to express powerful emotions.

p1.en: To react to something or reply to someone
p1.example: She responded confidently to the interviewer's major questions.
p1.ex1: He responded with a nod and a smile rather than speaking.
p1.ex2: Responding with suitable body language is a particularly powerful skill.

p1.en: Something that communicates information or shows a particular meaning
p1.example: A frown is a major signal of confusion or anxiety.
p1.ex1: She maintained eye contact as a signal of confident communication.
p1.ex2: Every gesture and movement sends a powerful nonverbal signal.

p1.en: Only one; not more than one
p1.example: A single nod can replace an entire spoken response.
p1.ex1: She made a single major gesture that expressed her emotion clearly.
p1.ex2: A single facial expression can send a particularly powerful signal.

p1.en: Sitting or leaning in a collapsed or drooping position
p1.example: She looked slumped in her chair, clearly signalling anxiety.
p1.ex1: His slumped posture made a negative impression on the interviewer.
p1.ex2: A slumped position replaces confident body language with a weak signal.

p1.en: Right or appropriate for a particular purpose or situation
p1.example: She chose a suitable posture for the important interview.
p1.ex1: His gestures were particularly suitable for the formal presentation.
p1.ex2: Suitable body language sends a major signal of confidence.

p1.en: For that reason; as a result or consequence
p1.example: She remained anxious; therefore, her body language was not confident.
p1.ex1: He was well qualified; therefore, he responded to every question clearly.
p1.ex2: Body language is major; therefore, it frequently replaces spoken words.

p1.en: The sound produced when speaking or singing
p1.example: Her voice remained clear and confident throughout the presentation.
p1.ex1: He relied on his voice to express emotion alongside body language.
p1.ex2: A powerful voice matched with suitable gestures makes a major impression.

p1.en: To fold your arms across your chest, often signalling defence or discomfort
p1.example: She crossed her arms during the interview, signalling anxiety.
p1.ex1: He crossed his arms, which replaced a confident open posture.
p1.ex2: Crossing your arms sends a major negative signal to the interviewer.

p1.en: Used to introduce a statement that is true in most cases
p1.example: Generally speaking, eye contact signals confidence and purpose.
p1.ex1: Generally speaking, body language frequently replaces spoken meaning.
p1.ex2: Generally speaking, a slumped posture sends a negative signal.

p1.en: To communicate an idea successfully so someone understands it
p1.example: She used confident gestures to get her message across clearly.
p1.ex1: He relied on body language to get the message across to the interviewer.
p1.ex2: Getting a message across without words is a particularly powerful skill.

p1.en: To cause someone to believe something about you
p1.example: She gave the impression of being well qualified and confident.
p1.ex1: His slumped posture gave the impression of anxiety and low confidence.
p1.ex2: Maintaining eye contact gives the impression of a particularly powerful signal.

p1.en: Sometimes; depending on the particular situation
p1.example: In certain cases, a single gesture can replace an entire spoken response.
p1.ex1: In certain cases, a frown is a suitable signal of serious thought.
p1.ex2: In certain cases, body language is more major than voice alone.

p1.en: To raise and lower your shoulders to show you do not know or care
p1.example: She shrugged her shoulders to signal she did not know the answer.
p1.ex1: He shrugged his shoulders instead of responding to the interviewer.
p1.ex2: Shrugging your shoulders is a particularly powerful nonverbal signal.

p2.en: A strong feeling of displeasure or rage towards someone or something
p2.example: Her anger was clearly visible from her facial expression and voice.
p2.ex1: He struggled to suppress his anger during the stressful presentation.
p2.ex2: Anger is a major emotion that frequently shows in body language.

p2.en: Feeling slightly angry or irritated by something
p2.example: She was annoyed when the audience kept yawning during her talk.
p2.ex1: He appeared annoyed because the volunteer kept interrupting him.
p2.ex2: An annoyed expression frequently replaces a spoken complaint.

p2.en: A group of people watching or listening to a performance or speech
p2.example: The audience clapped enthusiastically at the end of the presentation.
p2.ex1: She was relieved when the audience responded positively to her joke.
p2.ex2: A confused audience frequently shows puzzled facial expressions.

p2.en: The state of feeling uninterested and unengaged with something
p2.example: The audience's yawning was a major signal of boredom.
p2.ex1: She noticed boredom in the audience and changed her approach.
p2.ex2: Boredom is frequently expressed through yawning and looking away.

p2.en: To shout with enthusiasm to show support or happiness
p2.example: The audience cheered and clapped when the speaker finished.
p2.ex1: She was relieved to hear the audience cheer after the presentation.
p2.ex2: He told a joke and was relieved when the audience cheered.

p2.en: To bring your palms together repeatedly to show approval
p2.example: The audience clapped enthusiastically after the sign language performance.
p2.ex1: She was relieved when the audience clapped at the end.
p2.ex2: He encouraged the audience to clap to express their excitement.

p2.en: To give an opinion or make a remark about something
p2.example: She commented on the volunteer's particularly powerful presentation.
p2.ex1: He discussed and commented on each facial expression in turn.
p2.ex2: The interviewer asked her to comment on the meaning of the gesture.

p2.en: Unable to understand something; not sure what is happening
p2.example: She looked confused when the presenter used sign language unexpectedly.
p2.ex1: He was confused by the puzzled expression on the audience's faces.
p2.ex2: A confused expression frequently replaces a spoken question.

p2.en: A state of not understanding something clearly
p2.example: The confusion on her face clearly expressed her emotion.
p2.ex1: He tried to discuss the source of confusion with the audience.
p2.ex2: Confusion is a major emotion that frequently shows in facial expressions.

p2.en: To think carefully about something before deciding or acting
p2.example: She considered how to express her emotion without using words.
p2.ex1: He asked the audience to consider the meaning of each gesture.
p2.ex2: Consider how body language frequently replaces spoken communication.

p2.en: Unable to hear, either partially or completely
p2.example: The volunteer was deaf and communicated using sign language.
p2.ex1: She was relieved to learn that sign language could replace speech entirely.
p2.ex2: The audience included several deaf members who relied on sign language.

p2.uz: Umidi puchga chiqqan / hafsalasi pir bo'lgan
p2.en: Feeling sad because something was not as good as expected
p2.example: She was disappointed when the audience yawned during her presentation.
p2.ex1: He was disappointed that the volunteer did not clap at the end.
p2.ex2: A disappointed expression is a major nonverbal signal of sadness.

p2.en: To talk about something with other people, sharing ideas and opinions
p2.example: She discussed the meaning of each gesture with the audience.
p2.ex1: He asked the volunteer to discuss the emotion behind the sign language.
p2.ex2: They discussed how sadness and confusion frequently appear in facial expressions.

p2.en: A feeling of great enthusiasm and eagerness
p2.example: Her excitement was clearly visible from her smile and body language.
p2.ex1: The audience expressed their excitement by clapping and cheering.
p2.ex2: Excitement is a major emotion that frequently replaces boredom.

p2.en: Able to speak a language very naturally and confidently
p2.example: She was fluent in sign language and communicated with deaf students.
p2.ex1: He was relieved to be fluent enough to respond to every question.
p2.ex2: The volunteer was fluent in three languages and several sign language dialects.

p2.en: An attempt to give a correct answer without being certain
p2.example: She made a guess about the meaning of the puzzling gesture.
p2.ex1: His guess was surprisingly accurate — the signal meant confusion.
p2.ex2: Consider your guess carefully before responding to the audience's question.

p2.en: A feeling of pleasure, contentment and joy
p2.example: Her happiness was clearly expressed through her smile and gestures.
p2.ex1: The audience's clapping and cheering signalled their happiness.
p2.ex2: Happiness is a major emotion that frequently shows in facial expressions.

p2.en: To say something amusing to make people laugh
p2.example: She joked with the audience to reduce confusion and boredom.
p2.ex1: He joked about the puzzled expression on the volunteer's face.
p2.ex2: Joking is a suitable way to express happiness and reduce anxiety.

p2.en: Probable (likely) or improbable (unlikely) to happen
p2.example: It is likely that the audience will respond with clapping or cheering.
p2.ex1: She was unlikely to remain fluent under such stressful conditions.
p2.ex2: It is unlikely that a single gesture can replace every spoken emotion.

p2.en: To have a particular meaning or to intend to communicate something
p2.example: The gesture means confusion in certain sign language systems.
p2.ex1: She asked the audience what the movement of the head meant.
p2.ex2: A frown frequently means anxiety, confusion or disappointment.

p2.en: To say something briefly without discussing it in detail
p2.example: She mentioned the role of sign language in the presentation.
p2.ex1: He mentioned that a puzzled expression frequently replaces spoken confusion.
p2.ex2: The interviewer mentioned the importance of suitable body language.

p2.en: A formal talk given to an audience about a particular topic
p2.example: She gave a powerful presentation about sign language and emotion.
p2.ex1: The audience clapped enthusiastically after his confident presentation.
p2.ex2: Her presentation discussed the major role of body language in communication.

p2.en: A confusing problem or situation that is difficult to understand
p2.example: The gesture was a puzzle that the audience could not easily solve.
p2.ex1: She set the audience a puzzle about the meaning of sign language.
p2.ex2: His puzzled expression remained a puzzle to the interviewer throughout.

p2.en: Feeling confused or unable to understand something
p2.example: She looked puzzled when the presenter suddenly switched to sign language.
p2.ex1: He was puzzled by the audience's confused reaction to his joke.
p2.ex2: A puzzled expression frequently replaces a spoken question or confusion.

p2.en: To mention or direct attention to something
p2.example: She referred to sign language as a major form of communication.
p2.ex1: He referred to the volunteer's emotion when discussing facial expressions.
p2.ex2: Consider the gestures he referred to when discussing body language.

p2.en: Feeling happy because a worry or difficulty has ended
p2.example: She was relieved when the audience clapped at the end of her talk.
p2.ex1: He was relieved to hear the audience cheer rather than yawn.
p2.ex2: She felt relieved after the stressful presentation was finally over.

p2.en: To cause someone to remember something
p2.example: The gesture reminded her of a sign language movement she had seen.
p2.ex1: He reminded the audience to consider the meaning behind each expression.
p2.ex2: Remind yourself to maintain suitable body language during a presentation.

p2.en: To make someone think of something similar they have seen before
p2.example: His puzzled expression reminded her of a confused audience member.
p2.ex1: She was reminded of the excitement she felt at her first presentation.
p2.ex2: The gesture reminded the audience of a major sign language signal.

p2.en: A feeling of unhappiness or sorrow
p2.example: Her sadness was clearly visible from her expression and body language.
p2.ex1: The audience remained silent to show their sadness at the news.
p2.ex2: Sadness is a major emotion frequently expressed through facial expressions.

p2.en: To breathe out slowly and deeply, often to express sadness or relief
p2.example: She sighed with relief when the audience began to clap.
p2.ex1: He sighed when the volunteer gave a puzzled and confused response.
p2.ex2: Sighing is a major nonverbal signal of sadness or confusion.

p2.en: A language that uses hand movements and gestures for deaf people
p2.example: She was fluent in sign language and communicated clearly with deaf students.
p2.ex1: The presentation discussed how sign language replaces spoken communication.
p2.ex2: Sign language relies on gesture and movement to express every emotion.

p2.en: Causing feelings of anxiety and worry
p2.example: The presentation was stressful because the audience seemed confused.
p2.ex1: He remained confident despite the stressful and anxious atmosphere.
p2.ex2: Stressful situations frequently cause people to yawn, sigh or frown.

p2.en: To believe or assume something is likely to be true
p2.example: She supposed the audience was bored because they kept yawning.
p2.ex1: He supposed the gesture meant confusion in a specific sign language.
p2.ex2: Consider what you suppose the emotion is before you respond.

p2.en: A person who offers to do something freely without being asked
p2.example: A volunteer from the audience demonstrated the sign language gesture.
p2.ex1: She asked a volunteer to express a major emotion without words.
p2.ex2: The volunteer remained relieved after the stressful presentation ended.

p2.en: To move your hand from side to side as a greeting or to get attention
p2.example: She waved at the audience to signal the start of the presentation.
p2.ex1: He waved to replace a spoken greeting at the beginning of the talk.
p2.ex2: Waving is a particularly powerful gesture that frequently replaces words.

p2.en: To close one eye briefly as a friendly or secret signal
p2.example: She winked at the volunteer to signal that the joke was intentional.
p2.ex1: He winked at the audience to express excitement before the surprise.
p2.ex2: A wink is a single gesture that can replace a spoken signal.

p2.en: To open your mouth wide and breathe in deeply due to tiredness or boredom
p2.example: Several audience members yawned, which clearly signalled boredom.
p2.ex1: She yawned during the stressful and confusing presentation.
p2.ex2: Yawning is a major nonverbal signal that frequently replaces spoken boredom.

p2.en: To look sad or disappointed without speaking
p2.example: She had a long face after the audience failed to clap and cheer.
p2.ex1: He had a long face when the volunteer gave a confused response.
p2.ex2: Having a long face is a major signal of sadness or disappointment.

p2.en: Using something with no useful result or benefit
p2.example: She said yawning during a presentation is a waste of everyone's time.
p2.ex1: He considered the confused discussion a waste of a major opportunity.
p2.ex2: A stressful presentation with no clear message is a waste of effort.

p2.en: In order to help or benefit someone; out of consideration for them
p2.example: She remained calm for the sake of the anxious volunteer.
p2.ex1: He maintained confident body language for the sake of the audience.
p2.ex2: For the sake of clear communication, rely on suitable body language.

p2.en: To find it hard to do something; to struggle with a task
p2.example: She had difficulty expressing her emotion clearly without words.
p2.ex1: He had difficulty remaining fluent under such stressful conditions.
p2.ex2: Deaf volunteers often have difficulty relying on voice alone to communicate.

p2.en: Used to say that you will keep something completely secret
p2.example: She smiled and said my lips are sealed when asked about the surprise.
p2.ex1: He winked and said my lips are sealed to the confused volunteer.
p2.ex2: My lips are sealed — consider the gesture and guess the meaning.

p2.en: To lift your eyebrows as a sign of surprise, disbelief or interest
p2.example: She raised her eyebrows when the audience began to yawn.
p2.ex1: He raised his eyebrows to express surprise without saying a word.
p2.ex2: Raising your eyebrows is a major nonverbal signal of excitement or confusion.

p2.en: To move your eyes upward to show annoyance, boredom or disbelief
p2.example: She rolled her eyes when the volunteer gave a particularly puzzled response.
p2.ex1: He rolled his eyes to signal annoyance at the stressful confusion.
p2.ex2: Rolling your eyes frequently replaces a spoken expression of boredom.

p2.en: To rub the top of your head to show confusion or uncertainty
p2.example: She scratched her head to signal confusion about the sign language gesture.
p2.ex1: He scratched his head when the audience asked a particularly major question.
p2.ex2: Scratching your head is a particularly powerful signal of puzzled confusion.

p2.en: To move your head from side to side to signal no or disagreement
p2.example: She shook her head to signal she disagreed with the volunteer.
p2.ex1: He shook his head to replace a spoken refusal to the audience.
p2.ex2: Shaking your head is a major gesture that frequently replaces spoken words.

p1.en: To have an effect on someone or something; to cause a change
p1.example: Her cheerful attitude greatly affected the atmosphere in the team.
p1.ex1: Negative behaviour can affect a colleague's confidence and success.
p1.ex2: Being impatient with others affects relationships and causes issues.

p1.en: A particular part or feature of something
p1.example: Being reliable is an important aspect of a good personality trait.
p1.ex1: She described every aspect of her colleague's ambitious behaviour.
p1.ex2: The most important aspect of success is having a hopeful attitude.

p1.en: The mood or feeling created in a particular place or situation
p1.example: Her enthusiastic and outgoing nature created a positive atmosphere.
p1.ex1: An impolite colleague can cause a negative and stressful atmosphere.
p1.ex2: She dealt with the difficult atmosphere by remaining cheerful.

p1.en: The way you think or feel about something; your general outlook
p1.example: A positive and optimistic attitude is a major personality trait.
p1.ex1: His bossy attitude affected the atmosphere and disappointed his colleagues.
p1.ex2: She dealt with every issue with a hopeful and energetic attitude.

p1.en: The way a person acts in a particular situation
p1.example: His disorganised behaviour caused several issues for the team.
p1.ex1: She described her colleague's stubborn behaviour to the director.
p1.ex2: Selfish behaviour disappoints others and affects the team atmosphere.

p1.en: To have a good effect on someone; to gain an advantage
p1.example: A sociable and reliable colleague benefits the whole team greatly.
p1.ex1: She benefited from her colleague's enthusiastic support and guidance.
p1.ex2: Being honest and helpful always benefits every aspect of a relationship.

p1.en: To make something happen, especially something bad
p1.example: Stubborn behaviour can cause major issues in a team atmosphere.
p1.ex1: His impatient attitude caused disappointment among his colleagues.
p1.ex2: Being disorganised often causes delays and affects overall success.

p1.en: A person you work with, especially in an office or organisation
p1.example: She dealt with every issue honestly alongside her trusted colleague.
p1.ex1: Her enthusiastic and outgoing colleague created a positive atmosphere.
p1.ex2: A reliable and sociable colleague is a major benefit to any team.

p1.en: Totally and entirely; used to emphasise a statement
p1.example: She was completely disappointed by her colleague's selfish behaviour.
p1.ex1: He succeeded completely because of his ambitious and energetic attitude.
p1.ex2: The atmosphere changed completely when the optimistic colleague arrived.

p1.en: To take action to handle a problem or difficult situation
p1.example: She dealt with the difficult issue calmly and with a cheerful attitude.
p1.ex1: He dealt with his colleague's stubborn behaviour by remaining patient.
p1.ex2: Dealing with negative aspects of behaviour requires a hopeful attitude.

p1.en: To need something or someone; to rely on them
p1.example: Success depends on having a reliable and enthusiastic attitude.
p1.ex1: She depended on her colleague's helpful and honest nature.
p1.ex2: Whether you succeed depends on your attitude and personality traits.

p1.en: To say what something or someone is like in detail
p1.example: She described every aspect of her colleague's ambitious personality.
p1.ex1: He described the atmosphere as completely disorganised and stressful.
p1.ex2: Describe the personality traits that cause issues in the workplace.

p1.en: To make someone feel sad because something did not meet expectations
p1.example: His stubborn and impolite behaviour completely disappointed his colleague.
p1.ex1: She was disappointed that the issue affected the team atmosphere.
p1.ex2: Being unreliable disappoints others and causes major relationship issues.

p1.en: Well known for a particular quality, achievement or behaviour
p1.example: She was famous for her cheerful and outgoing personality trait.
p1.ex1: He was famous for being completely honest and reliable at work.
p1.ex2: Their team was famous for a positive atmosphere and great success.

p1.en: In a hopeful way; used to express a wish or expectation
p1.example: Hopefully, his stubborn attitude will improve with encouragement.
p1.ex1: She dealt with the issue hopefully, believing success was possible.
p1.ex2: Hopefully, every aspect of the atmosphere will improve completely.

p1.ex1: The announcement caught everyone's attention.
p1.ex2: Please pay attention to the safety instructions.

p1.en: Bags and suitcases that you take on a journey.
p1.example: You can check your baggage at the counter.
p1.ex1: They lost my baggage on the connecting flight.
p1.ex2: Baggage allowance depends on your ticket class.

p1.en: A document that allows a passenger to board a plane or train.
p1.example: Please show your boarding pass at the gate.
p1.ex1: I forgot to print my boarding pass at home.
p1.ex2: You can download your boarding pass as a PDF.

p1.en: To decide that something planned will not happen.
p1.example: The flight was cancelled due to the storm.
p1.ex1: We had to cancel our hotel reservation.
p1.ex2: They cancelled the trip at the last minute.

p1.en: To hand over your luggage to airline staff before a flight.
p1.example: We arrived early enough to check our bags in.
p1.ex1: You need to check in your suitcase at the desk.
p1.ex2: She checked in her luggage and went to security.

p1.en: To make something definite or say it is true.
p1.example: Please confirm your booking 24 hours before departure.
p1.ex1: She confirmed her reservation by email.
p1.ex2: The airline confirmed the new departure time.

p1.en: A situation in which something happens later than expected.
p1.example: There was a two-hour delay due to technical problems.
p1.ex1: The delay caused us to miss our connection.
p1.ex2: Passengers were frustrated by the long delay.

p1.en: To leave a place, especially at the start of a journey.
p1.example: The train departs from platform 3 at noon.
p1.ex1: The flight is scheduled to depart at 6 AM.
p1.ex2: Guests should depart by 11 o'clock.

p1.en: To leave a ship, aircraft, or train at the end of a journey.
p1.example: Passengers are asked to disembark through the front exit.
p1.ex1: We disembarked as soon as the plane landed.
p1.ex2: It took an hour for everyone to disembark.

p1.en: Because of; caused by something.
p1.example: The flight was delayed due to heavy fog.
p1.ex1: Due to the strike, many trains were cancelled.
p1.ex2: She missed the bus due to heavy traffic.

p1.en: In the end, after a long time or series of events.
p1.example: We eventually found our gate after walking for twenty minutes.
p1.ex1: He eventually got on the right train.
p1.ex2: Eventually the storm passed and flights resumed.

p1.en: The money you pay to travel on a bus, train, or plane.
p1.example: The train fare is cheaper if you book in advance.
p1.ex1: Bus fares have gone up this year.
p1.ex2: We compared fares on several different airlines.

p1.en: To feel nauseous because of the movement of a boat on water.
p1.example: She started to feel seasick as soon as the ferry left port.
p1.ex1: I always get seasick on rough crossings.
p1.ex2: He took medicine so he would not feel seasick.

p1.en: The place at an airport where passengers board their aircraft.
p1.example: Please proceed to gate 14 for your flight.
p1.ex1: The gate number changed at the last minute.
p1.ex2: We ran to the gate but the doors were already closed.

p1.en: At exactly the same time as something else happens.
p1.example: Just as we arrived, the train doors closed.
p1.ex1: Just as I sat down, my name was called.
p1.ex2: The announcement came just as we reached the gate.

p1.en: A person who travels in a vehicle but does not drive it.
p1.example: All passengers must fasten their seatbelts.
p1.ex1: There were over 300 passengers on the flight.
p1.ex2: Passengers were asked to remain seated.

p1.en: To collect someone from a place in a car or other vehicle.
p1.example: I will pick you up from the airport at 9 PM.
p1.ex1: Can you pick me up from the train station?
p1.ex2: She was picked up by her family after arrival.

p1.en: The raised surface at a train station where passengers wait.
p1.example: Your train leaves from platform 6 in five minutes.
p1.ex1: We stood on the platform waiting for the express.
p1.ex2: There was a large crowd on platform 2.

p1.en: To delay an event to a later time or date.
p1.example: They postponed the trip because of the bad weather.
p1.ex1: The meeting was postponed until next week.
p1.ex2: We had to postpone our holiday due to illness.

p1.en: Coming or happening before something else in time or order.
p1.example: On the previous flight, my seat was next to the window.
p1.ex1: My previous train journey took six hours.
p1.ex2: She had visited the city on a previous trip.

p1.en: To give information about something officially or formally.
p1.example: You must report any suspicious items to the staff.
p1.ex1: Please report to the check-in desk immediately.
p1.ex2: Passengers are required to report missing luggage.

p1.en: An arrangement to keep something (like a room or seat) for you.
p1.example: I'd like to make a reservation for two adults.
p1.ex1: We cancelled our reservation the day before.
p1.ex2: She made a reservation at the airport hotel.

p1.en: A ticket for a journey to a place and back again.
p1.example: A return ticket to Paris is cheaper than two singles.
p1.ex1: I bought a return ticket so I could come back on Friday.
p1.ex2: Return tickets must be used within 30 days.

p1.en: To do something even though something bad might happen.
p1.example: Do not risk missing your flight — arrive early!
p1.ex1: She risked losing her luggage by checking in late.
p1.ex2: He risked his seat by not confirming the reservation.

p1.en: To be very busy doing many different things in a rushed way.
p1.example: We spent an hour running around the terminal looking for the gate.
p1.ex1: She was running around packing at the last minute.
p1.ex2: Stop running around and check the departures board.

p1.en: To move or do something very quickly, often in a hurry.
p1.example: We had to rush to the gate before it closed.
p1.ex1: Do not rush — you still have plenty of time.
p1.ex2: He rushed through security to catch his train.

p1.en: To begin a journey.
p1.example: We set off for the airport at 5 in the morning.
p1.ex1: They set off early to avoid the traffic.
p1.ex2: Let us set off now so we do not miss the train.

p1.en: A ticket for a journey to one place only, without a return.
p1.example: I just need a single ticket to Manchester.
p1.ex1: Single tickets are usually cheaper for short trips.
p1.ex2: She bought a single ticket — she was not coming back.

p1.en: A small label attached to something, with information on it.
p1.example: Make sure the tag on your suitcase has your name.
p1.ex1: The luggage tag fell off during the journey.
p1.ex2: They put a tag on each bag at the check-in desk.

p1.en: Relating to machines, equipment, or how something works.
p1.example: The delay was caused by a technical fault with the engine.
p1.ex1: There was a technical problem with the check-in system.
p1.ex2: Technical issues grounded several flights that day.

p1.en: A building at an airport where passengers arrive and depart.
p1.example: Our flight departs from Terminal 2.
p1.ex1: The shuttle takes you between the two terminals.
p1.ex2: Terminal 5 is used for international flights only.

p1.en: Very surprising or hard to believe; used to express strong emotion.
p1.example: The queues at security were absolutely unbelievable!
p1.ex1: The delay was unbelievable — six hours!
p1.ex2: It was unbelievable how quickly we got through customs.

p1.en: Impossible to find; completely missing.
p1.example: I searched everywhere — my passport was nowhere to be found.
p1.ex1: The conductor was nowhere to be found when we needed help.
p1.ex2: Our bags were nowhere to be found after landing.

p2.en: A seat in a plane or theatre next to the central walkway.
p2.example: I prefer an aisle seat so I can stretch my legs.
p2.ex1: She always books an aisle seat on long flights.
p2.ex2: There were no aisle seats left when he checked in.

p2.en: To tell people officially or publicly about something.
p2.example: The captain announced that the flight would be delayed.
p2.ex1: They announced the gate change over the loudspeaker.
p2.ex2: The conductor announced the next stop.

p2.en: An official or public statement giving information.
p2.example: Did you hear the announcement about the gate change?
p2.ex1: An announcement was made about the delay.
p2.ex2: The announcement came through clearly on the loudspeaker.

p2.en: A statement saying you are sorry for something you did wrong.
p2.example: The airline issued a formal apology for the disruption.
p2.ex1: We received a written apology from the hotel.
p2.ex2: His apology seemed genuine and heartfelt.

p2.en: The act of reaching a place at the end of a journey.
p2.example: On arrival at the hotel, you must show your passport.
p2.ex1: The arrival of the train was announced on the board.
p2.ex2: Our arrival was delayed by two hours due to fog.

p2.en: To get onto a plane, ship, train, or bus.
p2.example: Passengers in rows 20–30 may now board the aircraft.
p2.ex1: We boarded the ferry just before it left.
p2.ex2: All passengers must board by 10:45.

p2.en: The area inside a plane where passengers sit, or a room on a ship.
p2.example: The cabin crew will demonstrate safety procedures.
p2.ex1: Please stow your luggage in the overhead compartment.
p2.ex2: The ship's cabin was small but comfortable.

p2.en: One of the separate sections of a passenger train.
p2.example: First class is in carriage A at the front of the train.
p2.ex1: We found seats in the last carriage.
p2.ex2: The dining car is between carriage 4 and carriage 5.

p2.en: To register your arrival at a hotel or airport.
p2.example: You need to check in at least two hours before departure.
p2.ex1: We checked in online the night before.
p2.ex2: Check-in closes 45 minutes before the flight.

p2.en: To pay your bill and leave a hotel.
p2.example: What time do we need to check out tomorrow?
p2.ex1: They checked out early to catch the morning train.
p2.ex2: Checkout is at noon — please be ready.

p2.en: To say you are unhappy or dissatisfied about something.
p2.example: Several passengers complained about the long delay.
p2.ex1: He complained to the manager about the noise.
p2.ex2: She complained that her room had no hot water.

p2.en: To formally state that you are unhappy about something.
p2.example: I'd like to make a complaint about my missing luggage.
p2.ex1: If you're not satisfied, you can make a complaint online.
p2.ex2: He made a complaint to the airline after his flight was cancelled.

p2.en: A person on a train who checks tickets and helps passengers.
p2.example: The conductor came through the carriage to check our tickets.
p2.ex1: Ask the conductor which stop is yours.
p2.ex2: The conductor announced the delay over the intercom.

p2.en: A long, narrow passage inside a building or train.
p2.example: The corridor between the carriages was very narrow.
p2.ex1: Please do not leave bags in the corridor.
p2.ex2: He walked down the corridor to find his seat.

p2.en: The people who work on a plane or ship.
p2.example: The cabin crew will serve refreshments during the flight.
p2.ex1: The crew handled the emergency calmly.
p2.ex2: All crew members were highly professional.

p2.en: The act of leaving a place to start a journey.
p2.example: Departure is scheduled for 14:35 from gate 7.
p2.ex1: Check the departures board for your gate number.
p2.ex2: The departure was delayed by bad weather.

p2.en: A screen at an airport showing flight or train times and gates.
p2.example: I checked the departures board for our gate number.
p2.ex1: The departures board showed our flight was on time.
p2.ex2: Look at the departures board — our gate has changed!

p2.en: A carriage on a train where meals are served.
p2.example: Let us go to the dining car for lunch.
p2.ex1: The dining car was fully booked for dinner.
p2.ex2: They served hot meals in the dining car.

p2.en: A hotel room designed for two people with a double bed.
p2.example: We booked a double room with a sea view.
p2.ex1: Is a double room available for two nights?
p2.ex2: The double room had a balcony and ensuite bathroom.

p2.en: The length of time that something lasts.
p2.example: The duration of the flight is approximately four hours.
p2.ex1: For the duration of the journey, phones must be on silent.
p2.ex2: What is the duration of the cruise?

p2.en: To come to the end of a valid period (of a document or ticket).
p2.example: My passport expires next month — I need to renew it.
p2.ex1: The ticket expired before we could use it.
p2.ex2: Check when your visa expires before booking.

p2.en: To close or secure something firmly.
p2.example: Please fasten your seatbelt for take-off.
p2.ex1: Fasten your bag before placing it in the overhead compartment.
p2.ex2: The crew checked that all doors were fastened.

p2.en: A person whose job is to look after passengers on a plane.
p2.example: The flight attendant brought us extra pillows.
p2.ex1: A flight attendant demonstrated the oxygen mask.
p2.ex2: She has been a flight attendant for ten years.

p2.en: A device used to remove creases from clothes using heat.
p2.example: Is there an iron available in the room?
p2.ex1: I asked reception for an iron to press my shirt.
p2.ex2: The iron in the hotel room was broken.

p2.en: Tiredness felt after a long flight across time zones.
p2.example: I always suffer from terrible jet lag after flying to Asia.
p2.ex1: It took her three days to recover from jet lag.
p2.ex2: Drink plenty of water to help with jet lag.

p2.en: A device that makes sound louder so people can hear announcements.
p2.example: The gate change was announced over the loudspeaker.
p2.ex1: Passengers could hear the delay on the loudspeaker.
p2.ex2: A message was broadcast over the airport loudspeaker.

p2.en: On the open upper area of a ship.
p2.example: We went on deck to watch the coast disappear.
p2.ex1: It was windy on deck but the view was amazing.
p2.ex2: Passengers gathered on deck as the ship entered port.

p2.en: The storage space above seats in a plane for carry-on luggage.
p2.example: Please place your hand luggage in the overhead compartment.
p2.ex1: The overhead compartment was already full when we boarded.
p2.ex2: He struggled to close the overhead compartment.

p2.en: To go forward or move towards a place, especially formally.
p2.example: Please proceed to the boarding gate immediately.
p2.ex1: Passengers are asked to proceed to customs.
p2.ex2: After security, proceed directly to your gate.

p2.en: The area in a hotel where visitors arrive and check in.
p2.example: Please leave your key at reception when you check out.
p2.ex1: I called reception to ask for a wake-up call.
p2.ex2: The reception desk is open 24 hours.

p2.en: A person who works at the reception desk of a hotel.
p2.example: The receptionist gave us our room key and a map.
p2.ex1: She asked the receptionist about nearby restaurants.
p2.ex2: A friendly receptionist greeted us at check-in.

p2.en: To extend the period of validity of a document like a passport.
p2.example: I need to renew my driving licence before the trip.
p2.ex1: She renewed her passport six months before it expired.
p2.ex2: You can renew your season ticket online.

p2.en: Describing the sea when it has large, violent waves.
p2.example: The crossing was rough and many passengers felt seasick.
p2.ex1: It was too rough to go on deck.
p2.ex2: The rough weather delayed the ferry by three hours.

p2.en: A strong, locked metal box in a hotel room for storing valuables.
p2.example: You can put your passport in the safe in your room.
p2.ex1: I kept my money in the hotel room safe.
p2.ex2: The safe requires a 4-digit code to open.

p2.en: Happy or content with the result or quality of something.
p2.example: I was not satisfied with the service at the hotel.
p2.ex1: Were you satisfied with your room?
p2.ex2: She was satisfied with how the complaint was handled.

p2.en: A hotel room designed for one person.
p2.example: I'd like to book a single room for three nights.
p2.ex1: A single room costs less than a double.
p2.ex2: Single rooms are sometimes smaller but perfectly comfortable.

p2.en: To experience pain, illness, or something unpleasant.
p2.example: He suffers from motion sickness on long bus journeys.
p2.ex1: Many travellers suffer from jet lag.
p2.ex2: She suffered from terrible headaches during the flight.

p2.en: The moment when a plane leaves the ground and begins to fly.
p2.example: Please fasten your seatbelts for take-off.
p2.ex1: Take-off was smooth despite the cloudy conditions.
p2.ex2: Children are often nervous at take-off.

p2.en: A long passage built underground, usually for trains or cars.
p2.example: The train goes through a tunnel under the mountains.
p2.ex1: There is a tunnel under the English Channel.
p2.ex2: It was dark inside the tunnel for several minutes.

p2.en: Sudden, irregular movements in the air that cause a plane to shake.
p2.example: We experienced heavy turbulence over the Atlantic.
p2.ex1: The pilot warned us about turbulence ahead.
p2.ex2: Turbulence made it difficult to walk in the cabin.

p2.en: Used to say that something is not important or not worth worrying about.
p2.example: It does not matter if we miss the earlier train — there is another one.
p2.ex1: That does not matter — we can book a later flight.
p2.ex2: It does not matter; we still have time.

p2.word: There's been some sort of mistake.
p2.en: Used politely to say something is wrong, often at a hotel or airline desk.
p2.example: There has been some sort of mistake — I booked a double room, not a single.
p2.ex1: There has been some sort of mistake with my reservation.
p2.ex2: Excuse me, I think there has been some sort of mistake with my seat.

p3.en: Making you feel slightly angry or impatient.
p3.example: It was really annoying when our flight was delayed again.
p3.ex1: The constant announcements were annoying.
p3.ex2: He found the waiting around very annoying.

p3.en: To understand how good something is; to be grateful for it.
p3.example: I really appreciate the extra help you gave us.
p3.ex1: We appreciated the free upgrade to business class.
p3.ex2: She appreciated how quickly the problem was solved.

p3.en: A small amount or degree of something.
p3.example: It was a bit cold on the deck at night.
p3.ex1: I was a bit nervous about the turbulence.
p3.ex2: Can you wait a bit? I am not ready yet.

p3.en: Extremely beautiful or impressive, taking your breath away.
p3.example: The view of the Alps from the plane was breathtaking.
p3.ex1: The scenery from the train window was breathtaking.
p3.ex2: We were amazed by the breathtaking sunset from the deck.

p3.en: To communicate with someone by phone, email, etc.
p3.example: Please contact us if your plans change.
p3.ex1: You can contact the hotel directly to confirm.
p3.ex2: She contacted the airline to claim compensation.

p3.en: To include someone in an activity or plan.
p3.example: We are going on a day trip to the mountains — count me in!
p3.ex1: If you are going sightseeing, count me in.
p3.ex2: She said count her in for the evening tour.

p3.en: To find or learn about something for the first time.
p3.example: We discovered a wonderful hidden beach on our last day.
p3.ex1: He discovered a fantastic local restaurant.
p3.ex2: Travelling lets you discover new cultures.

p3.en: Not interesting or exciting; boring.
p3.example: The journey was long and dull without any entertainment.
p3.ex1: The tour was a bit dull — nothing unusual.
p3.ex2: The hotel was clean but rather dull and plain.

p3.en: Not harmful to the environment.
p3.example: We stayed at an eco-friendly resort that used solar energy.
p3.ex1: The tour company used eco-friendly transport.
p3.ex2: More travellers are choosing eco-friendly options.

p3.en: A form of energy used to power lights, machines, and devices.
p3.example: There was no electricity in the cabin for the first night.
p3.ex1: The campsite had no electricity after 10 PM.
p3.ex2: Solar panels provided electricity for the whole resort.

p3.en: Giving pleasure; pleasant to experience.
p3.example: It was a very enjoyable trip — everything went smoothly.
p3.ex1: The cruise was enjoyable from start to finish.
p3.ex2: She found the workshop really enjoyable.

p3.en: A public display of objects, art, or information.
p3.example: We visited a fascinating photography exhibition at the museum.
p3.ex1: The travel exhibition had maps and artefacts.
p3.ex2: There is a free exhibition about local history in the town.

p3.en: To give someone all the information they need about something.
p3.example: Can you fill me in on what I missed while I was away?
p3.ex1: Fill me in on the details of the itinerary.
p3.ex2: She filled us in on the changes to the programme.

p3.en: The best or most exciting part of something.
p3.example: The highlight of the trip was sailing through the fjords.
p3.ex1: For me, the highlight was visiting the old market.
p3.ex2: She said the food tour was the highlight of her holiday.

p3.en: Perfect for a particular purpose or situation.
p3.example: The location was ideal — close to everything we wanted to see.
p3.ex1: It was ideal weather for walking.
p3.ex2: That hotel is ideal for families with children.

p3.en: Making you feel admiration because it is very good or large.
p3.example: The ancient cathedral was truly impressive.
p3.ex1: The scale of the city was impressive.
p3.ex2: Her knowledge of local history was very impressive.

p3.en: Extremely good, large, or remarkable; hard to believe.
p3.example: The food at the local restaurant was absolutely incredible.
p3.ex1: We had an incredible time in the mountains.
p3.ex2: The view from the summit was just incredible.

p3.en: A connection between two people, places, or things.
p3.example: There is a direct link between the airport and the city centre.
p3.ex1: The bus provides a link to the ferry terminal.
p3.ex2: Send me the link to the hotel booking page.

p3.en: To manage to arrive somewhere or achieve something.
p3.example: We were not sure we would make it in time for the last train.
p3.ex1: Did you make it to the airport on time?
p3.ex2: I am glad we made it — the views were worth the effort.

p3.en: To succeed in doing something despite difficulties.
p3.example: We managed to find a taxi even though it was very late.
p3.ex1: She managed to get tickets for the sold-out show.
p3.ex2: Did you manage to book the last cabin?

p3.en: Smelling or looking so delicious that it makes you want to eat.
p3.example: The market was full of mouth-watering local food.
p3.ex1: The menu had mouth-watering seafood dishes.
p3.ex2: The smell of fresh bread was mouth-watering.

p3.en: Used to say that something is not a problem.
p3.example: No worries if you cannot make the tour — we will go another day.
p3.ex1: No worries, we will sort it out when we arrive.
p3.ex2: Sorry for being late. — No worries at all!

p3.en: Easy to see or understand; clear.
p3.example: It was obvious that we were in the tourist area.
p3.ex1: It was obvious they had never been to the city before.
p3.ex2: The best route is obvious on the map.

p3.en: New and different; also meaning the first version of something.
p3.example: The restaurant served original dishes you could not find elsewhere.
p3.ex1: She liked the original itinerary better.
p3.ex2: The tour guide had a very original style.

p3.en: Completely full of something or someone.
p3.example: The museum was packed with tourists on Saturday.
p3.ex1: The beach was packed with families.
p3.ex2: The itinerary was packed with exciting activities.

p3.en: To take part in an activity or event.
p3.example: Everyone was encouraged to participate in the workshop.
p3.ex1: She participated in every activity on the tour.
p3.ex2: Would you like to participate in the cooking class?

p3.en: Belonging to or for the use of one person; not public.
p3.example: We hired a private guide for the day.
p3.ex1: The villa had a private pool and garden.
p3.ex2: He arranged a private tour of the palace.

p3.en: The natural features of an area, especially beautiful countryside.
p3.example: The train passed through spectacular mountain scenery.
p3.ex1: The scenery in the national park was stunning.
p3.ex2: We stopped several times to admire the scenery.

p3.en: Very exciting and enjoyable.
p3.example: White water rafting was absolutely thrilling!
p3.ex1: The roller coaster was thrilling but a bit frightening.
p3.ex2: It was a thrilling end to an amazing trip.

p3.en: To happen in a particular way or to have a particular result.
p3.example: The weather turned out to be perfect for sightseeing.
p3.ex1: The trip turned out better than we expected.
p3.ex2: It turned out the tour was fully booked.

p3.en: So impressive or special that you cannot forget it.
p3.example: It was an unforgettable holiday — the best of my life.
p3.ex1: The sunset over the ocean was truly unforgettable.
p3.ex2: We had an unforgettable experience at the festival.

p3.en: A session where people learn a skill by practising it.
p3.example: We attended a local cooking workshop during the trip.
p3.ex1: There was a pottery workshop at the cultural centre.
p3.ex2: The workshop lasted two hours and we loved it.

p3.en: A number of things or people, often used informally.
p3.example: There was a bunch of tourists gathered at the entrance.
p3.ex1: We bought a bunch of souvenirs at the market.
p3.ex2: A bunch of friends joined us for the tour.

p3.en: A polite response when someone thanks you, meaning it was no trouble.
p3.example: Thank you so much for helping with my bags. — Do not mention it!
p3.ex1: Do not mention it — I was happy to help.
p3.ex2: Do not mention it, really — it was nothing.

p3.en: Without any cost; for free.
p3.example: Children under five travel free of charge.
p3.ex1: The hotel offered airport transfers free of charge.
p3.ex2: The museum entry was free of charge on Sundays.

p3.en: To develop problems or fail to happen as planned.
p3.example: Everything went wrong when we missed our connection.
p3.ex1: Something went wrong with our booking.
p3.ex2: What can go wrong if we do not confirm in advance?

p3.en: To have a very enjoyable or exciting time.
p3.example: We had an absolute blast at the beach festival.
p3.ex1: Everyone had a blast at the end-of-trip party.
p3.ex2: I hope you have a blast on your adventure!

p3.en: The latest possible time; just before a deadline.
p3.example: We booked the hotel at the last minute and got a great deal.
p3.ex1: Do not leave packing to the last minute.
p3.ex2: She always buys gifts at the last minute.

p1.en: Relating to education, schools, or scholarly study.
p1.example: She has strong academic results and wants to study abroad.
p1.ex1: The academic year begins in September.
p1.ex2: He received an academic award for his research.

p1.en: To be able to reach, enter, or use something.
p1.example: Students can access the library resources online.
p1.ex1: You need a password to access the course materials.
p1.ex2: Not everyone can access higher education easily.

p1.en: To succeed in doing or completing something.
p1.example: She accomplished all her goals by the end of the year.
p1.ex1: It is hard to accomplish anything without focus.
p1.ex2: He accomplished the task faster than expected.

p1.en: Something that has been successfully achieved or completed.
p1.example: Graduating from university is a great accomplishment.
p1.ex1: Winning the competition was her greatest accomplishment.
p1.ex2: List your accomplishments on your CV.

p1.en: A formal request to join a course, job, or programme.
p1.example: She submitted her application for the exchange programme.
p1.ex1: Fill in the application form carefully.
p1.ex2: His application was accepted by the university.

p1.en: To make a formal request for something such as a job or course.
p1.example: He decided to apply for a summer internship.
p1.ex1: You should apply for the scholarship before the deadline.
p1.ex2: She applied for three different universities.

p1.en: Forming the simplest or most essential part of something.
p1.example: The course covers the basic principles of economics.
p1.ex1: You need basic computer skills for this job.
p1.ex2: The instructions are written in basic English.

p1.en: To take part in an activity or become connected to something.
p1.example: She got involved in several volunteer projects at college.
p1.ex1: Try to get involved in extracurricular activities.
p1.ex2: He became involved in student government.

p1.en: An official document proving that you have completed a course or qualification.
p1.example: You will receive a certificate after completing the programme.
p1.ex1: She has a certificate in business administration.
p1.ex2: The certificate is recognised by employers worldwide.

p1.en: Something difficult that requires effort and determination.
p1.example: Learning a new language is always a big challenge.
p1.ex1: The biggest challenge was managing time effectively.
p1.ex2: She rose to every challenge during the course.

p1.en: To focus your attention and effort on something.
p1.example: It is hard to concentrate when there is background noise.
p1.ex1: She concentrated on her studies before the exam.
p1.ex2: Try to concentrate on one task at a time.

p1.en: The ability to focus attention on something for a period of time.
p1.example: Online learning requires a high level of concentration.
p1.ex1: Loud music affects her concentration.
p1.ex2: His concentration improved after regular breaks.

p1.en: Fitting in well with your needs, without causing difficulty.
p1.example: Online courses are very convenient for working adults.
p1.ex1: Is Tuesday convenient for our meeting?
p1.ex2: The campus is in a convenient location near the station.

p1.en: To work together with someone to achieve a shared goal.
p1.example: Students need to cooperate with their teammates on projects.
p1.ex1: The two schools agreed to cooperate on the research.
p1.ex2: It is important to cooperate during group activities.

p1.en: The act of working together towards a shared goal.
p1.example: The project was a success thanks to excellent cooperation.
p1.ex1: Cooperation between students leads to better results.
p1.ex2: International cooperation helped fund the programme.

p1.en: The latest time or date by which something must be done.
p1.example: The deadline for applications is the 15th of March.
p1.ex1: Do not miss the deadline for submitting your essay.
p1.ex2: She always finishes her work before the deadline.

p1.en: A qualification given by a university after completing a course of study.
p1.example: He is studying for a degree in computer science.
p1.ex1: She earned her degree after four years of study.
p1.ex2: A degree opens many doors in the job market.

p1.en: A spoken or written account that says what something is like.
p1.example: Read the course description carefully before applying.
p1.ex1: The job description listed the required qualifications.
p1.ex2: Her description of the lecture was very detailed.

p1.en: A person who is paid to work for a company or organisation.
p1.example: Every employee must complete the training programme.
p1.ex1: The company values each employee's contribution.
p1.ex2: New employees receive a welcome pack on their first day.

p1.en: Words or actions that give someone confidence to do something.
p1.example: Her teacher's encouragement helped her apply for university.
p1.ex1: A little encouragement can make a big difference.
p1.ex2: He needed encouragement to speak up in class.

p1.en: The same in size, amount, or level; treating everyone the same.
p1.example: Everyone deserves equal access to education.
p1.ex1: Both teams have an equal chance of winning.
p1.ex2: The school promotes equal opportunities for all students.

p1.en: An arrangement that allows students to study in another country.
p1.example: She joined an exchange programme and spent a year in Spain.
p1.ex1: The exchange programme improved his language skills enormously.
p1.ex2: Apply early if you want a place on the exchange programme.

p1.en: A statement that makes something clear or easy to understand.
p1.example: The teacher gave a clear explanation of the grammar rule.
p1.ex1: Can you give me an explanation for your absence?
p1.ex2: The explanation in the textbook was confusing.

p1.en: An amount of money charged for a service or course.
p1.example: The course fee includes all study materials.
p1.ex1: International students pay a higher tuition fee.
p1.ex2: The registration fee must be paid in advance.

p1.en: A visit made by students to a place away from school for learning.
p1.example: The class went on a field trip to the science museum.
p1.ex1: The field trip gave students hands-on experience.
p1.ex2: We learned more on the field trip than in a week of lessons.

p1.en: Able to change or be adapted to suit different needs or situations.
p1.example: Online learning offers a more flexible schedule.
p1.ex1: The course timetable is flexible for part-time students.
p1.ex2: She appreciates a flexible approach to deadlines.

p1.en: Completely; to the greatest possible degree.
p1.example: The course is fully funded for eligible students.
p1.ex1: Are you fully prepared for the exam?
p1.ex2: The hall was fully booked for the graduation ceremony.

p1.en: To stop doing or trying something; to admit defeat.
p1.example: Do not give up if you find the subject difficult at first.
p1.ex1: She never gave up on her dream of becoming a doctor.
p1.ex2: He gave up the course after the first month.

p1.en: Something you aim to achieve; a target you set for yourself.
p1.example: Setting a goal helps you stay focused during your studies.
p1.ex1: Her goal was to finish the degree in three years.
p1.ex2: He set a goal to improve his grades each semester.

p1.en: The ceremony or occasion when you receive your degree or diploma.
p1.example: Her parents flew in from abroad to attend her graduation.
p1.ex1: Graduation takes place in July each year.
p1.ex2: He wore a cap and gown at the graduation ceremony.

p1.en: Taking place face to face, not online or by phone.
p1.example: Some students prefer in-person classes to online ones.
p1.ex1: The interview will be held in-person at the office.
p1.ex2: In-person learning helps students interact more.

p1.en: A student or recent graduate who works temporarily to gain experience.
p1.example: She worked as an intern at a marketing company last summer.
p1.ex1: The intern was given real responsibilities from day one.
p1.ex2: Many interns are offered a job after the placement.

p1.en: A period of work experience at a company, usually for students.
p1.example: He completed a six-month internship before graduating.
p1.ex1: The internship gave her valuable practical experience.
p1.ex2: She found the internship through a university careers fair.

p1.en: To stop someone while they are speaking or doing something.
p1.example: Please do not interrupt the lecturer during the presentation.
p1.ex1: He interrupted the teacher to ask a question.
p1.ex2: It is rude to interrupt when someone is talking.

p1.en: To not have enough of something; to be without something needed.
p1.example: She lacks confidence when speaking in front of a large group.
p1.ex1: He lacks the experience needed for the role.
p1.ex2: The school lacks proper equipment for science classes.

p1.en: The state of not having enough of something.
p1.example: A lack of preparation led to poor results in the exam.
p1.ex1: The project failed due to a lack of funding.
p1.ex2: His lack of attendance was noted by the teacher.

p1.en: A talk given to a group of students at a university or college.
p1.example: The lecture on climate change lasted two hours.
p1.ex1: She takes detailed notes at every lecture.
p1.ex2: The professor gave an inspiring lecture on history.

p1.en: To control or reduce the amount or extent of something.
p1.example: Try to limit the time you spend on social media while studying.
p1.ex1: The teacher limited the essay to 500 words.
p1.ex2: We should limit screen time before exams.

p1.en: Not large in number or amount; restricted.
p1.example: There are only a limited number of places on the course.
p1.ex1: Her experience with technology is limited.
p1.ex2: Limited resources made the project difficult.

p1.en: To fail to experience or take advantage of something good.
p1.example: If you do not attend, you will miss out on important information.
p1.ex1: He missed out on the scholarship by one point.
p1.ex2: Do not miss out on the chance to apply early.

p1.en: A time or set of circumstances that makes it possible to do something.
p1.example: Studying abroad is a great opportunity to grow.
p1.ex1: Take every opportunity to practise your English.
p1.ex2: The internship was an opportunity she could not refuse.

p1.en: The act of taking part in an activity or event.
p1.example: Active participation in class improves your grade.
p1.ex1: Her participation in the debate was impressive.
p1.ex2: Participation in the exchange programme is voluntary.

p1.en: The main idea or purpose of something; a single fact or argument.
p1.example: The main point of the lecture was about time management.
p1.ex1: What is the point of submitting work late?
p1.ex2: She made a very good point about online learning.

p1.en: Of a low quality or standard; not good enough.
p1.example: Poor concentration leads to poor results in exams.
p1.ex1: The essay received a poor grade due to lack of structure.
p1.ex2: He performed poorly because he lacked preparation.

p1.en: To show or describe something formally to a group.
p1.example: Each student will present their project to the class.
p1.ex1: She was nervous when she had to present her research.
p1.ex2: He presented his findings clearly and confidently.

p1.en: To encourage or support the growth of something.
p1.example: The programme aims to promote cooperation between universities.
p1.ex1: Schools should promote equal opportunities for all.
p1.ex2: The campaign promotes healthy study habits.

p1.en: The process of officially signing up for a course or event.
p1.example: Registration for the new semester opens next Monday.
p1.ex1: Complete your online registration before the deadline.
p1.ex2: The registration fee is 50 dollars per course.

p1.en: To arrange for something to be kept or saved for your use.
p1.example: You can reserve a place on the course by filling in the form.
p1.ex1: She reserved a seat for the graduation ceremony.
p1.ex2: Reserve your spot early as places are limited.

p1.en: Something given in recognition of effort or achievement.
p1.example: Hard work during your studies brings great rewards in the future.
p1.ex1: The reward for completing the course was a certificate.
p1.ex2: She worked hard and deserved the reward.

p1.en: Used to introduce examples of something.
p1.example: The course covers topics such as grammar, writing, and speaking.
p1.ex1: Skills such as teamwork are valued by employers.
p1.ex2: You can take electives such as art or music.

p1.en: To be right or appropriate for a particular person or situation.
p1.example: Online learning suits students who have busy schedules.
p1.ex1: Does Monday suit you for the meeting?
p1.ex2: This course suits people who want a flexible schedule.

p1.en: A person who teaches or trains people in a particular skill.
p1.example: The trainer explained each exercise step by step.
p1.ex1: She worked as a fitness trainer at the university gym.
p1.ex2: The corporate trainer ran a full-day workshop.

p1.en: The ability to comprehend something; knowledge of a subject.
p1.example: This course will deepen your understanding of economics.
p1.ex1: She has a good understanding of grammar rules.
p1.ex2: A clear understanding of the topic helped him write a better essay.

p1.en: In or to whatever place; no matter where.
p1.example: Online learning lets you study wherever you have internet access.
p1.ex1: You can access the course materials wherever you are.
p1.ex2: She takes notes wherever she goes.

p1.word: from the comfort of one's home
p1.en: Without needing to leave your house; used about remote activities.
p1.example: You can now attend lectures from the comfort of your own home.
p1.ex1: She completed the whole degree from the comfort of her home.
p1.ex2: Working from the comfort of home suits many people.

p1.en: A small number of things or people, usually two or a few.
p1.example: I have a couple of questions about the homework.
p1.ex1: She finished the task in a couple of hours.
p1.ex2: We need a couple of volunteers for the project.

p1.en: The right or ability to use or enter something.
p1.example: Not all students have equal access to technology.
p1.ex1: The library provides free access to online resources.
p1.ex2: He gained access to the database through his university account.

p1.en: To change your behaviour or approach to suit a new situation.
p1.example: It took her a while to adapt to working from home.
p1.ex1: New employees must adapt quickly to the company culture.
p1.ex2: He adapted his teaching style for online lessons.

p1.en: To believe something is true without having proof.
p1.example: Do not assume everyone has access to fast internet.
p1.ex1: She assumed the meeting had been cancelled.
p1.ex2: He assumed the job would be easy, but it was not.

p1.en: A healthy division between time spent on work and personal life.
p1.example: Good work-life balance is important for mental health.
p1.ex1: She struggles to maintain a work-life balance.
p1.ex2: The company promotes a healthy work-life balance.

p1.en: The information or material included in something such as a course or website.
p1.example: The digital content of the course is available 24 hours a day.
p1.ex1: Students can access course content from their phones.
p1.ex2: The content of the lesson was very useful.

p1.en: Requiring a lot of effort, skill, or time.
p1.example: Working as a teacher can be very demanding.
p1.ex1: The job is demanding but rewarding.
p1.ex2: She found the course more demanding than expected.

p1.en: Relating to or using computer technology and the internet.
p1.example: Digital skills are now essential in most workplaces.
p1.ex1: The digital age has changed how we learn.
p1.ex2: She completed a digital marketing course online.

p1.en: To separate something into parts or groups.
p1.example: The class was divided into groups for the project.
p1.ex1: Divide the tasks equally between team members.
p1.ex2: The digital divide affects access to education.

p1.en: A person or organisation that pays people to work for them.
p1.example: Many employers now offer remote working options.
p1.ex1: The employer valued teamwork and communication skills.
p1.ex2: Her employer paid for her training course.

p1.en: To make it possible for someone to do something.
p1.example: Technology enables people to work from anywhere.
p1.ex1: The grant enabled her to study abroad.
p1.ex2: Online tools enable students to collaborate more easily.

p1.en: In the same amount or degree; in a fair way.
p1.example: Tasks should be shared equally among all team members.
p1.ex1: Both candidates were equally qualified for the role.
p1.ex2: The prize money was divided equally between the winners.

p1.en: Relating to money or the management of money.
p1.example: Many students face financial difficulties during their studies.
p1.ex1: She received financial support from the university.
p1.ex2: The company is in a strong financial position.

p1.en: Not needing help from others; able to think or act for yourself.
p1.example: Online learning requires students to be more independent.
p1.ex1: She became more independent after moving abroad.
p1.ex2: Independent learners tend to do well in higher education.

p1.en: To form or compose something; also to invent a story.
p1.example: Online students make up a large percentage of the course.
p1.ex1: Women make up the majority of the teaching workforce.
p1.ex2: He made up an excuse for missing the deadline.

p1.en: In a way that is normal or expected; without effort.
p1.example: Naturally, working from home requires good self-discipline.
p1.ex1: She naturally assumed the role of team leader.
p1.ex2: Naturally, the results improved after more practice.

p1.en: A proportion or share expressed as a part of 100.
p1.example: A large percentage of workers now work remotely.
p1.ex1: What percentage of students passed the exam?
p1.ex2: The percentage of online learners has grown each year.

p1.en: A job or role in a company; also a place or point of view.
p1.example: She applied for a position as a marketing assistant.
p1.ex1: He was offered a senior position at the firm.
p1.ex2: What is your position on remote working?

p1.en: To make or create something.
p1.example: The team produced a detailed report on digital learning.
p1.ex1: She produced an excellent presentation for the client.
p1.ex2: The factory produces thousands of units per day.

p1.en: Forward movement or improvement towards a goal.
p1.example: She is making excellent progress in her English course.
p1.ex1: We need to review the progress of each student.
p1.ex2: He made great progress after switching to online learning.

p1.en: A fixed regular payment for a job, usually paid monthly.
p1.example: Her salary increased after she completed the training.
p1.ex1: He negotiated a higher salary before accepting the job.
p1.ex2: The starting salary for graduates is quite competitive.

p1.en: A piece of work that needs to be done.
p1.example: Each student was given a different task to complete.
p1.ex1: Break the project into smaller tasks to manage it better.
p1.ex2: She completed every task ahead of schedule.

p1.en: Working together with others to achieve a shared goal.
p1.example: Teamwork is one of the most valued skills by employers.
p1.ex1: Good teamwork helped the group finish the project on time.
p1.ex2: The course includes activities that develop teamwork skills.

p1.en: Payment for work, usually calculated by the hour or day.
p1.example: The minimum wage was raised at the start of the year.
p1.ex1: He earns a good wage working in construction.
p1.ex2: Many part-time workers are paid an hourly wage.

p1.en: The place where you go to do your job.
p1.example: Digital technology has transformed the modern workplace.
p1.ex1: A positive workplace culture improves productivity.
p1.ex2: She felt comfortable and supported in her workplace.

p1.en: The current period in history defined by digital technology.
p1.example: We live in a digital age where everything is connected.
p1.ex1: In the digital age, communication is instant.
p1.ex2: Education has changed dramatically in the digital age.

p1.en: Happening or calculated once every year.
p1.example: The company holds an annual review of all employees.
p1.ex1: She receives an annual bonus at the end of December.
p1.ex2: The annual report showed strong financial growth.

p1.en: At this moment in time; currently.
p1.example: At present, most students attend lectures online.
p1.ex1: At present, the position has not been filled.
p1.ex2: We are not accepting new applications at present.

p1.en: A period of one hundred years.
p1.example: Distance learning has grown enormously in the twenty-first century.
p1.ex1: The university was founded in the nineteenth century.
p1.ex2: Many jobs that exist today did not exist a century ago.

p1.en: A period of ten years.
p1.example: Online learning has expanded rapidly over the past decade.
p1.ex1: She has worked at the company for over a decade.
p1.ex2: The last decade has seen huge changes in technology.

p1.en: Used to refer to a time in the past that is now different.
p1.example: In those days, most people worked in factories.
p1.ex1: In those days, there was no internet or email.
p1.ex2: People worked six days a week in those days.

p1.en: At the present time, compared to the past.
p1.example: Nowadays, many companies allow employees to work remotely.
p1.ex1: Nowadays, digital skills are a requirement in most jobs.
p1.ex2: Nowadays, students can study from anywhere in the world.

p1.en: At some unspecified point in the future or past.
p1.example: One day, remote working may become the global standard.
p1.ex1: Some day she hopes to run her own business.
p1.ex2: One day he decided to change his career completely.

p1.en: A length of time with a particular quality or feature.
p1.example: The period after graduation can be a stressful time.
