p1.ex1: There was a short period when the company worked fully remotely.
p1.ex2: She studied abroad for a period of six months.

p1.en: Arriving or doing things at the expected or agreed time.
p1.example: It is important to be punctual for job interviews.
p1.ex1: She is always punctual and never misses a deadline.
p1.ex2: Being punctual shows respect for other people's time.

p1.en: A fixed period of time, especially a division of the school year.
p1.example: The results will be published at the end of the term.
p1.ex1: She improved her grades each term.
p1.ex2: The internship runs for one full term.

p1.en: A few days ago; recently.
p1.example: I read an interesting article about remote work the other day.
p1.ex1: The other day she received an offer for a new job.
p1.ex2: He mentioned the other day that he was thinking of changing careers.

p2.en: The fact of not being present at a place or event.
p2.example: His absence from the meeting was noticed by everyone.
p2.ex1: Frequent absence from class affects your grade.
p2.ex2: She sent an email to explain her absence.

p2.en: A professional who manages financial records and accounts.
p2.example: She trained as an accountant after graduating from university.
p2.ex1: The company hired an accountant to manage their finances.
p2.ex2: He works as an accountant at a large law firm.

p2.en: A quantity of something; how much there is of something.
p2.example: The amount of time students spend online has increased greatly.
p2.ex1: A large amount of effort is needed to succeed.
p2.ex2: The total amount of fees must be paid in advance.

p2.en: The route a person takes through their working life.
p2.example: She is still deciding which career path to follow.
p2.ex1: An internship can help you choose your career path.
p2.ex2: His career path took him from teaching to management.

p2.en: Difficult in a way that tests your abilities.
p2.example: The job was challenging but she enjoyed every moment.
p2.ex1: Managing a remote team can be very challenging.
p2.ex2: He found the interview questions challenging but fair.

p2.en: A competition to find the best team or player in a sport.
p2.example: Winning the championship was the highlight of his school career.
p2.ex1: She trained for years before winning the national championship.
p2.ex2: The team celebrated after winning the regional championship.

p2.en: Required by law or rules; something you must do.
p2.example: Attendance at the training session is compulsory for all staff.
p2.ex1: Physical education is compulsory in most schools.
p2.ex2: The course includes both compulsory and optional modules.

p2.en: The assistance and support given to people before, during, and after buying.
p2.example: She started her career in customer service at a hotel.
p2.ex1: Good customer service is essential in any business.
p2.ex2: He trained in customer service before becoming a manager.

p2.en: To leave a course or activity before finishing it.
p2.example: He dropped out of university in his second year.
p2.ex1: Several students dropped out due to financial difficulties.
p2.ex2: She nearly dropped out but continued after getting extra support.

p2.en: Having a job (employed) or not having a job (unemployed).
p2.example: He was unemployed for six months before finding a new role.
p2.ex1: She has been employed at the same company for ten years.
p2.ex2: The course helps unemployed people retrain for new careers.

p2.en: The state of having a job (employment) or not having one (unemployment).
p2.example: Youth unemployment remains a major challenge in many countries.
p2.ex1: Employment opportunities have grown in the tech sector.
p2.ex2: The government introduced schemes to reduce unemployment.

p2.en: Having knowledge or skill gained from doing something for a long time.
p2.example: The company is looking for an experienced project manager.
p2.ex1: She is an experienced teacher with over fifteen years in the classroom.
p2.ex2: Experienced staff are expected to mentor new employees.

p2.en: A lack of success; not achieving what was intended.
p2.example: Failure is often the first step towards success.
p2.ex1: He saw his failure as a learning opportunity.
p2.ex2: The project was considered a failure due to poor planning.

p2.en: To dismiss someone from their job.
p2.example: He was fired after missing several important deadlines.
p2.ex1: The manager fired two employees for breaking company rules.
p2.ex2: She was shocked when she was fired without warning.

p2.en: To give special attention to one particular thing.
p2.example: This term, try to focus on improving your writing skills.
p2.ex1: The course focuses on practical workplace communication.
p2.ex2: She decided to focus on her studies instead of working part-time.

p2.en: The power to act, speak, or think as you want without restriction.
p2.example: Remote working gives employees more freedom to manage their time.
p2.ex1: She valued the freedom of being self-employed.
p2.ex2: Academic freedom is essential in higher education.

p2.en: Involving the standard number of working hours, usually 35 to 40 per week.
p2.example: He moved from part-time to full-time work after graduation.
p2.ex1: She is a full-time student and does not work.
p2.ex2: Full-time employees receive more benefits than part-time ones.

p2.en: Money received regularly from work or investments.
p2.example: Her income increased after she was promoted to manager.
p2.ex1: Many freelancers have an irregular income.
p2.ex2: The family relied on a single income.

p2.en: The feeling of happiness or contentment you get from your work.
p2.example: High job satisfaction often leads to better performance.
p2.ex1: She earns less but has much more job satisfaction now.
p2.ex2: Job satisfaction is more important to him than salary.

p2.en: A person who writes news reports or articles for media.
p2.example: She has always dreamed of becoming a journalist.
p2.ex1: The journalist interviewed the CEO about remote working.
p2.ex2: He trained as a journalist and now works for a national newspaper.

p2.en: The process of controlling or organising a business or team.
p2.example: She studied business management at university.
p2.ex1: Good management is key to a successful company.
p2.ex2: He worked his way up to a senior management position.

p2.en: The activity of promoting and selling products or services.
p2.example: He works in marketing and manages the company's social media.
p2.ex1: She studied marketing as part of her business degree.
p2.ex2: Good marketing is essential for any new product launch.

p2.en: Something that you can choose; a possibility.
p2.example: Remote work is now an option for most office employees.
p2.ex1: She had several options after finishing her degree.
p2.ex2: Taking a gap year is a popular option for young people.

p2.en: Not required; available to choose but not compulsory.
p2.example: The second workshop is optional but highly recommended.
p2.ex1: The course includes two optional modules.
p2.ex2: Attendance at the afternoon session is optional.

p2.en: Involving fewer hours than a standard full working week.
p2.example: She works part-time while studying for her degree.
p2.ex1: He took a part-time job to support himself during university.
p2.ex2: Part-time positions are often more flexible.

p2.en: Lasting for a long time or forever; not temporary.
p2.example: After six months she was offered a permanent contract.
p2.ex1: He is looking for a permanent position in teaching.
p2.ex2: The company converted temporary staff to permanent employees.

p2.en: The state of being in a particular place at a particular time.
p2.example: Your presence at the training session is required.
p2.ex1: Her presence at the meeting was very reassuring.
p2.ex2: Online learning reduces the need for physical presence.

p2.en: Official certificates showing that you have completed a course.
p2.example: He gained valuable qualifications during his apprenticeship.
p2.ex1: You need formal qualifications to apply for this role.
p2.ex2: She spent two years gaining qualifications in project management.

p2.en: Connected to or about the same subject.
p2.example: She is looking for a job related to her university degree.
p2.ex1: The tasks were closely related to real workplace situations.
p2.ex2: He prefers reading books related to business and leadership.

p2.en: To politely or formally ask for something.
p2.example: She requested a meeting with her line manager.
p2.ex1: He requested time off to attend his sister's graduation.
p2.ex2: Students can request an extension on their deadlines.

p2.en: Involving the possibility of something bad happening.
p2.example: Leaving a stable job to start a business can be risky.
p2.ex1: It was risky to accept the offer without reading the contract.
p2.ex2: She decided it was too risky to drop out before finding work.

p2.en: Money given to a student to pay for their studies, based on merit.
p2.example: He won a scholarship to study at a top university abroad.
p2.ex1: She applied for a scholarship to cover her tuition fees.
p2.ex2: Winning a scholarship made it possible for him to go to university.

p2.en: Developing or happening gradually and regularly without sudden changes.
p2.example: She made steady progress throughout the academic year.
p2.ex1: A steady income helps with financial planning.
p2.ex2: He looked for steady work after graduation.

p2.en: A specific method or way of doing something requiring skill.
p2.example: The trainer taught us a useful technique for managing stress.
p2.ex1: She uses a technique called mind mapping to organise her notes.
p2.ex2: Learning good study techniques can improve your results significantly.

p2.en: Lasting for only a short time; not permanent.
p2.example: He took a temporary job while looking for something permanent.
p2.ex1: The contract was temporary, lasting only three months.
p2.ex2: She worked as a temporary assistant during the summer.

p2.en: Not receiving or involving payment for work done.
p2.example: Many internships are unpaid, which makes them difficult to afford.
p2.ex1: She did six months of unpaid work experience at a law firm.
p2.ex2: Unpaid overtime is common in some industries.

p2.en: Not able to be predicted or foreseen; likely to change unexpectedly.
p2.example: Freelance income can be unpredictable.
p2.ex1: The job market has become increasingly unpredictable.
p2.ex2: Her boss was unpredictable, which made the job stressful.

p2.en: To experience stress or urgency because of demands placed on you.
p2.example: Employees often feel under pressure to meet tight deadlines.
p2.ex1: She was under pressure to finish the report by Monday.
p2.ex2: He performs well even when he is under pressure.

p2.en: Without planning; as a result of luck or accident.
p2.example: She found her dream job by chance at a careers fair.
p2.ex1: By chance, he met his future business partner on a train.
p2.ex2: I came across the job listing by chance while browsing online.

p2.en: To make money in order to pay for the things you need.
p2.example: She earns her living as a freelance graphic designer.
p2.ex1: He earns his living by teaching English online.
p2.ex2: It is difficult to earn a living with an unpaid internship.

p2.en: To feel doubt or uncertainty about a decision you have already made.
p2.example: She had second thoughts about leaving her job.
p2.ex1: He had second thoughts about accepting the offer.
p2.ex2: Are you having second thoughts about the course?

p3.en: A choice or option that is different from what you are currently doing.
p3.example: Online learning is a good alternative to attending classes in person.
p3.ex1: Is there an alternative route to the city centre?
p3.ex2: She looked for alternatives to the expensive textbook.

p3.en: Former students of a school, college, or university.
p3.example: The alumni of the university meet every year for a reunion.
p3.ex1: He joined the alumni network to make professional connections.
p3.ex2: Many alumni donate money to support current students.

p3.en: As soon as possible — used to show something is urgent.
p3.example: Please reply to the email ASAP as the deadline is tomorrow.
p3.ex1: The manager asked for the report ASAP.
p3.ex2: Contact us ASAP if you have any questions.

p3.en: Help or support given to someone.
p3.example: Students can request financial assistance from the university.
p3.ex1: She offered her assistance with the research project.
p3.ex2: If you need assistance, please contact the student support team.

p3.en: The act of being present at a place, such as school or a meeting.
p3.example: Regular attendance is required to pass the course.
p3.ex1: Her attendance record was perfect throughout the year.
p3.ex2: Low attendance led to the cancellation of the afternoon session.

p3.en: A person who is a member of a particular country or community.
p3.example: Every citizen has the right to access public education.
p3.ex1: She became a citizen of the UK after living there for ten years.
p3.ex2: As a digital citizen, you should protect your online data.

p3.en: Long-term shifts in global temperatures and weather patterns.
p3.example: Climate change is one of the biggest challenges of our century.
p3.ex1: Many universities now offer courses on climate change.
p3.ex2: Students organised a campaign to raise awareness of climate change.

p3.en: A document listing your education, experience, and skills, used for job applications.
p3.example: She updated her CV before applying for the internship.
p3.ex1: Include your work experience and qualifications on your CV.
p3.ex2: A well-written CV increases your chances of getting an interview.

p3.en: A person who checks and corrects written content before publication.
p3.example: She works as an editor for an educational publishing company.
p3.ex1: The editor reviewed the report and suggested several changes.
p3.ex2: He became the editor of the university newspaper in his second year.

p3.en: Producing the intended result; working well.
p3.example: Online tools can help students communicate more effectively.
p3.ex1: She managed her time effectively and finished ahead of schedule.
p3.ex2: An effective study plan includes regular breaks.

p3.en: A sudden, serious situation that requires immediate action.
p3.example: In an emergency, students should contact the university helpline.
p3.ex1: The school had an emergency drill in case of a fire.
p3.ex2: She left the meeting early due to a family emergency.

p3.en: Feeling or showing thanks for something someone has done.
p3.example: She was grateful to her tutor for the extra help.
p3.ex1: He was grateful for the scholarship that funded his studies.
p3.ex2: We are grateful for your patience and understanding.

p3.en: A situation that causes difficulty or trouble.
p3.example: We apologise for the inconvenience caused by the system update.
p3.ex1: The delay caused a great deal of inconvenience for students.
p3.ex2: She accepted the inconvenience of commuting to attend in-person classes.

p3.en: Allowing active participation; responding to the user's actions.
p3.example: The course uses interactive videos and quizzes to engage students.
p3.ex1: Interactive lessons are more engaging than traditional lectures.
p3.ex2: The software includes interactive exercises for self-study.

p3.en: To continue for a period of time.
p3.example: The online session lasted for two hours.
p3.ex1: How long does the course last?
p3.ex2: The workshop lasted longer than expected.

p3.en: In or to a foreign country, especially one across the sea.
p3.example: She studied overseas for a year as part of her degree programme.
p3.ex1: He found a job overseas after graduating.
p3.ex2: Many companies now hire overseas workers through online platforms.

p3.en: Concerning or about something — used in formal writing.
p3.example: I am writing regarding my application for the summer programme.
p3.ex1: Please contact us regarding any changes to your booking.
p3.ex2: She sent an email regarding the upcoming schedule change.

p3.en: A polite or formal act of asking for something.
p3.example: We received your request and will respond within 24 hours.
p3.ex1: His request for extra time on the exam was approved.
p3.ex2: She submitted a formal request to change her course.

p3.en: A person who lives in a particular place.
p3.example: All residents of the student dormitory must follow the house rules.
p3.ex1: She became a permanent resident after working in the country for five years.
p3.ex2: Residents can access the gym facilities free of charge.

p3.en: A reaction or reply to something.
p3.example: We have not yet received a response to our email.
p3.ex1: Her response to the question was clear and well-structured.
p3.ex2: The university sent a prompt response to his application.

p3.en: A gathering of people who have not seen each other for some time.
p3.example: The university holds an annual alumni reunion every October.
p3.ex1: She attended her school reunion after twenty years.
p3.ex2: The reunion brought together graduates from five different years.

p3.en: A period of time set aside for a particular activity.
p3.example: The online session will begin at 10 AM and last ninety minutes.
p3.ex1: She attended every training session without missing one.
p3.ex2: The study session was very productive.

p3.en: Programs and other operating information used by a computer.
p3.example: The course requires students to download specific software.
p3.ex1: She learned to use new software as part of her training.
p3.ex2: The company developed its own software for project management.

p3.en: Clearly defined or identified; particular.
p3.example: Please follow the specific instructions on the application form.
p3.ex1: The job advert listed specific qualifications required.
p3.ex2: Can you give me a specific example of your experience?

p3.en: Something used to help you do a task or achieve a goal.
p3.example: Online platforms are a powerful tool for language learning.
p3.ex1: She uses productivity tools to manage her workload.
p3.ex2: The course introduces digital tools for collaboration.

p3.en: Informal word for university.
p3.example: He is in his second year at uni studying economics.
p3.ex1: She met her best friend at uni.
p3.ex2: What are you planning to do after uni?

p3.en: To be happening soon; approaching in time.
p3.example: The deadline for the scholarship is coming up fast.
p3.ex1: An important exam is coming up next week.
p3.ex2: There is a careers fair coming up at the university.

p3.en: To keep someone interested and focused.
p3.example: A good lecturer can hold the attention of a large audience.
p3.ex1: The interactive presentation held everyone's attention.
p3.ex2: She struggled to hold the students' attention during the long session.

p3.en: As a reaction or reply to something.
p3.example: In response to student feedback, the course was redesigned.
p3.ex1: She wrote the email in response to his request.
p3.ex2: In response to the emergency, the university cancelled all classes.

p3.en: A polite and formal way of saying you are happy to do something.
p3.example: It would be my pleasure to help you with your application.
p3.ex1: It would be my pleasure to present at the conference.
p3.ex2: Can you assist with the tour? It would be my pleasure.

p3.en: An informal way of admitting that you made a mistake.
p3.example: Oh, I sent the email to the wrong person. My bad!
p3.ex1: I forgot to attach the file. My bad!
p3.ex2: My bad! I thought the meeting was tomorrow.

p3.en: To think about a particular fact or detail before making a decision.
p3.example: Please take the deadline into consideration when planning your work.
p3.ex1: We took all factors into consideration before choosing a candidate.
p3.ex2: Her experience was taken into consideration during the interview.

p3.word: take sth to the next level
p3.en: To improve something or make it more advanced or successful.
p3.example: This advanced course will take your English to the next level.
p3.ex1: She wanted to take her career to the next level.
p3.ex2: The new software will take our productivity to the next level.

p1.en: Ready to do dangerous or difficult things without being afraid.
p1.example: You have to be brave to jump out of a plane for the first time.
p1.ex1: She was brave enough to try bungee jumping alone.
p1.ex2: It takes a brave person to face their fears head-on.

p1.en: A light, gentle wind.
p1.example: A cool breeze made the hot day feel more pleasant.
p1.ex1: They felt a gentle breeze as they floated above the fields.
p1.ex2: The breeze from the mountains kept us cool during the hike.

p1.en: To stop being visible; to go out of sight.
p1.example: The clouds disappeared and the sun came out just in time.
p1.ex1: His fear disappeared once the balloon left the ground.
p1.ex2: The landscape disappeared beneath them as they rose higher.

p1.en: Very enthusiastic and keen to do something.
p1.example: She was eager to try the hot air balloon experience.
p1.ex1: The children were eager to start the adventure course.
p1.ex2: He was eager to overcome his fear of heights.

p1.en: A strong feeling of excitement and interest in something.
p1.example: Her enthusiasm for outdoor adventures is contagious.
p1.ex1: He approached the challenge with great enthusiasm.
p1.ex2: Their enthusiasm made the whole team feel motivated.

p1.en: Extremely interesting or attractive.
p1.example: The view from the top was absolutely fascinating.
p1.ex1: She found the history of the region fascinating.
p1.ex2: It was fascinating to watch the landscape change from above.

p1.en: An unpleasant feeling caused by the belief that something dangerous might happen.
p1.example: He had a fear of heights, but decided to face it.
p1.ex1: Her biggest fear was falling, so she wore extra safety gear.
p1.ex2: Overcoming fear is often the first step to real adventure.

p1.en: To move slowly and gently through air or water without sinking.
p1.example: The balloon began to float silently above the hills.
p1.ex1: It felt magical to float over the countryside in a balloon.
p1.ex2: Leaves floated gently down from the trees in the breeze.

p1.en: Feeling fear; scared by something.
p1.example: She was frightened at first but soon began to enjoy the ride.
p1.ex1: He looked frightened as the balloon began to rise.
p1.ex2: The frightened passengers held each other's hands tightly.

p1.en: Mild, soft, and not rough or violent.
p1.example: The landing was gentle and smooth, much to everyone's relief.
p1.ex1: A gentle push was all it took to send the raft downstream.
p1.ex2: The instructor spoke in a gentle voice to calm the nervous group.

p1.en: To take hold of something suddenly and firmly.
p1.example: He grabbed the rope tightly as the wind picked up speed.
p1.ex1: She grabbed her camera to capture the breathtaking view.
p1.ex2: Grab the harness before you step out of the plane.

p1.en: The quality of being hot; a high temperature.
p1.example: The heat from the burner filled the balloon with warm air.
p1.ex1: The intense heat of the desert made the hike very challenging.
p1.ex2: They could feel the heat rising from the engine as they flew.

p1.en: Feeling admiration because something is better than expected.
p1.example: She was impressed by how calm her instructor remained throughout.
p1.ex1: Everyone was impressed by the spectacular views from above.
p1.ex2: He was impressed by how quickly he adapted to the new environment.

p1.en: In a situation where harm or risk is possible.
p1.example: The pilot assured us that we were never in danger.
p1.ex1: She felt in danger for a moment when the wind shifted suddenly.
p1.ex2: Stay close to the guide so you are never in danger.

p1.en: To present someone or something for the first time.
p1.example: The instructor introduced the safety procedures before take-off.
p1.ex1: She was introduced to rock climbing on a school trip.
p1.ex2: He introduced his family to the sport of paragliding.

p1.en: All the visible features of an area of land.
p1.example: The landscape below looked like a patchwork of fields and forests.
p1.ex1: She painted the dramatic mountain landscape from memory.
p1.ex2: Flying over the desert landscape was an unforgettable experience.

p1.en: At the same time as something else is happening.
p1.example: She took photos; meanwhile, her friend focused on staying calm.
p1.ex1: The balloon rose slowly; meanwhile, the crowd below cheered.
p1.ex2: Meanwhile, the weather was getting worse on the other side of the valley.

p1.en: A combination of different things.
p1.example: She felt a mixture of excitement and nervousness before the jump.
p1.ex1: The experience was a mixture of fear and pure joy.
p1.ex2: The landscape was a mixture of forests, rivers, and open fields.

p1.en: At one time in the past; also used to mean 'as soon as'.
p1.example: Once the balloon left the ground, all fear disappeared.
p1.ex1: Once you try skydiving, you will never forget it.
p1.ex2: She had once been afraid of flying but now loved it.

p1.en: To succeed in dealing with a problem or difficulty.
p1.example: She was determined to overcome her fear of heights.
p1.ex1: He overcame his nerves and completed the bungee jump.
p1.ex2: With practice, you can overcome almost any fear.

p1.en: To move upward; to go to a higher position.
p1.example: The hot air balloon began to rise slowly above the treetops.
p1.ex1: As the balloon rose, the sounds of the town faded away.
p1.ex2: The temperature rises quickly in the desert after sunrise.

p1.en: A thick, strong cord made of twisted fibres, used for climbing or tying.
p1.example: He held tightly to the rope as he descended the cliff face.
p1.ex1: The instructor checked every rope before the climb began.
p1.ex2: She used a rope to abseil down the steep rock face.

p1.en: The condition of being protected from danger or harm.
p1.example: Safety is the top priority on every adventure activity.
p1.ex1: All participants must wear safety equipment at all times.
p1.ex2: The guide explained the safety rules before the kayaking trip.

p1.en: In a way that is even and without difficulty or bumps.
p1.example: The balloon landed smoothly in the field below.
p1.ex1: Everything went smoothly despite the strong wind.
p1.ex2: The ride began smoothly, and the group quickly relaxed.

p1.en: Visually impressive and dramatic.
p1.example: The view from the summit was absolutely spectacular.
p1.ex1: They watched a spectacular sunset over the mountains.
p1.ex2: The fireworks display was truly spectacular.

p1.en: Extremely frightened.
p1.example: He was terrified during the first few seconds of freefall.
p1.ex1: She was terrified of the dark cave but went in anyway.
p1.ex2: The terrified passengers gripped their seats as the plane shook.

p1.en: Used to express relief that something good happened or something bad did not.
p1.example: Thankfully, the weather cleared up just before take-off.
p1.ex1: Thankfully, no one was injured during the unexpected landing.
p1.ex2: Thankfully, she remembered to bring her safety gear.

p1.en: Not expected or planned; surprising.
p1.example: An unexpected gust of wind made the landing more difficult.
p1.ex1: The trip included some unexpected moments of beauty.
p1.ex2: He handled the unexpected situation calmly and professionally.

p1.en: Not enjoyable or comfortable; causing a negative feeling.
p1.example: The turbulence was unpleasant, but it passed quickly.
p1.ex1: The smell near the lake was quite unpleasant in the heat.
p1.ex2: She found the experience unpleasant and decided not to repeat it.

p1.en: To be involved in or part of something (informal).
p1.example: Are you in for the skydiving trip next weekend?
p1.ex1: Count me in — I have always wanted to try rock climbing.
p1.ex2: She said she was in as soon as she heard about the adventure tour.

p1.en: To be extremely good or impressive; beyond normal experience.
p1.example: The view from the top of the mountain was out of this world.
p1.ex1: The food at the mountain lodge was out of this world.
p1.ex2: Her performance at the competition was out of this world.

p1.en: To become lively, active, or interesting.
p1.example: The city came to life as the sun set and the lights turned on.
p1.ex1: The old story came to life in the hands of a brilliant storyteller.
p1.ex2: The landscape came to life after the spring rains.

p1.en: To make a determined effort to achieve something; to do it boldly.
p1.example: She was nervous about jumping, but her friend said: go for it!
p1.ex1: If you have a dream, just go for it.
p1.ex2: He decided to go for it and signed up for the solo expedition.

p1.en: To feel a sudden strong emotion, usually excitement or fear.
p1.example: My heart skipped a beat when the balloon suddenly lurched sideways.
p1.ex1: Her heart skipped a beat as she stood at the edge of the cliff.
p1.ex2: His heart skipped a beat when he saw the incredible view.

p1.en: To stop breathing temporarily, often from tension or excitement.
p1.example: Everyone held their breath as the balloon rose above the clouds.
p1.ex1: She held her breath and jumped into the cold water.
p1.ex2: We held our breath waiting for the final results.

p1.en: To try hard to do something, even if it is difficult.
p1.example: Make an effort to enjoy the experience even if you feel nervous.
p1.ex1: He made a real effort to overcome his fear of water.
p1.ex2: She always makes an effort to push herself beyond her comfort zone.

p1.en: To breathe in deeply, often to calm yourself before something difficult.
p1.example: Take a deep breath before you step off the platform.
p1.ex1: She took a deep breath and walked to the edge.
p1.ex2: He told himself to take a deep breath and trust the equipment.

p2.en: In addition to; also used to add a new point.
p2.example: Besides swimming, she also enjoys running and cycling.
p2.ex1: Besides being good exercise, sport is also great for mental health.
p2.ex2: He did not want to go; besides, the weather was terrible.

p2.en: A place where people go to play bowling.
p2.example: We spent a fun evening at the bowling alley with friends.
p2.ex1: The bowling alley was packed on Friday night.
p2.ex2: She had never been to a bowling alley before.

p2.en: To take air into and send it out of the lungs.
p2.example: It is hard to breathe properly at high altitudes.
p2.ex1: Remember to breathe steadily when you are climbing.
p2.ex2: She stopped to breathe in the fresh mountain air.

p2.en: A state of physical or emotional exhaustion from too much stress.
p2.example: Many athletes suffer from burnout if they train too hard without rest.
p2.ex1: She took a break from competing to avoid burnout.
p2.ex2: Burnout is a serious risk for people who never take time off.

p2.en: Having a strong desire to win; involving competition.
p2.example: He is very competitive and always wants to finish first.
p2.ex1: The tournament was highly competitive this year.
p2.ex2: She thrives in competitive environments.

p2.en: A book in which you write personal events, thoughts, or experiences.
p2.example: She keeps a training diary to track her progress.
p2.ex1: His diary is full of notes from every race he has run.
p2.ex2: Writing in a diary after workouts helps her reflect on her goals.

p2.en: The way in which two things are not the same.
p2.example: What is the difference between a marathon and a half-marathon?
p2.ex1: Regular training makes a real difference to your performance.
p2.ex2: She noticed a big difference in her fitness after a month of exercise.

p2.en: A change or result produced by something.
p2.example: Exercise has a positive effect on both the body and the mind.
p2.ex1: The effects of overtraining can include injury and exhaustion.
p2.ex2: She felt the effects of the long race for several days afterward.

p2.en: Following established rules or conventions; official.
p2.example: The club has formal training sessions three times a week.
p2.ex1: You do not need formal qualifications to join the running club.
p2.ex2: He received formal coaching for the first time at age sixteen.

p2.en: Not doing much physical activity; not moving much.
p2.example: A sedentary lifestyle and being inactive can harm your health.
p2.ex1: Children who are inactive are more likely to be unfit.
p2.ex2: She became inactive during the winter months and lost fitness.

p2.en: Relating to one person rather than a group.
p2.example: Tennis can be played as an individual or a team sport.
p2.ex1: He preferred individual sports because he liked working alone.
p2.ex2: The coach gave each player individual feedback after the match.

p2.en: A long-distance running race of 42.195 kilometres.
p2.example: She trained for six months before running her first marathon.
p2.ex1: Completing a marathon is a huge personal achievement.
p2.ex2: The city marathon attracts thousands of runners every year.

p2.en: A way in which two things are alike or the same.
p2.example: There is a strong similarity between yoga and Pilates.
p2.ex1: She noticed many similarities between the two sports.
p2.ex2: The main similarity between running and cycling is that both improve endurance.

p2.en: A place where something is located or takes place.
p2.example: The sports centre is being built on the old factory site.
p2.ex1: The marathon route passes through several historic sites.
p2.ex2: She visited the site of the original Olympic Games in Greece.

p2.en: To slide accidentally and lose your balance.
p2.example: Be careful not to slip on the wet track after the rain.
p2.ex1: He slipped on the ice and injured his knee.
p2.ex2: She slipped during the warm-up and had to sit out the match.

p2.en: To spend time with other people in a friendly way.
p2.example: Team sports are a great way to socialise and make new friends.
p2.ex1: She joined the running club mainly to socialise.
p2.ex2: After the race, everyone socialised at the finish line celebration.

p2.en: A test or trial to see if someone is good enough for a team.
p2.example: She attended a tryout for the national athletics team.
p2.ex1: He was nervous before the football tryout but performed well.
p2.ex2: The tryout was tough, but she made the final squad.

p2.en: Gentle exercise done to prepare the body before more intense activity.
p2.example: Always do a proper warm-up before starting intense exercise.
p2.ex1: The coach led the team through a ten-minute warm-up.
p2.ex2: Skipping the warm-up increases the risk of injury.

p2.en: The state of the weather at a particular time and place.
p2.example: The race was cancelled due to dangerous weather conditions.
p2.ex1: Athletes need to adapt to different weather conditions.
p2.ex2: Poor weather conditions made the outdoor training session difficult.

p2.en: A period of physical exercise or training.
p2.example: She does a one-hour workout every morning before work.
p2.ex1: His workout routine includes running, cycling, and stretching.
p2.ex2: A good workout leaves you tired but energised.

p2.en: To improve or refresh a skill or area of knowledge you already have.
p2.example: He needed to brush up on his swimming technique before the race.
p2.ex1: She brushed up on her tennis skills before the tournament.
p2.ex2: Brush up on the rules before joining the competition.

p2.en: To move or progress at the same speed as someone or something.
p2.example: It was hard to keep up with the faster runners at first.
p2.ex1: She trained hard to keep up with her teammates.
p2.ex2: He struggled to keep up with the pace in his first marathon.

p2.en: To learn a skill gradually without formal instruction; also to increase speed.
p2.example: She picked up volleyball very quickly and is now on the school team.
p2.ex1: He picked up tennis at the age of six and never stopped playing.
p2.ex2: The pace picked up in the final kilometre of the race.

p3.en: In the direction you are facing; towards the front.
p3.example: Lean forwards slightly to pick up speed on the slope.
p3.ex1: She pushed forwards even when her legs were aching.
p3.ex2: The zorb rolled forwards and gathered pace quickly.

p3.en: Extremely cold; at or below the temperature at which water becomes ice.
p3.example: It was freezing at the top of the mountain, but the view was worth it.
p3.ex1: Her fingers were freezing after an hour on the ski slope.
p3.ex2: The lake was freezing — too cold for swimming.

p3.en: Extremely angry.
p3.example: She was furious when she fell just metres from the finish line.
p3.ex1: He was furious about the unfair call during the match.
p3.ex2: The coach was furious after the team missed three easy chances.

p3.en: To move smoothly and effortlessly through air or over a surface.
p3.example: She glided down the slope with perfect technique.
p3.ex1: The skier glided across the snow without making a sound.
p3.ex2: The zorb glided over the wet grass at impressive speed.

p3.en: Extremely funny; causing a lot of laughter.
p3.example: The video of him tumbling out of the zorb was absolutely hilarious.
p3.ex1: She found the whole situation hilarious, even though she had fallen.
p3.ex2: His commentary during the run was hilarious.

p3.en: Having physical damage to the body as a result of an accident.
p3.example: Two participants were injured when the zorb hit the barrier.
p3.ex1: She was injured during training and missed the competition.
p3.ex2: The rescue team arrived quickly to help the injured skier.

p3.en: To move your body or rest against something at an angle.
p3.example: Lean back slightly to slow down on the steepest section.
p3.ex1: She leaned forward to gain speed on the downhill stretch.
p3.ex2: He leaned against the fence to catch his breath.

p3.en: Very unhappy or uncomfortable.
p3.example: She felt miserable after falling in front of the whole crowd.
p3.ex1: The wet, cold weather made the hike absolutely miserable.
p3.ex2: He had a miserable time because he was too tired to enjoy anything.

p3.en: Short for professional; an expert or highly skilled person.
p3.example: She skis like a pro after years of training in the Alps.
p3.ex1: Even the pros find that slope challenging.
p3.ex2: He trained with a pro before his first competition.

p3.en: A group of people trained to help those in danger or difficulty.
p3.example: The rescue team arrived within minutes after the skier fell.
p3.ex1: She was grateful for the rescue team who found her on the mountain.
p3.ex2: The rescue team used a helicopter to reach the injured climber.

p3.en: A surface that is higher at one end than the other; a hillside.
p3.example: The beginners were advised to stick to the gentler slopes.
p3.ex1: She flew down the steep slope at terrifying speed.
p3.ex2: The slope was covered in fresh snow after the storm.

p3.en: To move or happen faster.
p3.example: The zorb began to speed up as the slope got steeper.
p3.ex1: She sped up in the final stretch and overtook her rival.
p3.ex2: The process sped up once the whole team was working together.

p3.en: Extremely hungry.
p3.example: After a full day on the slopes, everyone was absolutely starving.
p3.ex1: She was starving by the time they reached the mountain lodge.
p3.ex2: He had not eaten since morning and was starving.

p3.en: Rising or falling sharply; at a great angle.
p3.example: The steep slope made the descent exciting but dangerous.
p3.ex1: She was nervous about tackling the steep section of the run.
p3.ex2: The path became increasingly steep as they climbed higher.

p3.en: To continue doing or using something without changing.
p3.example: Stick to the marked route and do not go off-piste.
p3.ex1: He decided to stick to the beginner slope for his first visit.
p3.ex2: She stuck to her training plan even when it was difficult.

p3.en: Feeling very excited and pleased.
p3.example: She was absolutely thrilled when she made it to the bottom without falling.
p3.ex1: He was thrilled to be chosen for the national team.
p3.ex2: The crowd was thrilled by the skier's incredible performance.

p3.en: To tell someone about a possible danger or problem in advance.
p3.example: The instructor warned the group about the icy patch near the bottom.
p3.ex1: She warned him not to go too fast on his first run.
p3.ex2: The sign warned skiers about the steep drop ahead.

p3.en: To speak very quietly so only someone nearby can hear.
p3.example: She whispered to her friend that she was terrified of the slope.
p3.ex1: He whispered instructions to the nervous beginner.
p3.ex2: She could hear the wind whisper through the trees as she glided past.

p3.en: To be so surprised or moved that you cannot speak.
p3.example: She was speechless when she saw the view from the top of the mountain.
p3.ex1: He was speechless after crossing the finish line in record time.
p3.ex2: The crowd was speechless after the incredible final run.

p3.en: Soon; after a short period of time.
p3.example: Before long, she was gliding down the slope with confidence.
p3.ex1: Before long, the whole group was laughing and enjoying themselves.
p3.ex2: He struggled at first, but before long he found his balance.

p3.en: To feel very relieved after a stressful or difficult situation.
p3.example: She breathed a sigh of relief when the zorb finally stopped rolling.
p3.ex1: He breathed a sigh of relief when the rescue team arrived.
p3.ex2: Everyone breathed a sigh of relief when the storm passed.

p3.en: To stop moving completely.
p3.example: The zorb slowly came to a stop at the bottom of the hill.
p3.ex1: The ski lift came to a stop due to a technical fault.
p3.ex2: She came to a stop just before the barrier.

p3.en: To feel nervous or afraid before doing something and want to pull out.
p3.example: She got cold feet standing at the top of the ski slope.
p3.ex1: He got cold feet before his first bungee jump.
p3.ex2: Do not get cold feet now — you have trained for this!

p3.en: To feel very nervous or excited before doing something.
p3.example: She had butterflies in her stomach before the first run.
p3.ex1: He always has butterflies in his stomach before a big race.
p3.ex2: I had butterflies in my stomach waiting for the results.

p3.ru: я не мог поверить своим глазам / ушам
p3.en: Used to express extreme surprise at something you saw or heard.
p3.example: I couldn't believe my eyes when she skied down the black run on her first day.
p3.ex1: He couldn't believe his ears when they announced his name as the winner.
p3.ex2: I couldn't believe my eyes — she completed the jump perfectly.

p3.en: To do what you said you would do.
p3.example: He kept his promise and took his daughter zorbing on her birthday.
p3.ex1: She always keeps a promise, no matter how difficult.
p3.ex2: He kept his promise to reach the summit before sunset.

p3.en: To fail to keep your body steady and fall or nearly fall.
p3.example: She lost her balance on the icy section and slid to the side.
p3.ex1: He lost his balance trying to stop too quickly.
p3.ex2: The strong wind caused him to lose his balance on the slope.

p3.en: To cause a sudden fright; to startle someone.
p3.example: The sudden noise from the crowd made me jump.
p3.ex1: The zorb hitting the barrier made everyone in the group jump.
p3.ex2: A loud crack in the ice made her jump with fright.

p1.en: To plan or intend to achieve a particular thing.
p1.example: She aims to run a marathon before the end of the year.
p1.ex1: The programme aims to help people break unhealthy habits.
p1.ex2: He aims to improve his diet and exercise more regularly.

p1.en: A way of thinking about or dealing with something.
p1.example: A gradual approach is more effective than trying to change everything at once.
p1.ex1: Her approach to habit-building was based on small daily steps.
p1.ex2: The research suggests a different approach to motivation.

p1.en: Typical or ordinary; also the result of adding numbers and dividing by how many there are.
p1.example: On average, it takes about 66 days to form a new habit.
p1.ex1: The average person checks their phone over 100 times a day.
p1.ex2: Her daily step count is above the recommended average.

p1.en: The reason something happens.
p1.example: A lack of motivation is often the main cause of giving up too soon.
p1.ex1: Stress is a common cause of unhealthy eating habits.
p1.ex2: Understanding the cause of a habit helps you break it more easily.

p1.en: Extremely important; also meaning likely to find faults.
p1.example: The first week is critical — most people give up during this period.
p1.ex1: Consistency is critical when trying to build new habits.
p1.ex2: He gave a critical review of the habit-forming techniques.

p1.en: A series of events that repeat in the same order.
p1.example: The habit cycle consists of a cue, a routine, and a reward.
p1.ex1: Breaking the cycle of bad habits requires effort and awareness.
p1.ex2: She understood the cycle of behaviour that was holding her back.

p1.en: Done without difficulty or effort; seeming natural and easy.
p1.example: After months of practice, the routine felt completely effortless.
p1.ex1: She made the complex exercise look effortless.
p1.ex2: Good habits eventually become effortless parts of your day.

p1.en: To give something and receive something similar in return.
p1.example: He exchanged his unhealthy morning routine for a healthy one.
p1.ex1: She exchanged bad habits for productive ones over six months.
p1.ex2: Try exchanging one negative behaviour for a positive alternative.

p1.en: To be afraid of something or someone.
p1.example: Many people fear failure, which stops them from even trying.
p1.ex1: She feared that changing her habits would be too difficult.
p1.ex2: He feared the discomfort of early morning workouts.

p1.en: Happening or done without delay; at once.
p1.example: Habits with an immediate reward are easier to maintain.
p1.ex1: She needed immediate results to stay motivated.
p1.ex2: The immediate effect of exercise is a boost in energy.

p1.en: The process of becoming better; a change that makes something better.
p1.example: She noticed a significant improvement in her mood after cutting out sugar.
p1.ex1: Consistent effort leads to gradual improvement over time.
p1.ex2: His improvement in fitness was remarkable after three months.

p1.en: A hard-shelled fruit or seed, such as a walnut or almond, often eaten as a healthy snack.
p1.example: Replacing crisps with nuts is a simple habit that improves nutrition.
p1.ex1: She keeps a bag of mixed nuts at her desk as a healthy snack.
p1.ex2: Nuts are a great source of protein and healthy fats.

p1.en: To happen, especially without being planned.
p1.example: Most habit relapses occur when people are under stress.
p1.ex1: The change occurred gradually over several weeks.
p1.ex2: He noticed that cravings occurred most often in the evenings.

p1.en: Gradually, across a period of time.
p1.example: Over time, small daily habits lead to significant results.
p1.ex1: Over time, her new routine became completely natural.
p1.ex2: The benefits of exercise build up over time.

p1.en: Evidence that shows something is true.
p1.example: Her transformation is proof that small changes can have a big impact.
p1.ex1: The study provided scientific proof that habits are learned behaviour.
p1.ex2: He wanted proof that the method worked before he tried it.

p1.en: To stop doing something permanently.
p1.example: She decided to quit social media for a month to improve her focus.
p1.ex1: He quit smoking after reading about the long-term health risks.
p1.ex2: Many people try to quit bad habits but struggle without support.

p1.en: A person who carries out detailed study into a subject.
p1.example: Researchers have found that it takes on average 66 days to form a habit.
p1.ex1: The researcher published her findings on habit formation.
p1.ex2: A team of researchers studied the link between sleep and productivity.

p1.en: To give something good to someone in recognition of their effort.
p1.example: Rewarding yourself after completing a task helps reinforce the habit.
p1.ex1: She rewarded herself with a day off after a week of healthy eating.
p1.ex2: The brain rewards positive behaviours by releasing dopamine.

p1.en: A path or course taken to reach a destination.
p1.example: Finding the right route to building a habit takes patience.
p1.ex1: She planned a new running route through the park.
p1.ex2: The quickest route to success is consistency.

p1.en: One action in a series of actions needed to achieve something.
p1.example: The first step in breaking a habit is recognising the trigger.
p1.ex1: Take it one step at a time rather than trying to change everything.
p1.ex2: Each small step brings you closer to your goal.

p1.en: To make something stronger or more powerful.
p1.example: Repeating a behaviour daily strengthens the neural pathway in your brain.
p1.ex1: Exercise strengthens not just the body but also willpower.
p1.ex2: She worked to strengthen her morning routine over several weeks.

p1.en: Not having the ability, skill, or opportunity to do something.
p1.example: He felt unable to resist the urge to check his phone.
p1.ex1: She was unable to quit the habit without help.
p1.ex2: Many people feel unable to change because they do not know where to start.

p1.en: To be different or change according to the situation.
p1.example: The time it takes to form a habit varies from person to person.
p1.ex1: Results vary depending on how consistently you follow the routine.
p1.ex2: She varied her workout to avoid boredom.

p1.en: By many people, or over a large area or range.
p1.example: Habit loops are now widely accepted in psychology.
p1.ex1: The book on habits is widely read by coaches and managers.
p1.ex2: This technique is widely used in behaviour change programmes.

p1.en: To divide something complex into smaller, more manageable parts.
p1.example: Break the goal down into small daily actions to make it less overwhelming.
p1.ex1: She broke the habit down into three stages: cue, routine, reward.
p1.ex2: Breaking the task down made it much easier to start.

p1.en: To do or complete a task, plan, or order.
p1.example: Researchers carried out a study on how long it takes to break a habit.
p1.ex1: He carried out his daily routine without exception.
p1.ex2: She carried out all the steps in the habit-formation programme.

p1.en: To start or continue doing something, especially after a delay.
p1.example: Stop procrastinating and get on with your workout.
p1.ex1: She got on with her daily routine even when she was tired.
p1.ex2: He finally got on with writing the plan after weeks of putting it off.

p1.en: To have the opportunity or chance to do something.
p1.example: She got to try a new yoga class after changing her schedule.
p1.ex1: He got to present his research at the conference.
p1.ex2: I finally got to finish the book I had been meaning to read.

p1.en: To delay doing something until a later time.
p1.example: She kept putting off her morning run and eventually stopped altogether.
p1.ex1: He put off going to the gym for weeks before finally going.
p1.ex2: Stop putting it off — start the habit today, not tomorrow.

p1.en: To be prepared or happy to do something.
p1.example: You need to be willing to make small sacrifices to build good habits.
p1.ex1: She was willing to wake up earlier to fit in her morning run.
p1.ex2: He was not willing to give up his evening snacking habit.

p1.en: To stop doing something you have been doing regularly for a long time.
p1.example: Breaking a habit is much harder than forming one.
p1.ex1: She finally broke the habit of scrolling through her phone before bed.
p1.ex2: It took him six months to break the habit of eating late at night.

p1.en: Used to introduce an example.
p1.example: Many small habits add up. For instance, walking ten minutes a day improves health.
p1.ex1: For instance, replacing sugary drinks with water is a simple first step.
p1.ex2: There are many ways to build habits. For instance, habit stacking is very effective.

p1.en: To remove or eliminate something unwanted.
p1.example: She wanted to get rid of her habit of checking emails first thing in the morning.
p1.ex1: The goal of the programme is to help people get rid of unhealthy patterns.
p1.ex2: He got rid of junk food from his kitchen to avoid temptation.

p1.en: Each one separately and in order.
p1.example: She tackled her bad habits one by one rather than all at once.
p1.ex1: He replaced unhealthy foods one by one from his diet.
p1.ex2: They worked through the list of goals one by one.

p1.en: Used to add a further point that is even stronger or more surprising.
p1.example: Exercise improves fitness. What is more, it also boosts mental health.
p1.ex1: Habits save time. What is more, they reduce decision fatigue.
p1.ex2: The method is simple. What is more, it has been scientifically proven.

p2.en: A diet that contains the right amounts of all the necessary nutrients.
p2.example: A balanced diet is essential for maintaining energy and good health.
p2.ex1: She switched to a balanced diet after her doctor's advice.
p2.ex2: A balanced diet includes plenty of vegetables, protein, and whole grains.

p2.en: A sum of money paid as a penalty for breaking a rule.
p2.example: He received a fine for cycling in a pedestrian zone.
p2.ex1: She was given a fine for not returning the library books on time.
p2.ex2: Breaking the speed limit can result in a heavy fine.

p2.en: Physical harm or damage to the body.
p2.example: She suffered a knee injury from running without proper warm-up.
p2.ex1: Preventing injury is more important than training hard.
p2.ex2: The injury kept him out of sport for three months.

p2.en: The ability to remember things; also a stored recollection.
p2.example: Regular sleep and exercise are known to improve memory.
p2.ex1: She has an excellent memory for names and dates.
p2.ex2: Too much screen time before bed can negatively affect memory.

p2.en: Having a strong desire and enthusiasm to do something.
p2.example: She felt highly motivated after setting a clear weekly goal.
p2.ex1: He stays motivated by tracking his daily progress.
p2.ex2: It is hard to stay motivated when results are slow to appear.

p2.en: The process of eating the right food for health and growth.
p2.example: Good nutrition is just as important as regular exercise.
p2.ex1: She studied nutrition to better understand healthy eating habits.
p2.ex2: Poor nutrition can lead to tiredness and lack of concentration.

p2.en: An expert in the science of food and its effect on health.
p2.example: She visited a nutritionist who helped her plan a healthier diet.
p2.ex1: The nutritionist recommended cutting down on processed foods.
p2.ex2: A nutritionist can help you create a personalised meal plan.

p2.en: Taking everything into account; in general.
p2.example: Her overall health improved significantly after changing her daily routine.
p2.ex1: The overall results of the study were very encouraging.
p2.ex2: Overall, she felt much better after a month of regular exercise.

p2.en: The efficiency of a person or system in producing results.
p2.example: Taking regular breaks actually increases productivity rather than reducing it.
p2.ex1: He improved his productivity by planning his day the night before.
p2.ex2: Sleep deprivation has a significant negative effect on productivity.

p2.en: A regular sequence of actions you do every day.
p2.example: Sticking to a morning routine sets a positive tone for the whole day.
p2.ex1: She established a bedtime routine that helped her sleep better.
p2.ex2: His daily routine included stretching, reading, and a healthy breakfast.

p2.en: To plan something for a particular time.
p2.example: She scheduled her workouts for the same time every day to make them a habit.
p2.ex1: He scheduled a check-up with his doctor for next Monday.
p2.ex2: Schedule your meals in advance to avoid unhealthy last-minute choices.

p2.en: The amount of time spent looking at a phone, computer, or TV screen.
p2.example: Reducing screen time before bed leads to better quality sleep.
p2.ex1: She set a limit on her daily screen time to improve focus.
p2.ex2: Too much screen time in children is linked to shorter attention spans.

p2.en: To not do something that you normally do; to miss out.
p2.example: Try not to skip breakfast — it is the most important meal of the day.
p2.ex1: She skipped her workout only once and felt guilty about it.
p2.ex2: He skipped lunch and felt exhausted by mid-afternoon.

p2.en: To maintain regular contact with someone.
p2.example: She used social media to stay in touch with her fitness group.
p2.ex1: Staying in touch with a support group helps you maintain habits.
p2.ex2: He stayed in touch with his nutritionist throughout the programme.

p2.en: To feel or cause anxiety; also the state of anxiety itself.
p2.example: Overloading your schedule can stress you out and make habits harder to maintain.
p2.ex1: She stressed out about the deadline and abandoned her healthy routine.
p2.ex2: Exercise is a proven way to reduce stress.

p2.en: The ability to use your time effectively and productively.
p2.example: Good time management allows you to fit healthy habits into a busy day.
p2.ex1: She improved her time management by using a daily planner.
p2.ex2: Time management is one of the most valuable skills you can develop.

p2.en: Requiring immediate attention or action.
p2.example: Not everything that feels urgent is actually important.
p2.ex1: He dropped his gym session because of an urgent work deadline.
p2.ex2: She learned to distinguish between tasks that were urgent and those that were important.

p2.en: A natural substance found in food that is essential for good health.
p2.example: She took a vitamin D supplement during the winter months.
p2.ex1: A balanced diet provides all the vitamins your body needs.
p2.ex2: Vitamin C is found in citrus fruits and helps boost the immune system.

p2.en: The state of being comfortable, healthy, and happy.
p2.example: Regular exercise and good nutrition are key to overall well-being.
p2.ex1: Her well-being improved significantly after cutting down on sugar.
p2.ex2: Mental well-being is just as important as physical health.

p2.en: To give yourself or someone else a difficult goal to achieve.
p2.example: She set herself a challenge to exercise every day for 30 days.
p2.ex1: The coach set the team a challenge to improve their time by ten seconds.
p2.ex2: Set yourself a challenge that pushes you beyond your comfort zone.

p2.en: To decide on a specific day for something to happen.
p2.example: Set a date to start your new healthy routine and stick to it.
p2.ex1: They set a date for the first group workout session.
p2.ex2: He set a date to quit smoking and prepared for it in advance.

p2.en: To decide on a time by which something must be completed.
p2.example: Set a deadline for your goal so you have something to work towards.
p2.ex1: She set a deadline of three months to reach her fitness target.
p2.ex2: Without a deadline, goals often remain unachieved.

p2.en: To decide the maximum amount of something allowed.
p2.example: She set a limit of one hour of screen time per day.
p2.ex1: He set a limit on how much coffee he drank each day.
p2.ex2: Setting a limit on spending helped her save more money each month.

p2.en: To achieve the best result ever in a particular activity.
p2.example: She set a personal record for her 5km run after months of training.
p2.ex1: He set a record for the most consecutive days without missing a workout.
p2.ex2: The athlete set a new world record at the championship.

p2.en: To decide on an instruction that must be followed.
p2.example: She set a rule: no phone during dinner to improve family time.
p2.ex1: He set a rule to go to bed by 10 PM every weeknight.
p2.ex2: Setting clear rules for yourself helps maintain discipline.

p2.en: To behave in a way that others can learn from and copy.
p2.example: She set an example for her team by never skipping a training session.
p2.ex1: Parents set an example for their children through their daily habits.
p2.ex2: He set a positive example by always arriving on time.

p2.en: To arrange plates, cutlery, and glasses on a table before a meal.
p2.example: Setting the table before dinner is a simple habit that improves family routines.
p2.ex1: She asked the children to set the table while she finished cooking.
p2.ex2: He set the table carefully for the dinner guests.

p2.en: To fail to do something you said you would do.
p2.example: She never breaks a promise, which is why people trust her.
p2.ex1: He broke his promise to exercise every day after the first week.
p2.ex2: Breaking a promise to yourself is just as damaging as breaking one to others.

p2.en: To do something better than it has ever been done before.
p2.example: She broke her personal record for the 10km run by two minutes.
p2.ex1: He broke the school record for the longest plank hold.
p2.ex2: The team broke a record for the most wins in a single season.

p2.en: To do something that is not allowed.
p2.example: Breaking a simple rule like skipping warm-ups can lead to injury.
p2.ex1: He broke the rule of no phones during class.
p2.ex2: She never breaks a rule, even small ones, because she values discipline.

p2.en: To do or say something to make people feel more relaxed in a new situation.
p2.example: He suggested a group activity to break the ice at the fitness class.
p2.ex1: She broke the ice by asking everyone to share one health goal.
p2.ex2: A simple joke can break the ice in an uncomfortable situation.

p2.en: To do something that is illegal.
p2.example: Cycling without a helmet in some countries means you break the law.
p2.ex1: He did not realise that dumping waste there meant breaking the law.
p2.ex2: She would never break the law, even under pressure.

p2.en: To tell someone something important, especially something unpleasant.
p2.example: She had to break the news to her coach that she could not compete.
p2.ex1: He broke the news about the cancelled race to the team.
p2.ex2: It is never easy to break bad news to someone you care about.

p2.en: To say something after a period of quiet.
p2.example: After five minutes of silence, he finally broke it by sharing his goal.
p2.ex1: She broke the silence by asking who wanted to go first.
p2.ex2: The instructor broke the silence with an encouraging word.

p2.en: To drive faster than the legally allowed maximum speed.
p2.example: He received a fine for breaking the speed limit on the motorway.
p2.ex1: Breaking the speed limit is dangerous and irresponsible.
p2.ex2: Cameras were installed to catch drivers breaking the speed limit.

p2.en: To stop thinking about worries or problems, often through relaxation.
p2.example: She went for a walk to clear her mind before making a big decision.
p2.ex1: Meditation is a great way to clear your mind.
p2.ex2: He cleared his mind by focusing on his breathing for five minutes.

p2.en: To reduce the amount of something you consume or do.
p2.example: He cut down on sugar as part of his new healthy lifestyle.
p2.ex1: She cut down on screen time and started sleeping much better.
p2.ex2: The doctor advised him to cut down on fatty foods.

p2.en: To stop eating or drinking something completely.
p2.example: She cut processed food out of her diet completely.
p2.ex1: He cut sugary drinks out of his diet and lost weight quickly.
p2.ex2: Cutting junk food out of your diet can improve your energy levels.

p2.en: To find yourself in a difficult or problematic situation.
p2.example: He got in trouble for breaking the gym rules two days in a row.
p2.ex1: She got in trouble for skipping too many scheduled sessions.
p2.ex2: Getting in trouble with your health is easy if you ignore warning signs.

p2.en: To give work or something required to the person in charge.
p2.example: She handed in her food diary to the nutritionist at the end of the week.
p2.ex1: He handed in his progress report before the deadline.
p2.ex2: Make sure you hand in the form by Friday.

p2.en: To become heavier; to gain body weight.
p2.example: She put on weight during the holidays and decided to change her habits.
p2.ex1: He put on weight after stopping his daily runs.
p2.ex2: Skipping exercise and eating poorly is a quick way to put on weight.

p1.en: To put something into practice; to use a method or idea in a situation.
p1.example: Apply the same habit-forming principles to your fitness routine.
p1.ex1: She applied the technique she had learned in class to her daily schedule.
p1.ex2: He applied the rule of consistency to every area of his health.

p1.en: A strong feeling that something is true or real.
p1.example: The belief that exercise has to be painful is a common myth.
p1.ex1: Her belief in the power of small habits helped her stay consistent.
p1.ex2: He changed his belief about fitness after reading the research.

p1.en: To increase or improve something.
p1.example: Regular exercise boosts your energy levels and mood.
p1.ex1: A good night's sleep boosts concentration and productivity.
p1.ex2: She boosted her confidence by setting small, achievable goals.

p1.en: Relying on someone or something for support or survival.
p1.example: Becoming too dependent on supplements is not a healthy habit.
p1.ex1: She was dependent on caffeine to get through her mornings.
p1.ex2: He tried not to become dependent on his phone for motivation.

p1.en: A temporary fashion or craze, especially in health and fitness.
p1.example: Crash diets are just a fitness fad — sustainable habits work better.
p1.ex1: She tried every fitness fad before finding a routine that worked.
p1.ex2: The newest fitness fad promises results in just two weeks.

p1.en: To move from being awake into a state of sleep.
p1.example: She fell asleep within minutes of following her new bedtime routine.
p1.ex1: Too much screen time makes it harder to fall asleep quickly.
p1.ex2: He fell asleep on the sofa after skipping his workout.

p1.en: A person with an extreme and enthusiastic interest in something.
p1.example: He is a fitness fanatic who trains six days a week.
p1.ex1: She is not a fanatic — she just enjoys regular exercise.
p1.ex2: Being a fanatic can lead to overtraining and burnout.

p1.en: Gained directly from personal experience, not from what others say.
p1.example: She has first-hand experience of how habits can transform health.
p1.ex1: He spoke from first-hand knowledge about the effects of poor sleep.
p1.ex2: The best advice comes from people with first-hand experience.

p1.en: Causing or likely to cause damage or negative effects.
p1.example: Overexercising can be just as harmful as doing no exercise at all.
p1.ex1: Harmful habits are often hard to break because they feel rewarding.
p1.ex2: She read about the harmful effects of skipping meals regularly.

p1.en: Having faults or weaknesses; not completely perfect.
p1.example: An imperfect routine followed consistently beats a perfect one abandoned quickly.
p1.ex1: His plan was imperfect, but he improved it week by week.
p1.ex2: She accepted that her progress would be imperfect at times.

p1.en: Lacking warmth or human connection; not relating to personal feelings.
p1.example: Generic fitness apps can feel impersonal compared to working with a trainer.
p1.ex1: The advice was too impersonal to be useful for her specific situation.
p1.ex2: He preferred face-to-face coaching to impersonal online programmes.

p1.en: Not sensible or realistic in practice.
p1.example: Waking up at 4 AM to train is impractical for most people.
p1.ex1: Her fitness plan was impractical because it required too much equipment.
p1.ex2: He realised the two-hour daily workout was impractical with his schedule.

p1.en: Not suitable or proper for a particular situation.
p1.example: High-intensity training is inappropriate for beginners without guidance.
p1.ex1: It is inappropriate to compare your progress to someone at a different level.
p1.ex2: The exercise was inappropriate for people with back problems.

p1.en: Causing difficulty or trouble; not fitting well with your plans.
p1.example: Going to the gym at rush hour is inconvenient for many people.
p1.ex1: She found the early morning sessions inconvenient at first.
p1.ex2: The location of the sports centre was inconvenient for most participants.

p1.en: Lacking the knowledge or skill that comes from doing something for a long time.
p1.example: Inexperienced runners often start too fast and burn out early.
p1.ex1: He was inexperienced in weightlifting and needed expert guidance.
p1.ex2: Inexperienced athletes benefit most from working with a coach.

p1.en: To harm or damage part of the body.
p1.example: She injured her knee by skipping the warm-up before her run.
p1.ex1: He injured his shoulder trying to lift too much weight.
p1.ex2: If you injure yourself, stop immediately and seek advice.

p1.en: Not happening at consistent or expected times.
p1.example: Irregular sleep patterns can seriously affect your health and mood.
p1.ex1: His irregular eating schedule made it hard to maintain energy levels.
p1.ex2: Irregular exercise gives fewer benefits than a consistent routine.

p1.en: Not showing care for the consequences of actions.
p1.example: It is irresponsible to advise others on fitness without proper qualifications.
p1.ex1: Ignoring a doctor's advice is irresponsible when recovering from injury.
p1.ex2: She found his irresponsible attitude to warm-ups frustrating.

p1.en: To cause something to happen as a result.
p1.example: Poor sleep habits often lead to low energy and poor concentration.
p1.ex1: Overtraining can lead to injury and burnout.
p1.ex2: Consistent effort leads to lasting improvement.

p1.en: Permitted by law (legal) or not permitted by law (illegal).
p1.example: Some performance-enhancing substances are illegal in competitive sport.
p1.ex1: It is illegal to sell unlicensed supplements in many countries.
p1.ex2: The legal use of certain supplements varies between countries.

p1.en: Based on clear reasoning (logical) or not (illogical).
p1.example: It is illogical to expect instant results from a new fitness routine.
p1.ex1: Her approach to habit change was logical and well-structured.
p1.ex2: He made the illogical decision to skip rest days entirely.

p1.en: Fully developed and sensible (mature) or not yet developed (immature).
p1.example: An immature approach to fitness is expecting results without effort.
p1.ex1: She showed a mature attitude by accepting setbacks without giving up.
p1.ex2: His immature response to failure was to quit entirely.

p1.en: Relating to the mind or psychological processes.
p1.example: Regular exercise has significant benefits for both physical and mental health.
p1.ex1: She prioritised her mental well-being alongside her physical fitness.
p1.ex2: Mental strength is just as important as physical strength in sport.

p1.en: Making someone feel enthusiastic and determined to do something.
p1.example: Tracking your daily progress is one of the most motivating habits you can build.
p1.ex1: She found group exercise more motivating than training alone.
p1.ex2: His speech was incredibly motivating for the whole team.

p1.en: A tissue in the body that contracts to produce movement.
p1.example: Strength training builds muscle and improves overall body composition.
p1.ex1: She felt her muscles ache after the first week of training.
p1.ex2: Rest days allow muscles to recover and grow stronger.

p1.en: A widely believed but false idea or story.
p1.example: It is a myth that you need to exercise for hours every day to be healthy.
p1.ex1: The idea that carbs are always bad is a nutrition myth.
p1.ex2: She busted the myth that women should not lift heavy weights.

p1.en: To do something excessively or more than is necessary or healthy.
p1.example: It is easy to overdo exercise when you are highly motivated at the start.
p1.ex1: She overdid her training in the first month and injured her knee.
p1.ex2: Do not overdo the calorie restriction — it can harm your health.

p1.en: To exercise too much, beyond what is beneficial for the body.
p1.example: People who overexercise often end up more tired and more prone to injury.
p1.ex1: The trainer warned her not to overexercise during the first week.
p1.ex2: Overexercising without adequate rest can damage muscles rather than build them.

p1.en: Relating to the body rather than the mind.
p1.example: Physical activity should be enjoyable, not a punishment.
p1.ex1: Regular physical exercise improves both fitness and mood.
p1.ex2: She tracked both her physical and mental progress.

p1.en: Based on facts and achievable (realistic) or not (unrealistic).
p1.example: Setting unrealistic goals is one of the main reasons people give up.
p1.ex1: She set realistic targets and celebrated every small success.
p1.ex2: His plan was unrealistic because it required six hours of exercise a day.

p1.en: To return to a normal state of health after illness or injury.
p1.example: She took two weeks to recover from her knee injury.
p1.ex1: Rest and nutrition are essential to recover from intense training.
p1.ex2: He recovered quickly because he followed the physiotherapist's advice.

p1.en: Done or happening at consistent intervals; following a pattern.
p1.example: Regular exercise is more effective than occasional intense sessions.
p1.ex1: She regularly reviews her habits to see what is working.
p1.ex2: He goes to the gym regularly — three times a week without fail.

p1.en: To fix something that is damaged; also used for the body healing itself.
p1.example: Sleep is essential because it is when the body repairs itself.
p1.ex1: Protein helps repair muscles after a tough workout.
p1.ex2: She repaired her broken routine by making it simpler and more realistic.

p1.en: The possibility that something harmful or unpleasant may happen.
p1.example: There is a risk of injury if you skip the warm-up before exercise.
p1.ex1: She was aware of the risks of following an extreme diet.
p1.ex2: The risk of burnout increases when you ignore rest days.

p1.en: Based on or relating to science and its methods.
p1.example: There is scientific evidence that habits form through repetition and reward.
p1.ex1: She only followed scientifically proven methods of habit formation.
p1.ex2: The scientific research supports the idea of gradual habit change.

p1.en: To avoid a person, place, or thing.
p1.example: Stay away from extreme diets that promise overnight results.
p1.ex1: She stayed away from sugary snacks by keeping them out of the house.
p1.ex2: He stayed away from social media during his study sessions.

p1.en: Taking a large amount of time to complete.
p1.example: Cooking healthy meals from scratch can be time-consuming but rewarding.
p1.ex1: She found meal prepping time-consuming at first but efficient later.
p1.ex2: He gave up the habit because it was too time-consuming.

p1.en: The state of feeling tired and lacking energy.
p1.example: Tiredness is often a sign that your body needs more rest.
p1.ex1: She felt tiredness in her legs after three consecutive days of training.
p1.ex2: Chronic tiredness can be caused by poor sleep and overtraining.

p1.en: The most important thing that must be dealt with first.
p1.example: Making sleep a top priority is one of the best habits you can form.
p1.ex1: Her health became her top priority after the doctor's warning.
p1.ex2: He made exercise his top priority by scheduling it first thing in the morning.

p1.en: Not able to be used or reached; not free at a particular time.
p1.example: The gym is unavailable on public holidays.
p1.ex1: She was unavailable on Mondays due to work commitments.
p1.ex2: When your usual route is unavailable, adapt your plan.

p1.en: Not knowing or not noticing something.
p1.example: Many people are unaware of how much sugar is in their daily diet.
p1.ex1: She was unaware that her habit was affecting her sleep quality.
p1.ex2: He was completely unaware of the risks of overtraining.

p1.en: Not known or recognised; not previously encountered.
p1.example: Starting a new routine often feels unfamiliar and uncomfortable at first.
p1.ex1: She was unfamiliar with the concept of habit stacking.
p1.ex2: The unfamiliar exercises felt awkward during the first session.

p1.en: Harmful to health; not promoting good physical or mental condition.
p1.example: Unhealthy snacking habits are often formed during stressful periods.
p1.ex1: She replaced her unhealthy lunch with a balanced meal.
p1.ex2: An unhealthy relationship with food can be difficult to change.

p1.en: Not meeting the standards expected of a qualified professional.
p1.example: It is unprofessional to give medical advice without the right qualifications.
p1.ex1: His unprofessional attitude in the gym made others feel uncomfortable.
p1.ex2: She considered it unprofessional to promote unproven health products.

p1.en: Not right or appropriate for a particular person or purpose.
p1.example: High-impact exercise can be unsuitable for people with joint problems.
p1.ex1: The diet plan was unsuitable for her because it restricted key nutrients.
p1.ex2: He avoided exercises that were unsuitable for his fitness level.

p1.en: Used to say something is mostly true, though there may be exceptions.
p1.example: In general, a consistent routine is more effective than an intense but irregular one.
p1.ex1: In general, people who sleep well tend to make healthier choices.
p1.ex2: In general, habits formed slowly tend to last longer.

p1.en: Doing things gradually, one action at a time, rather than all at once.
p1.example: Do not try to change everything at once — take it one step at a time.
p1.ex1: She approached her fitness goals one step at a time.
p1.ex2: One step at a time, he transformed his daily routine.

p1.en: Used to introduce a specific topic being discussed.
p1.example: When it comes to building habits, consistency matters more than intensity.
p1.ex1: When it comes to nutrition, small changes make a big difference.
p1.ex2: When it comes to exercise, finding something you enjoy is key.

p2.en: The joint connecting the foot to the leg.
p2.example: She twisted her ankle during her morning run and had to stop.
p2.ex1: Ankle injuries are common in sports that involve jumping.
p2.ex2: He wore a support bandage around his ankle after the strain.

p2.en: Having a positive or helpful effect.
p2.example: Regular outdoor exercise is especially beneficial for mental health.
p2.ex1: A balanced diet is beneficial for both energy levels and skin health.
p2.ex2: She found that short walks throughout the day were very beneficial.

p2.en: The elected group of people responsible for managing a city or town.
p2.example: The city council approved a plan to build more cycling lanes.
p2.ex1: She contacted the city council to request a new sports facility.
p2.ex2: The city council invested in outdoor fitness equipment for the park.

p2.en: A group of people living in the same area or sharing common interests.
p2.example: Joining a running community helps you stay motivated and accountable.
p2.ex1: The local community came together to build a new sports court.
p2.ex2: She felt a strong sense of community at the fitness club.

p2.en: A thick substance applied to the skin for protection or healing.
p2.example: Apply sun cream before exercising outdoors in summer.
p2.ex1: She used a herbal cream to soothe her sore muscles after training.
p2.ex2: The pharmacist recommended a cream for her dry, irritated skin.

p2.en: To restore someone to health; to eliminate a disease or problem.
p2.example: Exercise cannot cure every illness, but it helps prevent many.
p2.ex1: Rest and good nutrition helped cure his fatigue after months of overtraining.
p2.ex2: No supplement can cure poor sleep habits.

p2.en: To cause harm or injury to something.
p2.example: Overtraining can damage muscles and slow recovery significantly.
p2.ex1: She damaged her knee by not warming up properly.
