p2.ex2: He queued up to be the first to buy the new limited edition trainers.

p2.en: Not cooked; also used to describe unprocessed or unfiltered content.
p2.example: She posts raw, unedited reviews because her audience values authenticity.
p2.ex1: He shared the raw footage of the unboxing before editing it.
p2.ex2: Raw data from customer reviews showed that the product had serious issues.

p2.en: The opinion that people generally have of someone or something.
p2.example: The brand damaged its reputation after several customers reported faulty products.
p2.ex1: She only buys from shops with a strong reputation for customer service.
p2.ex2: Building a good reputation takes years, but losing it can happen overnight.

p2.en: A small amount of a product given to people to try before they buy.
p2.example: She picked up a free sample of the new perfume at the cosmetics counter.
p2.ex1: The brand gave out samples at the farmer's market to attract new customers.
p2.ex2: He tried the sample before deciding whether to buy the full-sized product.

p2.en: To sell all available stock of a product.
p2.example: The limited edition trainers sold out within minutes of going on sale.
p2.ex1: She was disappointed to find that the item had sold out.
p2.ex2: He set an alarm to be notified the moment the product went back in stock.

p2.en: Able to connect to the internet and perform tasks automatically.
p2.example: Smart speakers have become one of the most popular consumer electronics.
p2.ex1: She bought a smart thermostat that she could control from her phone.
p2.ex2: He reviewed the latest smart home devices on his channel.

p2.en: The specific group of people a product or campaign is aimed at.
p2.example: The brand's target audience is young adults aged eighteen to thirty.
p2.ex1: She tailored her channel content to appeal to her target audience.
p2.ex2: Understanding your target audience is essential for effective marketing.

p2.en: Not wanting to do something; reluctant.
p2.example: She was unwilling to pay extra for express delivery.
p2.ex1: He was unwilling to leave a review unless the product truly impressed him.
p2.ex2: Many consumers are unwilling to share personal data with shopping apps.

p2.en: An image, video, or graphic used to represent or promote something.
p2.example: Strong visuals in an advertisement are more memorable than words alone.
p2.ex1: She used high-quality visuals in her review to show the product clearly.
p2.ex2: The brand invested in stunning visuals for their new social media campaign.

p2.en: A shop where bread, cakes, and pastries are made and sold.
p2.example: She stopped at the bakery every morning to buy fresh bread.
p2.ex1: The baker's on the corner is famous for its sourdough loaves.
p2.ex2: He picked up a box of pastries from the bakery as a gift.

p2.en: A small fashionable shop selling clothes or accessories.
p2.example: She found a beautiful dress in a small boutique near the market.
p2.ex1: The boutique specialises in handmade jewellery and accessories.
p2.ex2: He bought a custom-designed shirt from a boutique in the city centre.

p2.en: A shop where meat is sold.
p2.example: She bought fresh lamb from the local butcher's for Sunday dinner.
p2.ex1: The butcher's offers better quality meat than the supermarket.
p2.ex2: He asked the butcher to cut the steak to his preferred thickness.

p2.en: A small local shop that sells a variety of everyday goods.
p2.example: She ran to the corner shop to buy milk after running out at home.
p2.ex1: The corner shop stays open until midnight, which is very convenient.
p2.ex2: He always supports the local corner shop rather than the big supermarket.

p2.en: A shop selling high-quality cooked or prepared foods.
p2.example: She bought imported cheese and olives from the deli near her office.
p2.ex1: The delicatessen stocks unusual ingredients that are hard to find elsewhere.
p2.ex2: He grabbed a sandwich from the deli before heading to the meeting.

p2.en: An outdoor market where people sell old or second-hand goods.
p2.example: She found a vintage lamp at the flea market for just five pounds.
p2.ex1: He loves going to the flea market on Sunday mornings to find bargains.
p2.ex2: The flea market is a great place to buy unique items at low prices.

p2.en: A shop where flowers and plants are sold.
p2.example: He stopped at the florist's to buy roses for his mother's birthday.
p2.ex1: She ordered a bouquet from the florist's for the wedding decoration.
p2.ex2: The florist's arranges custom bouquets for any occasion.

p2.en: A shop that sells fresh fruit and vegetables.
p2.example: She buys seasonal produce from the greengrocer's rather than the supermarket.
p2.ex1: The greengrocer's on the high street sells locally grown vegetables.
p2.ex2: He preferred the greengrocer's because the produce was always fresh.

p2.en: A shop where eye tests are carried out and glasses are sold.
p2.example: She visited the optician's for an eye test and ordered new glasses.
p2.ex1: He picked up his prescription sunglasses from the optician's.
p2.ex2: The optician's offers a free eye test with every pair of glasses purchased.

p2.en: A shop that sells paper, pens, notebooks, and other office supplies.
p2.example: She went to the stationery shop to buy notebooks before the new term started.
p2.ex1: He found a beautiful planner at the stationery shop.
p2.ex2: The stationery shop stocks everything from art supplies to office equipment.

p2.en: The activity of looking for goods at reduced prices.
p2.example: She loves bargain hunting at the flea market every Saturday morning.
p2.ex1: Bargain hunting is easier during the January sales.
p2.ex2: He spent the afternoon bargain hunting online and saved a lot of money.

p2.en: One of a group of shops with the same name and owner.
p2.example: She prefers shopping at a chain store because of its consistent quality.
p2.ex1: The high street is dominated by chain stores rather than independent shops.
p2.ex2: He chose the chain store because he could return items at any branch.

p2.en: A rating or comment left by a person who has bought a product.
p2.example: She always reads at least ten customer reviews before making a purchase.
p2.ex1: The product received overwhelmingly positive customer reviews.
p2.ex2: He left a detailed customer review explaining both the pros and cons.

p2.en: A fashionable brand with a well-known name, often expensive.
p2.example: She splashed out on a designer label handbag for her birthday.
p2.ex1: He never buys designer labels because he thinks they are overpriced.
p2.ex2: The boutique stocks several designer labels alongside local brands.

p2.en: A room in a shop where you can try on clothes before buying.
p2.example: She took three sizes to the fitting room to find the best fit.
p2.ex1: The fitting room had a queue of ten people during the sale.
p2.ex2: He avoided online shopping for clothes because there was no fitting room.

p2.en: Items used in the home such as cleaning products, kitchenware, or furniture.
p2.example: She ordered household goods online to be delivered the next day.
p2.ex1: The corner shop sells a small range of everyday household goods.
p2.ex2: He went to the chain store to stock up on household goods for the new flat.

p2.en: The busiest time of day when most people are shopping or travelling.
p2.example: She avoids supermarkets during peak hours to skip the crowds.
p2.ex1: The checkout queues are longest during peak hours on Saturdays.
p2.ex2: Online deliveries during peak hours often take longer than expected.

p2.en: A label showing the price of an item; also used figuratively to mean the cost.
p2.example: She put the item back on the shelf when she saw the price tag.
p2.ex1: The price tag was hidden, which made her suspicious of the true cost.
p2.ex2: He was surprised by the high price tag given the product's poor reviews.

p2.en: The glass window at the front of a shop used to display products.
p2.example: She stopped to admire the shoes in the shop window before going inside.
p2.ex1: The shop window was decorated to attract customers during the festive season.
p2.ex2: He was lured into the boutique by a beautiful display in the shop window.

p2.en: A metal basket on wheels used to carry goods while shopping in a supermarket.
p2.example: She filled the shopping trolley with groceries for the week.
p2.ex1: He forgot to bring a coin for the shopping trolley and had to use a basket.
p2.ex2: The shopping trolley overflowed because she had bought so much on special offer.

p2.en: A product sold at a reduced price for a limited time.
p2.example: She bought three bottles of shampoo because they were on special offer.
p2.ex1: He always checks for special offers before doing his weekly shop.
p2.ex2: The supermarket had a two-for-one special offer on protein bars.

p2.en: Looking at goods in shop windows without intending to buy anything.
p2.example: She spent the afternoon window shopping along the high street.
p2.ex1: He enjoys window shopping but rarely actually buys anything.
p2.ex2: Window shopping online can easily lead to impulse purchases.

p2.en: To make someone notice something or become interested in it.
p2.example: Bright packaging and bold colours attract customers' attention on the shelf.
p2.ex1: The pop-up ad attracted her attention at exactly the right moment.
p2.ex2: He used eye-catching visuals to attract the attention of his target audience.

p2.en: To do better than other businesses or rivals.
p2.example: The brand offered free shipping to beat the competition during the sale season.
p2.ex1: She lowered her prices to beat the competition and attract more customers.
p2.ex2: To beat the competition, the company invested heavily in better customer service.

p1.en: A record of money held in a bank; also a user profile on an app or website.
p1.example: She checked her bank account and realised she had spent too much that month.
p1.ex1: He opened a savings account to put money aside each month.
p1.ex2: Make sure your account details are correct before making a payment.

p1.en: To make something start working or become operational.
p1.example: She activated her cashback card as soon as it arrived in the post.
p1.ex1: He activated the coupon code at checkout to get the discount.
p1.ex2: You need to activate your account before you can make a purchase.

p1.en: Done by itself without human action; happening as a natural result.
p1.example: The subscription fee is automatically charged to her account each month.
p1.ex1: Savings are automatically transferred to his account on payday.
p1.ex2: The app automatically tracks every purchase you make.

p1.en: The organ in your head that controls thoughts and actions; also used figuratively for intelligence.
p1.example: Shops use clever tricks to fool your brain into spending more than you planned.
p1.ex1: Marketing uses bright colours to trigger your brain's desire to buy.
p1.ex2: She learned how her brain responds to sales tactics and became a smarter shopper.

p1.en: Completely new and unused.
p1.example: She resisted buying a brand new phone when her old one still worked perfectly.
p1.ex1: He bought a brand new laptop instead of getting the old one repaired.
p1.ex2: There is no need to buy brand new when second-hand is just as good.

p1.en: Not giving enough attention or thought to what you are doing.
p1.example: Careless spending is one of the main reasons people get into debt.
p1.ex1: She was careless with her budget and ran out of money before the end of the month.
p1.ex2: He made a careless impulse buy that he regretted immediately.

p1.en: To ask someone to pay a certain amount; also to put electricity into a device.
p1.example: The shop charged her twice for the same item by mistake.
p1.ex1: He was charged a fee for withdrawing money from a foreign ATM.
p1.ex2: Some apps charge a monthly fee that is easy to forget about.

p1.en: A voucher that gives you a discount when buying something.
p1.example: She collected coupons and saved thirty per cent on her weekly shop.
p1.ex1: He used a coupon code at checkout to get a free delivery.
p1.ex2: The app sends coupons for products you have already been looking at.

p1.en: An agreement or arrangement; also a good offer at a reduced price.
p1.example: She spotted a great deal on trainers and bought them without thinking.
p1.ex1: He always waits for a deal before making a big purchase.
p1.ex2: The two-for-one deal convinced her to buy more than she had planned.

p1.en: The ability to control your behaviour and make yourself do difficult things.
p1.example: Financial discipline is the key to avoiding unnecessary debt.
p1.ex1: She showed great discipline by sticking to her monthly budget.
p1.ex2: Without discipline, it is easy to spend more than you earn.

p1.en: To pause before doing something because you are unsure.
p1.example: She hesitated before clicking the buy button and decided to wait.
p1.ex1: He never hesitates when he sees a bargain, which causes problems.
p1.ex2: Do not hesitate to ask the shop assistant for a better price.

p1.en: Unplanned purchases made suddenly without thinking about whether you need the item.
p1.example: Supermarkets place sweets near the checkout to encourage impulse buys.
p1.ex1: She came in for milk and left with five impulse buys.
p1.ex2: He deleted shopping apps from his phone to avoid impulse buys.

p1.en: To plan or mean to do something.
p1.example: She intended to spend fifty pounds but ended up spending double that.
p1.ex1: He intended to save the money but spent it on impulse buys.
p1.ex2: They intended to shop wisely but got carried away in the sale.

p1.en: To put money into something to make a profit or gain benefit over time.
p1.example: She decided to invest in quality items that would last rather than cheap ones.
p1.ex1: He invested a portion of his salary into a savings fund every month.
p1.ex2: Investing in a good budgeting app saved her hundreds of pounds a year.

p1.en: A sum of money that you borrow and must pay back, usually with interest.
p1.example: She took out a loan to buy the car, which she is still paying back.
p1.ex1: He regretted taking out a loan to pay for something he did not need.
p1.ex2: Always read the terms carefully before agreeing to a loan.

p1.en: To find the position of something.
p1.example: She used the app to locate the nearest ATM before withdrawing cash.
p1.ex1: He struggled to locate a shop that accepted cash only.
p1.ex2: The website helps you locate stores with the best current deals.

p1.en: To have an obligation to pay money back to someone.
p1.example: She owes her friend twenty pounds from the shopping trip last weekend.
p1.ex1: He owes three months of rent because he spent his salary carelessly.
p1.ex2: Always track how much you owe so debt does not build up.

p1.en: An unpleasant physical or emotional feeling; also used informally for something difficult.
p1.example: Researchers say paying by cash causes more mental pain than using a card.
p1.ex1: She felt the pain of her credit card bill at the end of the month.
p1.ex2: The pain of regret after an impulse buy is a well-known feeling.

p1.en: The action of paying someone money.
p1.example: She set up an automatic payment so she would never miss a bill.
p1.ex1: He made the final payment on his loan and felt enormous relief.
p1.ex2: Always check your payment has gone through before leaving the shop.

p1.en: Giving a sense of pleasure, fulfilment, or contentment.
p1.example: Shopping can feel satisfying in the moment but regretful later.
p1.ex1: She found it more satisfying to save for something than to buy it on impulse.
p1.ex2: Sticking to a budget and reaching a savings goal is genuinely satisfying.

p1.en: Showing good judgement; practical and reasonable.
p1.example: Making a shopping list before going to the supermarket is the sensible approach.
p1.ex1: She made a sensible decision to wait for the sale before buying.
p1.ex2: Being sensible with money when you are young sets you up for later life.

p1.en: To notice or see something, especially when it is not obvious.
p1.example: She spotted a hidden fee at the bottom of the checkout page.
p1.ex1: He spotted a discounted item at the back of the shelf.
p1.ex2: Learning to spot marketing tricks helps you spend more wisely.

p1.en: A plan designed to achieve a particular long-term goal.
p1.example: Her strategy for saving money was to transfer ten per cent of every payment straight to savings.
p1.ex1: He developed a strategy for shopping that helped him avoid impulse buys.
p1.ex2: A good financial strategy includes both saving and careful spending.

p1.en: To deceive someone into doing or believing something.
p1.example: Supermarkets trick shoppers by placing expensive items at eye level.
p1.ex1: She felt tricked when the sale price was actually the normal price.
p1.ex2: He learned to spot how ads trick people into thinking they need something.

p1.en: Not arranged or intended in advance.
p1.example: Most impulse buys are completely unplanned and driven by emotion.
p1.ex1: She made several unplanned purchases during the sale.
p1.ex2: Unplanned spending is the most common reason people go over budget.

p1.en: In a sensible, clever, and thoughtful way.
p1.example: She spent her bonus wisely by paying off part of her loan.
p1.ex1: He invested wisely and had enough saved to retire early.
p1.ex2: Choosing to spend wisely is a skill that takes time to develop.

p1.en: To take money out of a bank account.
p1.example: She withdrew fifty pounds from the ATM before going to the market.
p1.ex1: He forgot to withdraw cash before the bank closed.
p1.ex2: Withdrawing cash instead of using a card makes spending feel more real.

p1.en: To manage to live or deal with a situation, usually with limited resources.
p1.example: She was getting by on a very tight budget during her first year at university.
p1.ex1: He got by with just fifty pounds a week by cooking at home.
p1.ex2: It is difficult to get by in an expensive city on a low income.

p1.en: To give something to someone, often money.
p1.example: He reluctantly handed over his credit card at the checkout.
p1.ex1: She handed over the coupon and received her discount immediately.
p1.ex2: He hated handing over large amounts of cash for a single item.

p1.en: To return money that you have borrowed.
p1.example: She promised to pay back her friend as soon as she got paid.
p1.ex1: He is still paying back the loan he took out three years ago.
p1.ex2: Always agree on when you will pay back borrowed money.

p1.en: To finish paying a debt completely; also to produce a good result.
p1.example: She finally paid off her credit card debt after two years.
p1.ex1: He worked overtime to pay off his loan ahead of schedule.
p1.ex2: All her careful saving paid off when she could afford the holiday.

p1.en: To save an amount of money for a specific purpose.
p1.example: She puts aside a fixed amount every month for emergencies.
p1.ex1: He put aside money each week until he had enough for the deposit.
p1.ex2: Putting money aside regularly is the simplest saving strategy.

p1.en: To charge someone too much money or to cheat them.
p1.example: She felt completely ripped off when she found the same product cheaper elsewhere.
p1.ex1: The tourist was ripped off by a market seller who doubled the price.
p1.ex2: He always checks reviews to avoid being ripped off by dishonest sellers.

p1.en: To obtain something formally, such as a loan or insurance policy.
p1.example: She took out a loan to cover the cost of the course.
p1.ex1: He took out a subscription without realising it would auto-renew.
p1.ex2: Think carefully before taking out credit to buy something you want rather than need.

p1.en: Provided that; on the condition that.
p1.example: She was happy to spend more as long as the quality was worth it.
p1.ex1: He would lend her the money as long as she paid it back by Friday.
p1.ex2: As long as you budget carefully, you can enjoy shopping without guilt.

p1.en: To be in a more advantageous or comfortable situation.
p1.example: She would be better off saving the money than spending it on something she does not need.
p1.ex1: He realised he was better off buying second-hand than brand new.
p1.ex2: You are better off investing in quality than buying cheap items repeatedly.

p1.en: Used to show how two things are different or similar.
p1.example: Online shopping is much more convenient compared to going to a physical store.
p1.ex1: Compared to last year, she has reduced her impulse spending significantly.
p1.ex2: The price is high compared to similar products from other brands.

p1.en: To become so excited or enthusiastic that you lose control of your behaviour.
p1.example: She got carried away during the sale and spent twice her budget.
p1.ex1: He got carried away at the flea market and bought things he did not need.
p1.ex2: It is easy to get carried away when shopping online late at night.

p1.en: To stay aware of something over time by monitoring it regularly.
p1.example: She uses a budgeting app to keep track of every penny she spends.
p1.ex1: He kept track of his expenses in a notebook.
p1.ex2: Keeping track of your spending helps you avoid nasty surprises at the end of the month.

p1.en: To use something, especially something that is available to you.
p1.example: She made good use of her loyalty card to earn points on every purchase.
p1.ex1: He made use of every discount available before finalising his purchase.
p1.ex2: Make use of the free trial before committing to a paid subscription.

p1.en: To make good use of an opportunity; also to exploit someone unfairly.
p1.example: She took advantage of the special offer and saved forty per cent.
p1.ex1: He took advantage of the cashback scheme to get money back on purchases.
p1.ex2: Be careful that you are not being taken advantage of by misleading deals.

p2.en: The cost of entering a place; also the act of admitting something.
p2.example: She was shocked by the high admission price for the concert.
p2.ex1: The museum offers free admission on the first Sunday of every month.
p2.ex2: Admission to the theme park cost twice what she had expected.

p2.en: To have no money at all, usually temporarily.
p2.example: She was completely broke by the end of the month after several impulse purchases.
p2.ex1: He was broke after the holiday and had to borrow money for food.
p2.ex2: Being broke for a week made her realise she needed a better budget.

p2.en: Not expensive; suitable for people who do not want to spend much money.
p2.example: She found a budget-friendly alternative to the expensive designer brand.
p2.ex1: The farmer's market is one of the most budget-friendly places to shop.
p2.ex2: He looked for budget-friendly options when furnishing his new flat.

p2.en: A person whose job is to receive payment in a shop or bank.
p2.example: She asked the cashier if there were any active discount codes.
p2.ex1: The cashier noticed the overcharge and corrected it immediately.
p2.ex2: He thanked the cashier and asked for a receipt.

p2.en: To arise or occur, usually unexpectedly.
p2.example: An unexpected expense came up and she had to dip into her savings.
p2.ex1: Something came up at work and he had to cancel his shopping trip.
p2.ex2: Emergencies always come up, which is why having savings matters.

p2.en: Two people or things together; also an informal term for a small number.
p2.example: She only planned to buy a couple of things but left with a full trolley.
p2.ex1: He spent a couple of hours browsing the flea market.
p2.ex2: A couple of smart decisions can make a big difference to your finances.

p2.en: Money that you owe to someone or an institution.
p2.example: She worked hard to pay off her credit card debt within a year.
p2.ex1: Getting into debt is easy; getting out of it takes discipline.
p2.ex2: He was in debt for three years before finally clearing what he owed.

p2.en: Feeling self-conscious or ashamed in a social situation.
p2.example: She felt embarrassed when her card was declined at the checkout.
p2.ex1: He was embarrassed to admit he had spent all his salary in one week.
p2.ex2: She was embarrassed by how much she had spent compared to her friends.

p2.en: Having a reliable and secure financial situation.
p2.example: She worked towards being financially stable by paying off debts and building savings.
p2.ex1: He felt financially stable for the first time after a year of careful budgeting.
p2.ex2: Being financially stable gives you freedom to enjoy life without constant worry.

p2.en: Willing to give more than is necessary; kind with money or gifts.
p2.example: She was too generous with her money and often ended up broke by payday.
p2.ex1: He was generous with tips, which left him with little at the end of the week.
p2.ex2: Being generous is a wonderful quality as long as you can afford it.

p2.en: Made at home rather than bought in a shop.
p2.example: She saved money by bringing homemade lunches to work instead of buying food.
p2.ex1: Homemade gifts are often more meaningful and far cheaper.
p2.ex2: He started making homemade bread after realising how much he spent at the bakery.

p2.en: Buying or available during a period when shops sell goods at reduced prices.
p2.example: She always waits to buy winter clothes in the sales at the end of the season.
p2.ex1: He bought his new sofa in the sales and saved three hundred pounds.
p2.ex2: Shopping in the sales requires patience but can save a lot of money.

p2.en: One of a series of regular payments made over time for something.
p2.example: She paid for the laptop in monthly instalments rather than all at once.
p2.ex1: Paying in instalments can help manage large purchases without going into debt.
p2.ex2: He chose a zero per cent instalment plan to spread the cost of the holiday.

p2.en: Free time when you are not working, used for relaxation and enjoyment.
p2.example: She sets aside a small amount each month for leisure activities.
p2.ex1: He spends most of his leisure time and money on sports equipment.
p2.ex2: Budgeting for leisure is just as important as budgeting for essentials.

p2.en: To get or achieve something, often with effort.
p2.example: She managed to obtain a discount by speaking directly to the manager.
p2.ex1: He obtained a refund after proving the product was faulty.
p2.ex2: You can obtain a loyalty card at the customer service desk.

p2.en: Having very little money to spend.
p2.example: She fed her family well on a tight budget by planning all meals in advance.
p2.ex1: Travelling on a tight budget is possible if you research carefully.
p2.ex2: He learned to cook from scratch when he was on a tight budget at university.

p2.en: To decide which things are most important and deal with them first.
p2.example: She had to prioritize rent and food over leisure spending.
p2.ex1: He prioritized paying off debt before starting to save.
p2.ex2: Learning to prioritize your needs over your wants is a key financial skill.

p2.en: A regular payment made for using a property or building.
p2.example: After paying rent, she had very little money left for anything else.
p2.ex1: Rent in the city centre was so high that he had to share a flat.
p2.ex2: She set up a direct debit so her rent was always paid on time.

p2.en: A period when a shop sells goods at reduced prices.
p2.example: The January sales attract thousands of bargain hunters every year.
p2.ex1: She saved up specifically to take advantage of the summer sales.
p2.ex2: He never shops outside the sales if he can help it.

p2.en: Money that you have saved, especially in a bank account.
p2.example: She dipped into her savings to cover an unexpected repair bill.
p2.ex1: He built up his savings by cutting out all unnecessary spending.
p2.ex2: Having savings gives you confidence and security in difficult times.

p2.en: The importance of an object because of personal memories attached to it, not its financial worth.
p2.example: The old watch had no market value but enormous sentimental value to her.
p2.ex1: She kept the broken necklace because of its sentimental value.
p2.ex2: He explained that the gift had more sentimental value than monetary worth.

p2.en: To divide something between people.
p2.example: They split the cost of the meal between the four of them.
p2.ex1: She and her sister split the rent to make it more affordable.
p2.ex2: He suggested they split the bill rather than one person paying everything.

p2.en: To have great difficulty doing something.
p2.example: She struggled to make ends meet in her first year of living alone.
p2.ex1: He struggled to stick to his budget during the festive season.
p2.ex2: Many young people struggle to save when rent takes up most of their income.

p2.en: An amount of money paid to the government, usually based on income or purchases.
p2.example: She did not realise how much tax had been added to the price of the item.
p2.ex1: He was surprised to find that the final price was much higher due to import tax.
p2.ex2: Always check whether a quoted price includes tax before agreeing to pay.

p2.en: Extra money given voluntarily for good service; also a useful piece of advice.
p2.example: She left a generous tip because the service was excellent.
p2.ex1: He tipped the delivery driver because they arrived ahead of schedule.
p2.ex2: Her best money-saving tip is to wait twenty-four hours before any unplanned purchase.

p2.en: Difficult or demanding; requiring great effort.
p2.example: It was tough to stick to her budget when all her friends were shopping.
p2.ex1: He found it tough to say no to impulse buys during the sales.
p2.ex2: Living on a tight budget is tough, but it teaches you valuable skills.

p2.en: To have a very large amount of money; to be extremely wealthy.
p2.example: She acted as if she was rolling in money, but her savings were nearly gone.
p2.ex1: He spent money like he was rolling in it, despite his modest salary.
p2.ex2: Just because someone looks wealthy does not mean they are rolling in money.

p2.word: cost an arm and a leg
p2.en: To be extremely expensive.
p2.example: The designer jacket cost an arm and a leg but she bought it anyway.
p2.ex1: Eating out every day costs an arm and a leg in the city centre.
p2.ex2: He was shocked — the repair cost an arm and a leg.

p2.en: To earn a very small amount of money for work done.
p2.example: She was getting paid peanuts and could barely cover her rent.
p2.ex1: He felt undervalued because he was getting paid peanuts for long hours.
p2.ex2: Many interns get paid peanuts despite working as hard as full-time employees.

p2.en: To have just enough money to pay for the things you need.
p2.example: With rent so high, it was difficult for her to make ends meet each month.
p2.ex1: He worked two jobs just to make ends meet.
p2.ex2: Many families struggle to make ends meet when unexpected bills arrive.

p2.en: Used to remind someone that money is a limited resource that must be earned carefully.
p2.example: Her mum reminded her that money does not grow on trees when she asked for more.
p2.ex1: He spent recklessly until someone reminded him that money does not grow on trees.
p2.ex2: Remember, money does not grow on trees — think before you spend.

p2.ru: деньги не проблема / цена не имеет значения
p2.en: Used to say that you are willing to spend as much as necessary.
p2.example: She said money was no object when planning her wedding.
p2.ex1: For this project, money is no object — only the best will do.
p2.ex2: He treated his partner as if money were no object, which led to serious debt.

p2.uz: kelajak uchun tejash / qora kunga saqlamoq
p2.en: To save money for a time when you might need it unexpectedly.
p2.example: Her grandmother always told her to save for a rainy day.
p2.ex1: He put fifty pounds aside every month to save for a rainy day.
p2.ex2: She was glad she had saved for a rainy day when her car broke down.

p2.en: To spend money carelessly and in large amounts.
p2.example: He was throwing money around at the casino as if it meant nothing.
p2.ex1: She used to throw money around on designer labels before learning to budget.
p2.ex2: Throwing money around impresses no one and leaves you broke.

p3.en: To analyse something carefully and objectively rather than accepting it without question.
p3.example: She learned to think critically about advertising claims before making a purchase.
p3.ex1: He thinks critically about every deal he sees, which saves him from being tricked.
p3.ex2: Thinking critically about spending habits is the first step to financial freedom.

p3.en: Having no end; continuing without stopping.
p3.example: Social media provides endless opportunities for brands to target consumers.
p3.ex1: She felt overwhelmed by the endless stream of pop-up ads and notifications.
p3.ex2: The endless temptation of online shopping makes it hard to stick to a budget.

p3.en: A desire for something created by advertising rather than a genuine necessity.
p3.example: Marketers are skilled at creating false needs that make you feel you must buy something.
p3.ex1: She recognised the new phone as a false need because her old one still worked.
p3.ex2: He questioned whether his desire for the product was real or a false need created by the advert.

p3.en: Giving the wrong impression; likely to cause someone to have a false belief.
p3.example: The advertisement was misleading — the product looked much better in the images than in reality.
p3.ex1: She complained to the company because the product description was misleading.
p3.ex2: He learned to spot misleading price tags that made deals look better than they were.

p3.en: To cause someone to do something through argument, reasoning, or appeal.
p3.example: Advertisers use psychological tricks to persuade people to buy things they do not need.
p3.ex1: She persuaded herself that the purchase was a good investment.
p3.ex2: He was persuaded by a glowing review to spend more than he had planned.

p3.en: To increase or accumulate over time, especially in an unwanted way.
p3.example: Debt can pile up quickly if you use credit cards carelessly.
p3.ex1: Unopened packages piled up in her hallway after a period of excessive online shopping.
p3.ex2: He did not notice how much interest was piling up on his loan.

p3.en: Offered at a lower price than normal.
p3.example: She only buys clothes from the reduced section to stay within her budget.
p3.ex1: He spotted a reduced label on a product he had been waiting to buy.
p3.ex2: The reduced price made her feel she was getting a bargain, even if she did not need the item.

p3.ru: Под этим я имею в виду...
p3.en: Used to explain or clarify what you have just said.
p3.example: She lacks financial discipline — by this I mean she spends without thinking.
p3.ex1: The product is misleading; by this I mean the price shown does not include tax.
p3.ex2: He is impulsive — by this I mean he regularly buys things he does not need.

p3.en: Used to express something more simply or clearly.
p3.example: She spends more than she earns — in other words, she is living beyond her means.
p3.ex1: The deal is not genuine; in other words, the original price was inflated.
p3.ex2: He has no savings; in other words, he is financially vulnerable.

p1.en: Real and existing, not just imagined or theoretical.
p1.example: The detective needed to find the actual location of the stolen painting.
p1.ex1: The actual cost of the crime was far higher than first estimated.
p1.ex2: She was surprised by the actual number of break-ins in the neighbourhood.

p1.en: A device that makes a loud noise to warn of danger; also the feeling of fear.
p1.example: The alarm went off when the burglar broke the window.
p1.ex1: She installed a new alarm system after the break-in next door.
p1.ex2: The security alarm was triggered during the night but police found no one.

p1.en: Moving repeatedly in two opposite directions.
p1.example: The detective paced back and forth as he examined the crime scene.
p1.ex1: The suspect was seen moving back and forth near the entrance.
p1.ex2: She walked back and forth outside the shop before the theft was noticed.

p1.en: To cause someone trouble or worry; also to make the effort to do something.
p1.example: The thief did not bother to cover their tracks.
p1.ex1: She was bothered by the slight scratch she found on the door frame.
p1.ex2: He did not bother checking the footage until it was too late.

p1.en: An occasion when someone illegally enters a building by force.
p1.example: The police were called after a break-in at the jewellery shop.
p1.ex1: There had been several break-ins in the area over the past month.
p1.ex2: The break-in was discovered when the owner arrived at work in the morning.

p1.en: A set of facts or events investigated by the police or discussed in court.
p1.example: The detective was assigned to investigate a baffling theft case.
p1.ex1: The case had no clear suspect and very little evidence.
p1.ex2: She read about the famous unsolved case in a true crime book.

p1.en: A piece of information or evidence that helps solve a mystery.
p1.example: The detective found a single clue — a thread of fabric caught on the fence.
p1.ex1: She followed every clue until she identified the thief.
p1.ex2: The clue hidden in the surveillance footage solved the entire case.

p1.en: An illegal act that is punishable by law.
p1.example: Theft is one of the most commonly reported crimes in urban areas.
p1.ex1: She became interested in detective work after studying famous crimes.
p1.ex2: The crime was carried out in broad daylight, which shocked the community.

p1.en: A door, gate, or opening used to enter a building or place.
p1.example: The thief entered through a broken window near the back entrance.
p1.ex1: The surveillance camera at the entrance recorded the suspect clearly.
p1.ex2: She noticed the scratched lock at the entrance and reported it to security.

p1.en: Information or objects used to establish the facts of a crime.
p1.example: The detective carefully collected evidence before anyone else disturbed the scene.
p1.ex1: Without evidence, the police could not make an arrest.
p1.ex2: She preserved all the evidence by touching nothing at the crime scene.

p1.en: To inspect something carefully and in detail.
p1.example: The detective examined every inch of the crime scene for clues.
p1.ex1: She examined the fingerprints under a magnifying glass.
p1.ex2: He examined the footage frame by frame to identify the suspect.

p1.en: The unique pattern of lines on a person's finger, used to identify them.
p1.example: The investigators found a fingerprint on the safe door.
p1.ex1: His fingerprints were found at the scene of the theft.
p1.ex2: Modern labs can identify a suspect from a single fingerprint.

p1.en: Recorded video, especially from a security camera.
p1.example: The police reviewed the surveillance footage from the night of the break-in.
p1.ex1: Footage from the camera showed the thief entering through the side door.
p1.ex2: She spotted a figure in the footage that had gone unnoticed before.

p1.en: A person whose job is to protect a place or person.
p1.example: The security guard had left his post for only ten minutes when the theft occurred.
p1.ex1: She asked the guard if he had seen anything suspicious.
p1.ex2: The guard reviewed the camera footage as soon as the alarm sounded.

p1.en: To attach or be attached at the top so the lower part is free.
p1.example: A piece of torn fabric was hanging from the sharp edge of the broken fence.
p1.ex1: The painting that had been hanging on the wall was now missing.
p1.ex2: She noticed a key hanging near the door that had not been there before.

p1.en: To examine a situation carefully and officially to discover the truth.
p1.example: Detectives were sent to investigate the mysterious disappearance.
p1.ex1: She investigated the case for three months before finding the key evidence.
p1.ex2: Police are investigating several suspects in connection with the robbery.

p1.en: To form an opinion about someone or something; also to make a legal decision.
p1.example: Do not judge a suspect without solid evidence.
p1.ex1: She was judged unfairly before all the facts came to light.
p1.ex2: He was judged guilty by the court and sentenced to prison.

p1.en: Difficult to explain or understand; strange and secret.
p1.example: The mysterious disappearance of the necklace puzzled the entire detective team.
p1.ex1: A mysterious figure was seen leaving the building on the night of the theft.
p1.ex2: The case remained mysterious for years until new evidence emerged.

p1.en: To watch someone or something carefully and attentively.
p1.example: The detective observed the suspect's movements for several days.
p1.ex1: She observed a slight change in the door lock that others had missed.
p1.ex2: He had been observing the warehouse for a week before reporting his findings.

p1.en: The place where a crime has taken place.
p1.example: Investigators sealed off the crime scene to preserve the evidence.
p1.ex1: She was one of the first officers to arrive at the crime scene.
p1.ex2: Photographs of the crime scene were used as evidence in court.

p1.en: Measures taken to keep a place, person, or information safe.
p1.example: The museum increased its security after the theft was reported.
p1.ex1: She reviewed the security footage and identified the suspect within minutes.
p1.ex2: Better security systems could have prevented the break-in.

p1.en: Small in degree; not serious or obvious.
p1.example: There was only a slight scratch on the door, but it confirmed a forced entry.
p1.ex1: She noticed a slight smell of smoke near the back entrance.
p1.ex2: A slight movement caught on camera turned out to be the key piece of evidence.

p1.en: To be forgotten, usually temporarily.
p1.example: He admitted that checking the alarm had completely slipped his mind.
p1.ex1: The detail slipped her mind during the questioning.
p1.ex2: It slipped the guard's mind to reset the security system.

p1.en: A particular place or position; also a mark on a surface.
p1.example: The detective identified the exact spot where the thief had stood.
p1.ex1: She found a small dark spot on the floor that turned out to be ink.
p1.ex2: He marked the spot on the map where the evidence was discovered.

p1.en: Perfectly clean; completely without marks or blemishes.
p1.example: The room was suspiciously spotless — no fingerprints, no dust, nothing.
p1.ex1: She found it odd that the kitchen was spotless despite signs of a struggle elsewhere.
p1.ex2: A spotless crime scene suggested the thief had cleaned up carefully.

p1.en: To look fixedly at something or someone for a long time.
p1.example: He stared at the security footage for hours trying to spot a familiar face.
p1.ex1: She stared at the evidence board, looking for a connection she had missed.
p1.ex2: The witness stared at the suspect line-up in silence.

p1.en: A camera used to record activity in a public or private area for security.
p1.example: The surveillance camera outside the bank captured the robbery on film.
p1.ex1: She checked the footage from every surveillance camera in the area.
p1.ex2: Installing a surveillance camera at the entrance deterred future break-ins.

p1.en: A person who is believed to have committed a crime but has not been proved guilty.
p1.example: Police identified three suspects based on the surveillance footage.
p1.ex1: The main suspect had no alibi for the night of the theft.
p1.ex2: She refused to name a suspect without solid evidence.

p1.en: The act of stealing something from a person or place.
p1.example: The theft of the painting was not discovered until the next morning.
p1.ex1: She reported the theft of her laptop to the police immediately.
p1.ex2: The theft took place in broad daylight, which surprised investigators.

p1.en: An idea used to explain something, especially when not yet proved.
p1.example: The detective developed a theory about how the thief had escaped undetected.
p1.ex1: Her theory about a second suspect turned out to be correct.
p1.ex2: He shared his theory with the team, but they needed more evidence to confirm it.

p1.en: A person who steals things from others.
p1.example: The thief left no fingerprints and no witnesses — only a clue.
p1.ex1: Surveillance footage clearly showed the thief entering through the back door.
p1.ex2: She described the thief to the police in as much detail as she could remember.

p1.en: A thin strand of fibre used in sewing; also a small piece of fabric left as a clue.
p1.example: A single thread of wool caught on the fence was the only clue the detective had.
p1.ex1: She followed the thread of evidence until the full picture became clear.
p1.ex2: The tiny thread found at the crime scene matched the suspect's jacket.

p1.en: Feeling worried or anxious; experiencing difficulties.
p1.example: The detective looked troubled after reading the new evidence in the case.
p1.ex1: She was troubled by the inconsistency in the witness statements.
p1.ex2: He seemed troubled when questioned about his whereabouts that night.

p1.en: Below or directly under something.
p1.example: She found the missing key underneath the doormat at the crime scene.
p1.ex1: The suspect had hidden the stolen goods underneath the floorboards.
p1.ex2: Underneath the table, investigators discovered a crumpled receipt.

p1.en: Not significant or relevant; having little value.
p1.example: What seemed unimportant at first turned out to be the key piece of evidence.
p1.ex1: She discarded details that seemed unimportant but later regretted it.
p1.ex2: No clue is truly unimportant when investigating a serious crime.

p1.en: A person harmed or killed as a result of a crime or accident.
p1.example: The victim reported the theft as soon as she realised her wallet was gone.
p1.ex1: The police interviewed the victim at the hospital.
p1.ex2: She became an advocate for victims of theft after her own experience.

p1.en: Up to this time; used to indicate something has not happened but may happen.
p1.example: The case had not yet been solved when the detective was taken off it.
p1.ex1: They have not yet identified the suspect despite weeks of investigation.
p1.ex2: The stolen painting has not yet been recovered.

p2.en: To take someone into custody because they are suspected of a crime.
p2.example: The police arrested the suspect outside the shopping centre.
p2.ex1: She was arrested after being identified on surveillance footage.
p2.ex2: He was arrested and taken in for questioning about the robbery.

p2.en: Always; continuously without exception.
p2.example: Security staff are required to remain alert at all times.
p2.ex1: Visitors must wear their badge at all times when inside the building.
p2.ex2: The cameras monitor the area at all times, day and night.

p2.en: To enter a building by force, usually illegally.
p2.example: Someone had broken into the office and stolen several laptops.
p2.ex1: They broke into the warehouse through a damaged window.
p2.ex2: She discovered the car had been broken into when she returned from the shop.

p2.en: The crime of illegally entering a building to steal things.
p2.example: The neighbourhood had experienced three burglaries in one week.
p2.ex1: She reported the burglary to the police and an officer arrived within minutes.
p2.ex2: The burglary was discovered at six in the morning when the owner opened up.

p2.en: A person who enters a building illegally to steal things.
p2.example: The burglar had entered through a window left open on the ground floor.
p2.ex1: Security cameras captured the burglar's face clearly.
p2.ex2: She chased the burglar out of her house and called the police immediately.

p2.en: To illegally enter a building and steal things from it.
p2.example: The house had been burgled while the family were on holiday.
p2.ex1: Her shop was burgled twice in one year.
p2.ex2: The old warehouse was burgled and several valuable items were taken.

p2.en: To find and take hold of a criminal or someone trying to escape.
p2.example: The police caught the thief three days after the robbery.
p2.ex1: She was caught on camera committing the theft.
p2.ex2: He was finally caught after being recognised by a witness.

p2.en: To act dishonestly to gain an unfair advantage.
p2.example: He cheated customers by selling fake designer goods.
p2.ex1: She cheated her way through the online store by using a stolen card.
p2.ex2: The con artist cheated dozens of victims out of their savings.

p2.en: A person who has committed a crime.
p2.example: The criminal was sentenced to five years in prison for the robbery.
p2.ex1: She helped police identify the criminal through a witness statement.
p2.ex2: The criminal had a long record of previous offences.

p2.en: No longer alive; also used informally to describe a complete stop or end.
p2.example: The investigation reached a dead end when all leads ran out.
p2.ex1: She felt the case was dead after the key witness withdrew their statement.
p2.ex2: The only lead they had went dead when the suspect disappeared.

p2.en: To get away from a place or situation of danger or captivity.
p2.example: The suspect escaped from custody before the trial began.
p2.ex1: He escaped from the scene before police arrived.
p2.ex2: She helped the authorities reconstruct how the criminal escaped from the building.

p2.en: To gain unauthorised access to a computer system.
p2.example: A criminal gang hacked into the bank's database and stole customer data.
p2.ex1: She discovered her email had been hacked when she could no longer log in.
p2.ex2: He was arrested for hacking into a government security system.

p2.en: A person who illegally gains access to computer systems.
p2.example: The hacker stole thousands of personal records from the company's database.
p2.ex1: She hired a cybersecurity expert after a hacker targeted her business.
p2.ex2: The hacker was tracked down through their IP address.

p2.en: The act of gaining unauthorised access to computer systems.
p2.example: Hacking has become one of the most common forms of modern crime.
p2.ex1: She learned about hacking during a cybersecurity awareness course.
p2.ex2: The company suffered major losses due to a hacking attack on their servers.

p2.en: To take control of a vehicle or situation by force.
p2.example: The criminals hijacked a delivery van to steal the goods inside.
p2.ex1: Armed men hijacked the cargo plane on its way to the capital.
p2.ex2: The hijacking of the vehicle was caught on a road surveillance camera.

p2.en: A person who takes control of a vehicle or aircraft by force.
p2.example: The hijacker was overpowered by passengers before the plane landed.
p2.ex1: Police arrested the hijacker at the airport.
p2.ex2: She described the hijacker to investigators in great detail.

p2.en: The crime of taking control of a vehicle or aircraft by force.
p2.example: The hijacking of the lorry was connected to a wider organised crime network.
p2.ex1: He was charged with hijacking and armed robbery.
p2.ex2: The hijacking was resolved peacefully after several hours of negotiation.

p2.en: Who a person is; the qualities that make someone who they are.
p2.example: The thief disguised their identity by wearing a mask and gloves.
p2.ex1: Police confirmed the suspect's identity through DNA evidence.
p2.ex2: She had to prove her identity before the bank would release any information.

p2.en: The crime of using another person's personal information fraudulently.
p2.example: Identity theft can ruin a person's finances and reputation for years.
p2.ex1: She discovered she was a victim of identity theft when a loan appeared in her name.
p2.ex2: Protecting your personal data online helps prevent identity theft.

p2.en: To watch someone or something carefully.
p2.example: The detective asked a colleague to keep an eye on the main suspect.
p2.ex1: She kept an eye on the entrance while her partner examined the back room.
p2.ex2: He was asked to keep an eye on the package until the owner returned.

p2.en: The unlawful killing of another person.
p2.example: The detective was assigned to investigate an apparent murder case.
p2.ex1: She was horrified to learn that a murder had taken place in her street.
p2.ex2: He was convicted of murder and sentenced to life in prison.

p2.en: A person who has killed another person unlawfully.
p2.example: The murderer was finally identified through a DNA match twenty years later.
p2.ex1: She refused to believe her neighbour was the murderer.
p2.ex2: The murderer was caught after leaving forensic evidence at the scene.

p2.en: The act of allowing someone to do something.
p2.example: The hacker accessed private files without permission.
p2.ex1: She entered the building without permission and was detained.
p2.ex2: He insisted he had permission to be there, but no one could verify it.

p2.en: To steal something from a person's pocket without them noticing.
p2.example: A pickpocket picked her pocket on the crowded metro.
p2.ex1: He had his wallet picked in a busy market.
p2.ex2: She warned tourists that pickpockets often work in large crowds.

p2.en: A person who steals from other people's pockets in crowded places.
p2.example: A pickpocket was arrested near the shopping centre entrance.
p2.ex1: She spotted the pickpocket just as he was reaching into her bag.
p2.ex2: The area is known for pickpockets during the busy tourist season.

p2.en: The crime of stealing from people's pockets without them noticing.
p2.example: Pickpocketing is common at busy train stations and tourist sites.
p2.ex1: She was a victim of pickpocketing during the festival.
p2.ex2: The police launched a campaign to reduce pickpocketing in the city centre.

p2.en: To behave as if something is true when it is not.
p2.example: The thief pretended to be a delivery worker to gain access to the building.
p2.ex1: She pretended not to notice the suspect to avoid raising suspicion.
p2.ex2: He pretended to drop something in order to distract the shop assistant.

p2.en: A place where people are kept as punishment for a crime.
p2.example: The robber was sentenced to eight years in prison.
p2.ex1: She visited the prison as part of a rehabilitation programme.
p2.ex2: He was released from prison after serving half of his sentence.

p2.en: The process of asking someone questions, especially as part of a police investigation.
p2.example: The suspect was taken in for questioning but later released without charge.
p2.ex1: She broke down during questioning and admitted what she had seen.
p2.ex2: Hours of questioning failed to produce any new information.

p2.en: To take property from a person or place illegally, often using force.
p2.example: Two men robbed the jewellery store in broad daylight.
p2.ex1: She was robbed at gunpoint while walking home.
p2.ex2: He robbed the same shop twice before being caught on camera.

p2.en: A person who steals from others, often using force or threats.
p2.example: The robber was caught three miles from the scene.
p2.ex1: She gave a description of the robber to the police sketch artist.
p2.ex2: The robber escaped in a car waiting outside.

p2.en: The crime of stealing from a person or place, often with threats or force.
p2.example: The bank robbery was planned over several weeks.
p2.ex1: She was shaken by the robbery that occurred outside her workplace.
p2.ex2: The robbery was caught on three different surveillance cameras.

p2.en: To steal goods from a shop while pretending to be a customer.
p2.example: She was caught shoplifting a necklace and banned from the store.
p2.ex1: He shoplifted regularly for years before being caught.
p2.ex2: The security guard noticed her shoplifting and alerted staff.

p2.en: A person who steals from shops.
p2.example: The shoplifter was detained until the police arrived.
p2.ex1: She was labelled as a shoplifter despite insisting it was a mistake.
p2.ex2: Shoplifters are often caught by hidden cameras throughout the store.

p2.en: The crime of stealing from a shop.
p2.example: Shoplifting costs retailers billions of pounds every year.
p2.ex1: She was charged with shoplifting and given a caution.
p2.ex2: The shop installed extra cameras to deter shoplifting.

p2.en: To say you will harm someone if they do not do what you want.
p2.example: The robber threatened the cashier with a weapon during the hold-up.
p2.ex1: She was threatened by the criminal and too scared to report it.
p2.ex2: He was charged with threatening behaviour as well as robbery.

p2.en: A person who deliberately damages or destroys property.
p2.example: Vandals broke the windows of the community centre overnight.
p2.ex1: She identified the vandal from the footage and reported him.
p2.ex2: The vandal spray-painted graffiti across the entire wall of the building.

p2.en: To deliberately damage or destroy property.
p2.example: The phone box had been vandalised and was no longer working.
p2.ex1: She was horrified to find her car had been vandalised overnight.
p2.ex2: He was arrested for vandalising several shops in the high street.

p2.en: The crime of deliberately damaging public or private property.
p2.example: Vandalism in the park increased during the summer months.
p2.ex1: She reported the vandalism to the council and demanded better lighting.
p2.ex2: Anti-vandalism campaigns helped reduce graffiti in the area.

p2.en: A person who sees a crime or event happen and can give evidence about it.
p2.example: An eyewitness described the robber to the police in detail.
p2.ex1: She was the only eyewitness to the theft and gave a statement.
p2.ex2: The eyewitness account was crucial in securing a conviction.

p1.en: Extra; more than what is already there or expected
p1.example: She received additional punishment for the additional offence committed.
p1.ex1: The criminal record included additional incidents of cyberbullying.
p1.ex2: He faced additional consequences after being caught red-handed again.

p1.en: A person who frightens weaker people; or to frighten someone repeatedly
p1.example: The school bully laughed at younger students and committed daily offences.
p1.ex1: She witnessed the bully mistreat every new student without consequence.
p1.ex2: He was charged after bullying turned into a criminal record incident.

p1.en: Repeated and intentional behaviour that hurts or frightens someone
p1.example: Bullying online is a serious offence that can lead to criminal consequences.
p1.ex1: She stood up for her classmate and reported the bullying incident.
p1.ex2: Witnesses to bullying should speak out rather than turn a blind eye.

p1.en: To do something that is against the law
p1.example: He committed a crime by hacking into the company's login system.
p1.ex1: She witnessed him commit a crime and reported the incident immediately.
p1.ex2: Committing a crime as a minor can still result in a criminal record.

p1.en: A result that follows from an action, often a negative one
p1.example: The consequence of bullying is a criminal record and public shame.
p1.ex1: She faced serious consequences after the upsetting incident was reported.
p1.ex2: Commit a crime and the consequence will be swift punishment.

p1.en: An official list of the crimes someone has been found guilty of
p1.example: He was caught red-handed and immediately received a criminal record.
p1.ex1: The additional offence meant her criminal record was now very serious.
p1.ex2: A criminal record is a life-changing consequence of any committed crime.

p1.en: To gain illegal access to a computer system or account
p1.example: He hacked into the company's login system and committed a serious crime.
p1.ex1: She witnessed the hacker hack into additional accounts without consequence.
p1.ex2: Hacking into a login system is a criminal offence with serious punishment.

p1.en: Especially; more than others of the same type
p1.example: She was upsetting to witness, in particular the bullying incident at school.
p1.ex1: He committed several crimes, in particular hacking into login systems.
p1.ex2: The punishment, in particular the criminal record, had serious consequences.

p1.en: An event, especially an unpleasant or unusual one
p1.example: She witnessed the incident and immediately reported the bullying to staff.
p1.ex1: The upsetting incident involved hacking into a student's login details.
p1.ex2: The incident resulted in a criminal record and additional consequences.

p1.en: To make fun of someone in a mean or unkind way
p1.example: The bully laughed at the victim in front of witnesses without consequence.
p1.ex1: She stood up for her friend when classmates laughed at her.
p1.ex2: Laughing at someone is bullying and can result in serious punishment.

p1.en: The name and password used to access a computer or online account
p1.example: He hacked into her login and committed an additional criminal offence.
p1.ex1: She witnessed the hacker use her login to commit financial crimes.
p1.ex2: Hacking someone's login details is a serious and upsetting criminal offence.

p1.en: To treat someone badly or cruelly
p1.example: The bully mistreated every witness who stood up for the victim.
p1.ex1: She witnessed him mistreat additional students without any consequence.
p1.ex2: Mistreating others is bullying and results in severe criminal punishment.

p1.en: An act that breaks the law or a rule
p1.example: Hacking into a login system is a serious criminal offence.
p1.ex1: He committed an additional offence after his first criminal record.
p1.ex2: The upsetting incident was classified as a cyberbullying offence.

p1.en: To stop a vehicle at the side of the road, especially by police
p1.example: The officer pulled him over after witnessing the upsetting incident.
p1.ex1: She was pulled over behind the wheel for an additional traffic offence.
p1.ex2: He was pulled over and caught red-handed with evidence of the crime.

p1.en: A penalty given to someone who has broken a rule or law
p1.example: The punishment for the bullying offence was a criminal record.
p1.ex1: She faced additional punishment after committing the same crime again.
p1.ex2: A serious consequence and punishment followed the upsetting incident.

p1.en: The way someone responds to something that happens
p1.example: Her reaction to witnessing the bullying was to immediately speak out.
p1.ex1: He had a strong reaction after being pulled over for a traffic offence.
p1.ex2: The witness's reaction to the incident led to serious criminal consequences.

p1.en: To defend or support someone who is being treated badly
p1.example: She stood up for her classmate when the bully laughed at him.
p1.ex1: Witnesses to bullying must stand up for victims and speak out.
p1.ex2: He stood up for his colleague despite the consequences and punishment.

p1.en: A financial or business deal between parties
p1.example: He hacked into her login and made additional criminal transactions.
p1.ex1: She witnessed the upsetting financial transaction and reported the offence.
p1.ex2: The criminal record included evidence of unauthorised login transactions.

p1.en: Causing strong feelings of unhappiness or distress
p1.example: It was upsetting to witness the bullying incident without speaking out.
p1.ex1: She found the criminal record consequences upsetting but necessary.
p1.ex2: The upsetting transaction led to an additional offence and punishment.

p1.en: To see something happen; to be present at an event
p1.example: She witnessed the bully commit the upsetting incident and reported it.
p1.ex1: He witnessed additional offences but turned a blind eye to the consequences.
p1.ex2: Witnessing a crime and not speaking out can have serious consequences.

p1.en: Something that is absolutely necessary or essential
p1.example: Standing up for victims of bullying is a must, not just a good idea.
p1.ex1: Reporting a criminal offence is a must for every responsible witness.
p1.ex2: Speaking out against bullying is a must — better safe than sorry.

p1.en: To be someone's decision or responsibility
p1.example: It is up to every witness to report a bullying offence immediately.
p1.ex1: Whether to speak out or turn a blind eye is up to the individual.
p1.ex2: It is up to the authorities to decide the punishment for each crime.

p1.en: In control of a vehicle; in the act of driving
p1.example: He was pulled over behind the wheel after committing a traffic offence.
p1.ex1: She was caught red-handed behind the wheel without a valid licence.
p1.ex2: Being behind the wheel while distracted is a criminal offence.

p1.en: It is wiser to be cautious than to take risks and regret it
p1.example: Better safe than sorry — always report a bullying incident immediately.
p1.ex1: She spoke out about the offence because better safe than sorry.
p1.ex2: Better safe than sorry — do not turn a blind eye to criminal behaviour.

p1.en: To catch someone in the act of doing something wrong
p1.example: He was caught red-handed hacking into the company's login system.
p1.ex1: She was caught red-handed committing an additional financial transaction.
p1.ex2: The officer caught the bully red-handed mistreating the younger student.

p1.en: To make a different decision from the one you made before
p1.example: She changed her mind and stood up for the victim instead of watching.
p1.ex1: He changed his mind about turning a blind eye to the upsetting incident.
p1.ex2: The witness changed his mind and agreed to speak out about the offence.

p1.en: To end any possibility of doing or achieving something
p1.example: A criminal record can close the door on many important life opportunities.
p1.ex1: She closed the door on the bullying incident by reporting it formally.
p1.ex2: Turning a blind eye closes the door on justice and fair punishment.

p1.en: To accept and deal with the consequences of your own actions
p1.example: He had to face the music after being caught red-handed committing crime.
p1.ex1: She faced the music for her additional offence and accepted the punishment.
p1.ex2: Every bully must eventually face the music for their upsetting behaviour.

p1.en: To laugh at or joke about someone in a cruel or unkind way
p1.example: The bully made fun of the victim in front of every witness at school.
p1.ex1: She stood up for her classmate when they were made fun of.
p1.ex2: Making fun of others is bullying and results in serious punishment.

p1.ru: Не такое большое дело / ничего особенного
p1.en: Used to say that something is not important or serious
p1.example: Witnessing bullying is not no big deal — it is an upsetting offence.
p1.ex1: He thought hacking into a login was no big deal but faced punishment.
p1.ex2: Turning a blind eye is not no big deal — it has serious consequences.

p1.ru: Как гром среди ясного неба / неожиданно
p1.en: Happening suddenly and unexpectedly without any warning
p1.example: Out of the blue, the witness spoke out about the upsetting incident.
p1.ex1: The criminal record appeared out of the blue after the first offence.
p1.ex2: The punishment came out of the blue and had serious additional consequences.

p1.en: To say publicly what you think about something, especially a wrong
p1.example: She spoke out about the bullying incident despite the consequences.
p1.ex1: Witnesses must speak out about criminal offences rather than watch.
p1.ex2: Speaking out against bullying is a must — better safe than sorry.

p1.en: To deliberately ignore something wrong that is happening
p1.example: He turned a blind eye to the upsetting bullying incident at school.
p1.ex1: Turning a blind eye to a criminal offence has serious consequences.
p1.ex2: Witnesses who turn a blind eye allow bullying to continue unchecked.

p2.en: To say that someone has done something wrong or illegal
p2.example: She was accused of hacking into an additional login account.
p2.ex1: He was accused of committing the offence caught on a CCTV camera.
p2.ex2: The suspect was accused of the crime despite having a strong alibi.

p2.en: To take someone into police custody because of a suspected crime
p2.example: He was arrested for hacking into multiple login systems.
p2.ex1: She was arrested for the cybercrime offence caught on CCTV camera.
p2.ex2: The neighbourhood watch helped arrest the suspect for the crime.

p2.en: To officially say that something is not allowed
p2.example: The authorities banned the suspect from the area after the offence.
p2.ex1: She was banned from additional online transactions after the cybercrime.
p2.ex2: The court banned him from driving after his third criminal record.

p2.en: To actively look out for suspicious or criminal behaviour
p2.example: The neighbourhood watch was on watch for any suspicious criminal activity.
p2.ex1: She was on watch near the CCTV camera when the incident occurred.
p2.ex2: Officers were on watch and arrested the suspect red-handed.

p2.en: To say or think that someone is responsible for something bad
p2.example: She was blamed for the cybercrime despite having a strong alibi.
p2.ex1: He was blamed for the additional offence caught on the CCTV camera.
p2.ex2: The authorities blamed the scammer for the rising local crime rate.

p2.en: To find someone doing something wrong at the very moment they do it
p2.example: He was caught in the act of hacking into the company's login.
p2.ex1: The neighbourhood watch caught the suspect in the act near the CCTV.
p2.ex2: She was caught in the act and immediately charged with the offence.

p2.en: A camera used to record activity in public places for security
p2.example: The CCTV camera recorded the suspect committing the additional offence.
p2.ex1: She was caught in the act on a CCTV camera near the neighbourhood watch.
p2.ex2: Without CCTV camera evidence, it was difficult to prove the crime.

p2.en: To formally accuse someone of a crime so they can be tried
p2.example: He was charged with the cybercrime after the CCTV camera evidence.
p2.ex1: She was charged with hacking into additional login accounts.
p2.ex2: The suspect was charged with the offence after the neighbourhood watch report.

p2.en: A feeling of worry about something; something that worries you
p2.example: The rising crime rate was a major concern for the neighbourhood watch.
p2.ex1: She expressed concern about the lack of CCTV cameras in the area.
p2.ex2: His concern about privacy was set against the need to prevent crime.

p2.en: The number of crimes committed in an area over a period of time
p2.example: The neighbourhood watch significantly reduced the local crime rate.
p2.ex1: She was concerned about the rising crime rate despite the CCTV cameras.
p2.ex2: A high crime rate is a major concern for the local authorities.

p2.en: An attempt to damage or gain illegal access to a computer system
p2.example: The company suffered a major cyberattack on its login systems.
p2.ex1: She reported the cyberattack to the authorities and provided CCTV evidence.
p2.ex2: Cybercrime and cyberattacks increase the local digital crime rate.

p2.en: To try to stop someone from doing something; to reduce enthusiasm
p2.example: CCTV cameras discourage criminals from committing offences nearby.
p2.ex1: She discouraged the suspect from additional criminal transactions.
p2.ex2: The neighbourhood watch discouraged crime and reduced the crime rate.

p2.en: To officially decide that someone has committed a crime
p2.example: He was found guilty of the cybercrime based on CCTV camera evidence.
p2.ex1: She was found guilty of the additional offence and charged accordingly.
p2.ex2: The court found him guilty despite his claim of having an alibi.

p2.en: To officially decide that someone has not committed a crime
p2.example: She was found innocent after the alibi was confirmed by witnesses.
p2.ex1: He was found innocent because the CCTV camera proved his alibi.
p2.ex2: The suspect was found innocent of the additional cybercrime charge.

p2.en: To make someone pay money as a punishment for breaking a rule
p2.example: He was fined for the additional traffic offence caught on CCTV.
p2.ex1: She was fined by the authorities for the minor criminal record incident.
p2.ex2: The authorities fined the company after the cyberattack was discovered.

p2.en: To officially say that something must not be done
p2.example: The authorities forbid any additional criminal transactions online.
p2.ex1: She was forbidden from approaching the neighbourhood watch area.
p2.ex2: The court forbade the suspect from hacking into any login system.

p2.en: To speak formally to an audience about a particular topic
p2.example: She gave a speech about the dangers of cybercrime and rising crime rates.
p2.ex1: He gave a speech at the neighbourhood watch meeting about CCTV cameras.
p2.ex2: The authorities gave a speech about preventing cyberattacks and offences.

p2.en: To be able to prove you were elsewhere when a crime was committed
p2.example: She had an alibi and was found innocent of the additional offence.
p2.ex1: He had an alibi confirmed by CCTV camera footage from the area.
p2.ex2: The suspect claimed to have an alibi but the neighbourhood watch disagreed.

p2.en: To regularly check or observe something over a period of time
p2.example: The authorities monitored the crime rate using CCTV cameras.
p2.ex1: She monitored the suspect's additional login activity for evidence.
p2.ex2: The neighbourhood watch monitored suspicious activity near the area.

p2.en: An organised group of local residents who watch for and report crime
p2.example: The neighbourhood watch helped reduce the local crime rate significantly.
p2.ex1: She joined the neighbourhood watch after a cyberattack in the area.
p2.ex2: The neighbourhood watch reported the suspect to the authorities.

p2.en: A person who happens to be walking past a place
p2.example: A passer-by witnessed the incident and reported it to the authorities.
p2.ex1: She was a passer-by who was caught on CCTV camera near the offence.
p2.ex2: The passer-by gave a speech at the neighbourhood watch meeting.

p2.en: A group that regularly walks through an area to prevent crime; or to do this
p2.example: The neighbourhood watch patrolled the area near the CCTV cameras.
p2.ex1: She patrolled on behalf of the authorities to reduce the crime rate.
p2.ex2: A regular patrol discourages crime and helps catch suspects red-handed.

p2.en: Something that might happen or be true; a chance
p2.example: There is a possibility that the suspect will be found innocent.
p2.ex1: She raised the possibility of a cyberattack at the neighbourhood watch.
p2.ex2: The possibility of being caught on CCTV discouraged additional offences.

p2.en: A person who is kept in prison as a punishment for a crime
p2.example: He was sent to prison as a prisoner after being found guilty.
p2.ex1: The prisoner was charged with the additional cybercrime offence.
p2.ex2: A prisoner with a criminal record faces serious long-term consequences.

p2.en: The right to keep your personal information and life private
p2.example: She raised concerns about privacy in relation to CCTV camera monitoring.
p2.ex1: The cyberattack seriously violated her digital privacy and login security.
p2.ex2: Privacy is a major concern when using CCTV cameras in public areas.

p2.en: To show or demonstrate that something is true
p2.example: The CCTV camera footage proved the suspect was guilty of the offence.
p2.ex1: She proved she had an alibi and was found innocent.
p2.ex2: The authorities struggled to prove the cyberattack beyond reasonable doubt.

p2.ru: При условии что / при условии если
p2.en: On the condition that something is the case
p2.example: The suspect will be set free provided that the alibi holds up.
p2.ex1: She can avoid prison providing that no additional offences are committed.
p2.ex2: Provided that the CCTV camera evidence is clear, he will be found guilty.

p2.en: To capture something on film, audio or in writing
p2.example: The CCTV camera recorded the suspect committing the criminal offence.
p2.ex1: She recorded the additional transaction as evidence for the authorities.
p2.ex2: The neighbourhood watch recorded every suspicious incident in the area.

p2.en: To change the planned time of something to a different time
p2.example: The court appearance was rescheduled after the suspect found an alibi.
p2.ex1: She rescheduled the neighbourhood watch patrol due to an incident.
p2.ex2: The authorities rescheduled the trial after additional CCTV evidence emerged.

p2.en: To release someone from prison or captivity
p2.example: The prisoner was set free after the alibi was confirmed.
p2.ex1: She was set free provided that she committed no additional offences.
p2.ex2: The authorities set him free when the CCTV camera proved his innocence.

p2.ru: Не выходить на улицы / держаться подальше
p2.en: To avoid going out in public, especially in dangerous areas
p2.example: The authorities advised residents to stay off the streets during the patrol.
p2.ex1: She stayed off the streets after the neighbourhood watch warned of crime.
p2.ex2: Criminals are less likely to offend if residents stay off the streets.

p2.en: Used to consider a situation that might happen or be true
p2.example: Suppose the suspect has a strong alibi — would he still be found guilty?
p2.ex1: Supposing the CCTV camera evidence is inconclusive, what happens next?
p2.ex2: Suppose the authorities cannot prove the offence — the prisoner is set free.

p2.en: Causing a feeling that something wrong or illegal is happening
p2.example: The neighbourhood watch reported several suspicious additional incidents.
p2.ex1: She felt suspicious when the login was accessed from an unknown device.
p2.ex2: The CCTV camera captured a suspicious individual near the crime scene.

p2.en: To start legal proceedings against someone
p2.example: She took the scammer to court after the cyberattack on her login.
p2.ex1: The authorities took the suspect to court after the CCTV evidence.
p2.ex2: The victim took the bully to court for the additional criminal offences.

p2.en: To think very carefully before doing something risky
p2.example: She thought twice before reporting the incident to the neighbourhood watch.
p2.ex1: Think twice before hacking into someone's login — the consequences are severe.
p2.ex2: CCTV cameras make criminals think twice before committing any offence.

p2.en: Having plenty of light; bright and clearly visible
p2.example: A well-lit area discourages crime and supports neighbourhood watch efforts.
p2.ex1: She felt safer walking through the well-lit street near the CCTV camera.
p2.ex2: Well-lit public areas with CCTV cameras significantly reduce crime rates.

p3.en: To total a particular amount when combined
p3.example: The additional fines and penalties add up to a major financial consequence.
p3.ex1: Her criminal record added up to three separate offences over a year.
p3.ex2: The evidence added up to a convincing case that he committed the crime.

p3.en: A seat in a public place; or the judge's seat in a courtroom
p3.example: The suspect sat on the bench outside the court before the hearing.
p3.ex1: She sat on the bench and witnessed the investigation from a distance.
p3.ex2: The judge on the bench declared him innocent despite the CCTV evidence.

p3.en: The way someone behaves, especially in a formal or official setting
p3.example: His conduct during the investigation was suspicious and upsetting.
p3.ex1: The authorities investigated the suspect's conduct on CCTV footage.
p3.ex2: Good conduct in court can reduce the penalty and additional charges.

p3.en: Seeming likely to be true; making you believe something is real
p3.example: The scammer's fake story was convincing enough to deceive many victims.
p3.ex1: She presented a convincing case with CCTV footage and investigation notes.
p3.ex2: A convincing alibi made the authorities reconsider the additional charge.

p3.en: Not genuine; made to look real but actually false or fraudulent
