p3.example: The scammer used a fake login to commit additional financial offences.
p3.ex1: She reported the fake transaction to the authorities after the cyberattack.
p3.ex2: The investigation revealed that the convincing evidence was entirely fake.

p3.en: The paper or plastic packaging around a food item
p3.example: She littered a food wrapper near the bench and was fined by authorities.
p3.ex1: The investigation found the suspect's food wrapper near the CCTV camera.
p3.ex2: Dropping a food wrapper is a minor offence that carries a penalty.

p3.en: A picture; or the impression someone creates in others' minds
p3.example: The CCTV camera captured a clear image of the suspect near the scene.
p3.ex1: She used a fake image to create a convincing scam account online.
p3.ex2: The investigation relied on the image from the neighbourhood watch footage.

p3.en: A careful examination of facts to find out what happened
p3.example: The investigation revealed convincing evidence of a major cyberattack.
p3.ex1: She cooperated fully with the investigation to avoid additional charges.
p3.ex2: CCTV camera footage played a major role in the criminal investigation.

p3.en: To throw rubbish on the ground in a public place
p3.example: He littered a food wrapper near the bench and was fined on the spot.
p3.ex1: The authorities warned that littering carries a significant financial penalty.
p3.ex2: She was caught on CCTV camera littering near the neighbourhood watch area.

p3.en: A punishment given for breaking a rule or law
p3.example: The penalty for littering near a public bench is a significant fine.
p3.ex1: She faced an additional penalty after the investigation found new evidence.
p3.ex2: The judge on the bench increased the penalty based on the CCTV footage.

p3.en: To identify someone or something from past knowledge
p3.example: She recognised the scammer from the fake image in the investigation.
p3.ex1: He was recognised by a passer-by who had witnessed the earlier incident.
p3.ex2: The neighbourhood watch recognised the suspect from previous CCTV footage.

p3.en: A dishonest plan to get money from people; or to use such a plan
p3.example: The convincing scam involved fake login pages and additional cyberattacks.
p3.ex1: She reported the scam to the authorities and provided investigation evidence.
p3.ex2: The scammer's image was captured on CCTV committing the financial scam.

p3.en: A person who uses dishonest methods to get money from others
p3.example: The scammer created convincing fake accounts to commit financial crimes.
p3.ex1: She recognised the scammer from the investigation's CCTV camera footage.
p3.ex2: The authorities arrested the scammer for multiple criminal scam offences.

p3.en: The state of being important or having great significance
p3.example: The judge emphasised the seriousness of the criminal record and offences.
p3.ex1: She expressed the seriousness of the cyberattack during her investigation.
p3.ex2: The seriousness of the scam convinced the court to increase the penalty.

p3.en: The people or organisations with official power to make decisions
p3.example: The authorities investigated the convincing scam using CCTV footage.
p3.ex1: She reported the fake transaction to the authorities immediately.
p3.ex2: The authorities imposed additional penalties based on the investigation findings.

p3.en: Young people collectively; or a person in their early years
p3.example: Youth crime is a major concern that adds up to a high local crime rate.
p3.ex1: She gave a speech about the seriousness of scams targeting the youth.
p3.ex2: The investigation revealed that the scammer targeted vulnerable youth online.

p1.en: A person's signature, especially that of a celebrity written for a fan as a souvenir.
p1.example: After the concert, dozens of fans waited for the singer's autograph.
p1.ex1: She kept the actor's autograph in a frame on her wall.
p1.ex2: The footballer signed autographs for every child outside the stadium.

p1.en: Causing or feeling embarrassment or inconvenience; not smooth or graceful.
p1.example: There was an awkward silence when nobody knew what to say next.
p1.ex1: It felt awkward meeting my ex at the party.
p1.ex2: He gave an awkward smile and quickly changed the subject.

p1.en: Unable to see; or (figuratively) to prevent someone from seeing or thinking clearly.
p1.example: Fame can blind a person to what truly matters in life.
p1.ex1: Success sometimes blinds people to the needs of others.
p1.ex2: She was blind to his faults because she admired him so much.

p1.en: An event where an author signs copies of their book for readers, usually in a bookshop or library.
p1.example: The author held a book signing at a local bookshop after her novel was released.
p1.ex1: Hundreds of fans queued for the book signing event downtown.
p1.ex2: She was nervous before her first ever book signing.

p1.en: A strong belief that something will happen or that someone will achieve a certain standard.
p1.example: The film failed to meet the high expectations of its audience.
p1.ex1: She felt pressure from her parents' expectations.
p1.ex2: Living up to public expectation is one of the hardest parts of fame.

p1.en: The state of being known or recognised by many people, usually for an achievement or talent.
p1.example: She rose to fame after her first album became a worldwide hit.
p1.ex1: Fame brought him both opportunities and personal difficulties.
p1.ex2: Many young people dream of fame but underestimate its pressures.

p1.en: Something, especially a film or show, that is completely unsuccessful.
p1.example: Despite the huge budget, the film was a total flop at the box office.
p1.ex1: Her second novel was considered a flop by critics.
p1.ex2: Not every project succeeds — even great artists have flops.

p1.en: To make someone feel annoyed or upset because they cannot achieve what they want.
p1.example: Constant media attention began to frustrate the young star.
p1.ex1: It frustrated him that his ideas were never taken seriously.
p1.ex2: Slow progress can frustrate even the most patient performer.

p1.en: To deal with a situation or person in a particular way, especially a difficult one.
p1.example: Not every celebrity can handle the pressure of constant public attention.
p1.ex1: She handled the criticism with great maturity.
p1.ex2: Learning to handle failure is essential for any performer.

p1.en: Providing a lot of useful or interesting information.
p1.example: The documentary was both entertaining and highly informative.
p1.ex1: Her talk was so informative that everyone took notes.
p1.ex2: The guide wrote an informative article about life backstage.

p1.en: Making people feel motivated, enthusiastic, or full of creative energy.
p1.example: Her speech was deeply inspiring and moved the entire audience to tears.
p1.ex1: He found the artist's journey incredibly inspiring.
p1.ex2: Inspiring role models can change the direction of a young person's life.

p1.en: To send a written message to someone, especially via a phone or online platform.
p1.example: Thousands of fans messaged the singer after she posted about her new tour.
p1.ex1: She messaged her agent as soon as she heard the audition result.
p1.ex2: He messaged all his contacts to share the exciting news.

p1.en: An organisation that uses its income to pursue its goals rather than to make a profit for owners.
p1.example: The actor set up a non-profit organisation to support young artists.
p1.ex1: She donated all the proceeds to a non-profit organisation.
p1.ex2: Non-profit organisations often rely on volunteers and public donations.

p1.en: Happening very suddenly or within a very short time; during or for the night.
p1.example: The video went viral and she became an overnight sensation.
p1.ex1: Overnight success is rare — most stars work for years before being noticed.
p1.ex2: His overnight rise to fame surprised even his closest friends.

p1.en: Used to emphasise that something is genuine, real, or to a great degree.
p1.example: She was truly grateful for all the support she received from her fans.
p1.ex1: It was a truly unforgettable performance.
p1.ex2: He truly believed that hard work would lead to success.

p1.en: If something crosses your mind, you think of it briefly or it occurs to you suddenly.
p1.example: It never crossed my mind that she would quit the show so soon.
p1.ex1: Did it ever cross your mind that fame might change everything?
p1.ex2: The idea of giving up never once crossed his mind.

p1.en: A situation where every seat in a theatre, cinema, or venue is occupied.
p1.example: The band performed to a full house on the opening night of their world tour.
p1.ex1: Every performance this week has been a full house.
p1.ex2: Getting a full house for a debut show is every artist's dream.

p1.en: To start or begin to succeed after a difficult or slow beginning.
p1.example: The project took months to get off the ground due to a lack of funding.
p1.ex1: Their music career finally got off the ground after years of effort.
p1.ex2: Without public support, the campaign couldn't get off the ground.

p1.en: Receiving a lot of public attention or being the focus of interest.
p1.example: Being in the spotlight constantly is one of the hardest things about celebrity life.
p1.ex1: She thrives when she's in the spotlight.
p1.ex2: After winning the award, he found himself constantly in the spotlight.

p1.en: Feeling extremely happy and successful.
p1.example: After receiving a standing ovation, she felt on top of the world.
p1.ex1: Winning his first award made him feel on top of the world.
p1.ex2: She described feeling on top of the world after her debut performance.

p1.en: Beyond control; in a way that can no longer be managed or stopped.
p1.example: The media attention got completely out of hand after the video went viral.
p1.ex1: Security had to intervene when the crowd got out of hand.
p1.ex2: Fame can get out of hand quickly if you're not prepared for it.

p2.en: Full of exciting events or activity, used especially to describe films or stories.
p2.example: The film was action-packed from the very first scene to the final credits.
p2.ex1: They spent an action-packed weekend at the adventure park.
p2.ex2: Critics praised the action-packed plot of the summer blockbuster.

p2.en: A trial performance to assess whether someone is suitable for a role in a show, film, or band.
p2.example: She auditioned for the lead role three times before finally being cast.
p2.ex1: Hundreds of actors showed up to audition for the new drama series.
p2.ex2: His audition impressed the directors so much that they offered him the part immediately.

p2.en: The area behind or to the side of the stage in a theatre, not visible to the audience.
p2.example: The journalist was given a backstage pass to observe the show from behind the scenes.
p2.ex1: The performers gathered backstage before their entrance.
p2.ex2: Backstage, everyone was nervous despite looking calm in front of the cameras.

p2.en: A film, book, or other product that is hugely successful and very popular commercially.
p2.example: The studio invested over $200 million into their latest summer blockbuster.
p2.ex1: Every director dreams of making a blockbuster that defines a generation.
p2.ex2: The blockbuster broke box office records in its opening weekend.

p2.uz: qo'lga olmoq, suratga olmoq; ifodalab bermoq
p2.en: To record or represent something accurately; to attract and hold attention or imagination.
p2.example: The documentary perfectly captures the excitement of life on a film set.
p2.ex1: The photographer managed to capture the emotion of the moment.
p2.ex2: A great performance can capture the audience's hearts within seconds.

p2.en: All the actors and performers who appear in a film, play, or television programme.
p2.example: The film had an impressive cast including several Oscar-winning actors.
p2.ex1: The entire cast gathered on stage to take a bow after the final show.
p2.ex2: Casting the right people is one of the most important decisions a director makes.

p2.en: A famous person, especially one in entertainment, sport, or the media.
p2.example: The charity event attracted several celebrities from the world of film and music.
p2.ex1: Being a celebrity means your private life is constantly under public scrutiny.
p2.ex2: She became a celebrity almost overnight after her debut film was released.

p2.en: A formal public event held to mark an important occasion, such as an award show.
p2.example: The awards ceremony was broadcast live to millions of viewers around the world.
p2.ex1: She wore a stunning gown to the film industry's biggest ceremony.
p2.ex2: The opening ceremony of the festival attracted thousands of visitors.

p2.en: A person or organisation that uses the professional services of another, such as an agent or lawyer.
p2.example: The talent agent worked hard to find the best roles for her most famous client.
p2.ex1: Every client of the agency was a well-known name in the entertainment industry.
p2.ex2: He signed a contract with a new manager who had impressive clients on her list.

p2.en: The use of something (e.g. a photo, song, or video) in a way intended to generate profit.
p2.example: The photographer's contract prevented the studio from using the images for commercial use.
p2.ex1: Any song used for commercial use requires a proper licence.
p2.ex2: She discovered her image had been used for commercial use without her permission.

p2.en: A formal legal agreement between two or more parties, especially one in writing.
p2.example: The young actress signed a five-year contract with a major Hollywood studio.
p2.ex1: Always read a contract carefully before putting your signature on it.
p2.ex2: His contract included clauses about social media use and public appearances.

p2.en: To be in charge of making a film, play, or programme and supervise the actors and crew.
p2.example: She decided to direct her own short film after years of working as an actress.
p2.ex1: It takes great skill to direct a large-scale musical production.
p2.ex2: He will direct his third feature film later this year.

p2.en: The chief female character in a story, film, or play; or a woman admired for courage or achievements.
p2.example: The film's heroine overcomes enormous obstacles to save her community.
p2.ex1: She became the heroine of the story when she risked everything for the truth.
p2.ex2: Many young girls admired the confident heroine of the fantasy series.

p2.en: The words of a song.
p2.example: The songwriter spent months perfecting the lyrics of each track on the album.
p2.ex1: Fans memorised every line of the lyrics within hours of the song's release.
p2.ex2: The lyrics spoke about loss and hope in a way that resonated with millions.

p2.en: A special or important event or time; a suitable opportunity.
p2.example: The film premiere was a glamorous occasion attended by the world's biggest stars.
p2.ex1: She dressed elegantly, knowing it was a formal occasion.
p2.ex2: Award nights are occasions when the whole industry comes together to celebrate.

p2.en: Photographers who follow celebrities around to take pictures of them, often intrusively.
p2.example: The paparazzi gathered outside the hotel hoping to photograph the famous couple.
p2.ex1: She wore sunglasses and a hat to avoid being spotted by the paparazzi.
p2.ex2: The paparazzi followed him everywhere after his film became a global hit.

p2.en: A role played by an actor in a film, play, or television show.
p2.example: She auditioned for every available part until she finally landed a leading role.
p2.ex1: Playing the part of a villain was a completely new challenge for him.
p2.ex2: The director said it was the most difficult part to cast in the entire production.

p2.en: The act of entertaining an audience by acting, singing, dancing, or playing music.
p2.example: Her performance in the lead role earned her a nomination for Best Actress.
p2.ex1: The audience gave the cast a standing ovation after their final performance.
p2.ex2: His performance was so convincing that many forgot they were watching an actor.

p2.en: A person who entertains an audience by acting, singing, dancing, or other performance arts.
p2.example: She is one of the most talented live performers in the music industry today.
p2.ex1: A skilled performer knows how to read and respond to their audience.
p2.ex2: The young performer wowed the judges with her energy and stage presence.

p2.en: A small raised platform on which a person stands when giving a speech or receiving an award.
p2.example: She walked to the podium to accept her award, visibly moved by the applause.
p2.ex1: Standing at the podium, he thanked his family and the entire cast.
p2.ex2: The director stepped onto the podium and addressed the crowd with confidence.

p2.en: The first public showing of a new film, often attended by its cast and other celebrities.
p2.example: Hundreds of fans lined the red carpet at the film's premiere in Los Angeles.
p2.ex1: The director flew in from abroad to attend the premiere of his latest work.
p2.ex2: Critics and journalists gathered at the premiere hoping to interview the cast.

p2.en: A person responsible for the financial and managerial aspects of a film, show, or music project.
p2.example: The producer secured funding for the film and oversaw the entire production process.
p2.ex1: She worked as a producer on several award-winning documentaries.
p2.ex2: A good producer knows how to bring together the right creative team.

p2.en: Acknowledgement or appreciation of someone's work, achievements, or abilities.
p2.example: After years of hard work, she finally received the recognition she truly deserved.
p2.ex1: Winning the award brought him international recognition.
p2.ex2: She continued her work without seeking recognition or praise.

p2.en: A part of a film, play, or story in which the action takes place in one location or at one time.
p2.example: The opening scene of the film immediately drew the audience in.
p2.ex1: She had to film the same scene fifteen times before the director was satisfied.
p2.ex2: That scene where they say goodbye is the most emotional moment in the entire film.

p2.en: The scenery, furniture, and background used on stage or in a film to represent the place where the action occurs.
p2.example: The set was designed to look like a 1920s Paris street.
p2.ex1: All cast members were expected on set by 6 a.m.
p2.ex2: The set designer won an award for the stunning visuals she created.

p2.en: A single photograph or a continuous piece of film recorded by a camera without stopping.
p2.example: The director wanted one perfect wide shot to open the film.
p2.ex1: It took three hours to get the right shot of the sunset behind the mountains.
p2.ex2: The final shot of the film left the audience speechless.

p2.en: To have the most important role in a film, play, or television programme.
p2.example: The film stars two of the most celebrated actors of their generation.
p2.ex1: She will star in an upcoming thriller set in post-war Europe.
p2.ex2: He starred in over thirty films before winning his first major award.

p2.en: To produce liquid through the skin due to heat or effort; figuratively, to work very hard or worry.
p2.example: She sweated over every detail of her performance for weeks before the premiere.
p2.ex1: He could feel himself sweating as he waited backstage for his cue.
p2.ex2: Don't sweat the small details — focus on delivering an honest performance.

p2.en: A person who finds work and negotiates contracts on behalf of actors, musicians, or other performers.
p2.example: Her talent agent secured her a role in a major Hollywood production.
p2.ex1: A good talent agent can transform the career of a promising young performer.
p2.ex2: He signed with a new talent agent after his old deal expired.

p2.en: Not known, definite, or decided; feeling doubt about something.
p2.example: The future of the project remained uncertain after the lead actor withdrew.
p2.ex1: She felt uncertain about accepting the offer without reading the contract.
p2.ex2: Life in the entertainment industry can be exciting but deeply uncertain.

p2.en: To be known to or watched by the general public; to receive a lot of media attention.
p2.example: Being in the public eye means every mistake you make is reported in the press.
p2.ex1: She has been in the public eye since her debut role at the age of nineteen.
p2.ex2: Those who are in the public eye must be especially careful about their behaviour.

p2.en: Out of public view; referring to the hidden work that makes something happen.
p2.example: A huge team works hard behind the scenes to make every live show a success.
p2.ex1: Behind the scenes, the producers were dealing with serious budget problems.
p2.ex2: The documentary gave viewers a rare look at what happens behind the scenes of a film set.

p2.en: A theatrical expression used to wish a performer good luck before a show.
p2.example: Before she walked on stage, her co-star whispered, 'Break a leg!'
p2.ex1: It's a tradition in the theatre to say 'break a leg' rather than 'good luck'.
p2.ex2: All her friends texted her 'break a leg' before the opening night.

p2.en: The entertainment industry, including film, theatre, music, and television.
p2.example: She entered show business as a child dancer and never looked back.
p2.ex1: Show business can be glamorous, but it demands enormous personal sacrifices.
p2.ex2: His father always said, 'There's no business like show business.'

p2.en: To attract the most attention and admiration in a performance or event.
p2.example: The young supporting actress completely stole the show at the awards ceremony.
p2.ex1: His unforgettable dance routine stole the show at the talent competition.
p2.ex2: Even in a small role, she managed to steal the show every single night.

p2.en: A phrase referring to the cinema or films, as opposed to television or other screens.
p2.example: The beloved novel was finally brought to the big screen after ten years of development.
p2.ex1: Watching an epic film on the big screen is a completely different experience.
p2.ex2: She had always dreamed of seeing her story told on the big screen.

p2.en: A phrase meaning that a performance or activity must continue despite difficulties or problems.
p2.example: Despite the lead actor falling ill, the director insisted: the show must go on.
p2.ex1: Even after the technical failure, the cast remained calm — the show must go on.
p2.ex2: In show business, people learn early that no matter what happens, the show must go on.

p1.en: To officially give someone a prize, money, or honour in recognition of their achievement.
p1.example: She was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature for her extraordinary body of work.
p1.ex1: The film was awarded three Oscars at this year's ceremony.
p1.ex2: The committee decided to award him a special prize for lifetime achievement.

p1.en: A mixture of different things combined together to form a new whole.
p1.example: The novel was a brilliant blend of fantasy and historical fiction.
p1.ex1: Her writing style is a unique blend of humour and deep emotion.
p1.ex2: The film's soundtrack was a perfect blend of classical and modern music.

p1.en: The power, skill, or ability to do something.
p1.example: The young inventor showed an extraordinary capability for solving complex problems.
p1.ex1: Modern technology has expanded the capability of scientists to explore space.
p1.ex2: She never doubted her own capability to succeed in the field of journalism.

p1.en: A group or class of people or things that share similar qualities or characteristics.
p1.example: Her novel was shortlisted in the Best Fiction category at the national book awards.
p1.ex1: The awards ceremony had twelve different categories this year.
p1.ex2: Science fiction is the most popular category in our school library.

p1.en: The period of time when someone is a child, from birth to adolescence.
p1.example: Many great authors draw on memories from their childhood when writing their stories.
p1.ex1: His childhood in a small town inspired the setting of his most famous novel.
p1.ex2: She had a happy childhood filled with books, music, and adventure.

p1.en: To join or merge two or more things together to form a single thing.
p1.example: The author skilfully combines humour and tragedy throughout the novel.
p1.ex1: She managed to combine a career in journalism with raising a family.
p1.ex2: The scientist combined two different compounds to create an entirely new material.

p1.en: Something given or done to help achieve or improve something; a part played in a result.
p1.example: Her contribution to the field of literature was recognised with a lifetime achievement award.
p1.ex1: Every member of the team made a significant contribution to the project.
p1.ex2: His contribution to science changed the way we understand the universe.

p1.en: A strong desire to know or learn about something.
p1.example: A sense of curiosity is one of the most important qualities a writer can have.
p1.ex1: It was her natural curiosity that led her to investigate the strange disappearance.
p1.ex2: Children learn best when their curiosity is encouraged rather than suppressed.

p1.en: Eager to know or learn something; showing a desire to explore and find things out.
p1.example: He was always curious about how things worked, which eventually made him a great inventor.
p1.ex1: She gave him a curious look when he mentioned the mysterious package.
p1.ex2: Being curious about the world around you is the first step to becoming a scientist.

p1.en: The permanent end of life; the act or fact of dying.
p1.example: The death of his mentor inspired the writer to complete the novel they had worked on together.
p1.ex1: The poem explored themes of love, loss, and death with great sensitivity.
p1.ex2: After her death, her unpublished manuscripts were discovered and released to the public.

p1.en: An official document awarded by an educational institution to confirm the completion of a course of study.
p1.example: She received her journalism diploma after four years of dedicated study.
p1.ex1: He proudly hung his diploma on the wall of his new office.
p1.ex2: Earning a diploma in creative writing gave her the confidence to pursue her first novel.

p1.en: The feeling of pleasure or satisfaction from doing or experiencing something.
p1.example: She wrote purely for the enjoyment of storytelling, never expecting to be published.
p1.ex1: Reading for enjoyment is one of the best habits a child can develop.
p1.ex2: The audience's enjoyment of the performance was clear from their enthusiastic applause.

p1.en: To set up or start something on a firm or permanent basis; to show or prove something.
p1.example: She established herself as one of the leading voices in contemporary fiction.
p1.ex1: The organisation was established to support young writers from disadvantaged backgrounds.
p1.ex2: It took years of hard work to establish his reputation as a serious journalist.

p1.en: Not including; leaving out a particular person or thing.
p1.example: All the reviews were positive except for one critic who found the ending too predictable.
p1.ex1: Everyone came to the award ceremony except for the author herself.
p1.ex2: The book was well-structured except for the final chapter, which felt rushed.

p1.en: Unusually good or impressive; outstanding in quality or ability.
p1.example: Her exceptional talent for storytelling was recognised from a very early age.
p1.ex1: The committee agreed it was an exceptional piece of writing unlike anything they had read before.
p1.ex2: He was an exceptional student who consistently outperformed his peers.

p1.en: A genre of fiction involving imaginary worlds, magic, or supernatural elements; or the act of imagining impossible or unlikely things.
p1.example: The fantasy novel transported readers to a magical kingdom ruled by ancient dragons.
p1.ex1: Her love of fantasy began when she read her first adventure story at the age of seven.
p1.ex2: Science fiction and fantasy are among the most popular genres in modern literature.

p1.en: An area of study, activity, or work; a subject or domain of expertise.
p1.example: She dedicated her entire career to the field of environmental journalism.
p1.ex1: Einstein made a groundbreaking contribution to the field of theoretical physics.
p1.ex2: Breaking into a competitive field like literature requires both talent and persistence.

p1.en: The town or city where a person was born or grew up.
p1.example: The author returned to her home town to research the setting for her latest novel.
p1.ex1: He dedicated his first book to the people of his home town who had supported him.
p1.ex2: Her home town inspired the fictional village at the centre of her bestselling series.

p1.en: To have a strong effect on someone or something.
p1.example: Her debut novel impacted millions of readers around the world and sparked important conversations.
p1.ex1: How does social media impact the way stories are shared and consumed today?
p1.ex2: The discovery impacted the scientific community in ways no one had anticipated.

p1.en: Lacking the ability, skill, or quality needed to do something.
p1.example: He seemed incapable of writing anything that was not deeply personal and emotionally raw.
p1.ex1: She felt incapable of finishing the manuscript after losing her notes.
p1.ex2: Some critics said the director was incapable of handling such a complex story.

p1.en: An organisation or establishment, especially one that is important in society, such as a university, school, or government body.
p1.example: The library is one of the most important cultural institutions in any civilised society.
p1.ex1: She studied at a prestigious literary institution before publishing her first collection.
p1.ex2: The award is given annually by a well-respected international literary institution.

p1.en: A person who creates or designs something entirely new for the first time.
p1.example: Thomas Edison is one of the most celebrated inventors in the history of science and technology.
p1.ex1: She grew up wanting to be an inventor and eventually patented her own design.
p1.ex2: The inventor spent decades developing a solution to a problem no one else had noticed.

p1.en: The activity or profession of writing, editing, and reporting news for newspapers, magazines, television, or online media.
p1.example: She pursued a career in journalism because she believed in the power of the truth.
p1.ex1: Investigative journalism plays a vital role in holding powerful people accountable.
p1.ex2: His early interest in storytelling led him naturally into the world of journalism.

p1.en: The period during which someone is alive; the duration of a person's life.
p1.example: She spent a lifetime devoted to writing and was finally celebrated at the age of eighty.
p1.ex1: Meeting his literary hero was a once-in-a-lifetime experience he would never forget.
p1.ex2: The award was given in recognition of his lifetime of contribution to literature.

p1.en: The words of a script that an actor must memorise and perform; or rows of text in writing.
p1.example: She stayed up all night learning her lines before the opening performance.
p1.ex1: He forgot his lines during the first rehearsal but recovered brilliantly on opening night.
p1.ex2: The director told the cast to memorise their lines perfectly before the first read-through.

p1.en: Written creative works, especially those considered to have great artistic or intellectual value.
p1.example: She discovered a love of literature through the novels she read as a child.
p1.ex1: Classical literature has influenced countless writers across generations and cultures.
p1.ex2: He studied English literature at university before becoming a novelist himself.

p1.en: Worth remembering or easily remembered because of being special or remarkable.
p1.example: The final scene of the film was the most memorable moment of the entire year in cinema.
p1.ex1: She gave a memorable speech that left the whole audience deeply moved.
p1.ex2: A truly memorable book stays with you long after you have turned the last page.

p1.en: To learn something so thoroughly that you can remember it exactly, word for word.
p1.example: Actors must memorise hundreds of lines before they ever step onto a stage.
p1.ex1: She memorised an entire poem to recite at the school's literary evening.
p1.ex2: He found it easier to memorise facts when he connected them to stories.

p1.en: Something that is essential or absolutely required; an indispensable thing.
p1.example: The author believed that imagination was not a luxury but a necessity for human survival.
p1.ex1: Books are a necessity in any serious educational institution.
p1.ex2: She understood early on that discipline was a necessity for any aspiring writer.

p1.en: A long fictional narrative work, usually published as a book.
p1.example: Her debut novel won several international awards and was translated into thirty languages.
p1.ex1: He spent seven years writing his first novel before it was finally accepted for publication.
p1.ex2: Reading one classic novel a month is one of the best ways to improve your writing.

p1.en: A state of freedom from war or conflict; a feeling of calm and tranquillity.
p1.example: The Nobel Peace Prize is awarded to those who have made the greatest contribution to world peace.
p1.ex1: She found peace in writing, escaping the noise of the world through her stories.
p1.ex2: After years of conflict, the region finally achieved a lasting peace.

p1.en: To follow or chase a goal, career, or activity with determination and effort.
p1.example: Despite many setbacks, she continued to pursue her dream of becoming a published author.
p1.ex1: He decided to pursue a career in journalism after graduating from university.
p1.ex2: Nothing could stop her from pursuing her passion for storytelling.

p1.en: The quality of being consistently dependable and trustworthy, or the lack of it.
p1.example: Readers trust certain critics because of their reliability and consistent honesty.
p1.ex1: The unreliability of the narrator made the mystery novel even more compelling.
p1.ex2: His reliability as a journalist meant editors always trusted his facts.

p1.en: The state of things as they actually exist, as opposed to how they might be imagined.
p1.example: The novel blurs the boundary between reality and fantasy in fascinating ways.
p1.ex1: Sometimes literature helps us understand the reality of lives very different from our own.
p1.ex2: The documentary presented a harsh reality that audiences found difficult to ignore.

p1.en: The activity of telling or writing stories; the art or craft of constructing narratives.
p1.example: Oral storytelling is one of the oldest and most universal human traditions.
p1.ex1: She had a gift for storytelling that made even the simplest events sound extraordinary.
p1.ex2: Digital storytelling has created exciting new ways for authors to reach their audiences.

p1.en: A prize, usually a cup, statue, or plaque, awarded as recognition of victory or achievement.
p1.example: She lifted the trophy high above her head as the crowd cheered wildly.
p1.ex1: The trophy cabinet in his study was filled with awards from around the world.
p1.ex2: Winning the literary trophy confirmed that years of hard work had been worthwhile.

p1.en: Extending or occurring throughout the entire world.
p1.example: Her novel sold over ten million copies worldwide and was adapted into a major film.
p1.ex1: The campaign raised awareness of the issue on a worldwide scale.
p1.ex2: Social media allows authors to connect with readers worldwide instantly.

p2.en: Extremely surprising or impressive; causing great wonder or amazement.
p2.example: The performer's astonishing talent left the entire audience speechless.
p2.ex1: It was astonishing how quickly the young writer produced her second novel.
p2.ex2: The documentary revealed astonishing details about life on a professional film set.

p2.en: A close connection or feeling of friendship between people; a relationship built on shared experiences.
p2.example: The film beautifully explores the bond between a grandmother and her granddaughter.
p2.ex1: Reading the same books created a strong bond between the two friends.
p2.ex2: The bond formed between the cast members made their on-screen chemistry feel completely natural.

p2.en: Difficult to understand; making someone uncertain or unclear about something.
p2.example: The plot of the film was so confusing that many viewers had to watch it twice.
p2.ex1: She found the instructions for the new software confusing and asked for help.
p2.ex2: His explanation was more confusing than the original problem.

p2.en: A set of clothes worn by an actor for a role, or associated with a particular period or character.
p2.example: The elaborate costumes in the historical drama took three months to design and produce.
p2.ex1: She won an Oscar for Best Costume Design for her work on the epic fantasy film.
p2.ex2: The children dressed in Halloween costumes to watch the horror film screening.

p2.en: Failing to fulfil one's hopes or expectations; not as good as expected.
p2.example: Despite the high expectations, critics found the sequel deeply disappointing.
p2.ex1: It was disappointing that so few people attended the opening night of the play.
p2.ex2: She gave a disappointing performance that the director decided to cut from the final film.

p2.uz: eksklyuziv, maxsus, faqat bir kishiga tegishli
p2.en: Limited to a particular person or group; not available to everyone; highly restricted.
p2.example: The journalist was granted exclusive access to the director on the day of the premiere.
p2.ex1: Only members of the academy received an exclusive preview of the film.
p2.ex2: The magazine published an exclusive interview with the reclusive author.

p2.en: A showing of a film before its general release, usually for journalists, critics, or special guests.
p2.example: Tickets for the film preview sold out within minutes of going on sale.
p2.ex1: She attended the film preview and immediately predicted it would win several awards.
p2.ex2: The director gave a short speech at the film preview before the lights went down.

p2.en: To organise or be responsible for an event taking place.
p2.example: The festival will hold its annual ceremony in the city's grand theatre this November.
p2.ex1: The school will hold a special screening of the award-winning documentary next week.
p2.ex2: They decided to hold the book launch outdoors to accommodate more guests.

p2.en: Happening consecutively without a break; one after another.
p2.example: The studio produced three blockbusters in a row, breaking box office records each time.
p2.ex1: She won the award for Best Actress three years in a row.
p2.ex2: He read five novels in a row during his two-week holiday.

p2.en: Full of energy, excitement, or activity; animated and enthusiastic.
p2.example: The lively debate between the two authors kept the audience thoroughly entertained.
p2.ex1: Her lively writing style made even the dullest historical facts feel exciting.
p2.ex2: The festival had a lively atmosphere with music, food, and storytelling all day long.

p2.en: Causing strong feelings of sadness, sympathy, or admiration.
p2.example: The final chapter of the novel was so moving that she had to stop reading to compose herself.
p2.ex1: His moving tribute to his late mentor reduced the entire audience to tears.
p2.ex2: The film tells a moving story about love and loss in a war-torn city.

p2.en: A set of clothes chosen to be worn together for a particular occasion.
p2.example: She chose a stunning red outfit for the evening of the awards ceremony.
p2.ex1: The stylist put together the perfect outfit for each red carpet appearance.
p2.ex2: His outfit for the premiere was so memorable it appeared on every fashion website.

p2.en: Free from disturbance, conflict, or unpleasant activity; calm and quiet.
p2.example: She spent a peaceful morning in her garden writing the final pages of her novel.
p2.ex1: The countryside retreat provided the peaceful environment she needed to finish the book.
p2.ex2: After years of touring, he was grateful for a peaceful life away from the spotlight.

p2.en: Making you feel satisfied that you have done something useful, valuable, or worthwhile.
p2.example: Teaching creative writing to young students is one of the most rewarding things she has ever done.
p2.ex1: Writing a novel is incredibly rewarding, even if it takes years to complete.
p2.ex2: He found volunteering at the literary festival deeply rewarding.

p2.en: Meeting or failing to meet the required level of quality or expectation.
p2.example: The editor found the first draft unsatisfactory and asked for major revisions.
p2.ex1: A satisfactory ending is essential for readers to feel the story has been resolved.
p2.ex2: The committee deemed the proposal unsatisfactory and requested further research.

p2.en: A person who visits interesting or famous places as a tourist.
p2.example: The city became popular with sightseers after the award-winning film was set there.
p2.ex1: Thousands of sightseers arrive each year hoping to see the locations featured in the novel.
p2.ex2: As a sightseer, she visited every literary landmark mentioned in the guidebook.

p2.en: A person who watches an event, show, or performance without taking part in it.
p2.example: Thousands of spectators gathered for the open-air film screening in the main square.
p2.ex1: As a spectator at the debate, she found herself moved by both arguments.
p2.ex2: The spectators applauded loudly when the director stepped onto the stage.

p2.en: Making you feel physically or mentally exhausted.
p2.example: Filming a major blockbuster is an exciting but incredibly tiring process.
p2.ex1: The long award season was thrilling but also extremely tiring for the cast.
p2.ex2: She found the constant interviews tiring and began to crave quiet and solitude.

p2.en: Arousing feelings of sympathy, tenderness, or gratitude; emotionally moving.
p2.example: The most touching moment in the film was when the two characters finally reconciled.
p2.ex1: He gave a touching acceptance speech that mentioned every person who had helped him.
p2.ex2: The book's touching dedication to his late mother moved many readers before they had even begun.

p2.en: Not attractive or interesting; failing to appeal to one's tastes or preferences.
p2.example: The cover design was considered unappealing by the publisher and was redesigned before release.
p2.ex1: She found the antagonist's behaviour so unappealing that she almost stopped reading.
p2.ex2: The film's unappealing premise kept audiences away despite positive early reviews.

p2.en: Not easy to understand or see; uncertain or ambiguous.
p2.example: The film's ending was deliberately unclear, leaving audiences to draw their own conclusions.
p2.ex1: Her instructions were unclear, so the cast had to ask several follow-up questions.
p2.ex2: It remains unclear whether the sequel will be released next year or the year after.

p2.en: A set of standardised clothes worn by members of an organisation, school, or profession.
p2.example: The actor wore a military uniform throughout the entire production.
p2.ex1: The school required all students to wear a uniform to maintain a sense of equality.
p2.ex2: She instantly recognised the uniform of the festival volunteers and approached them for help.

p2.en: About to happen or appear in the near future.
p2.example: Fans are already excited about the upcoming sequel to last year's biggest blockbuster.
p2.ex1: The magazine published a preview of all upcoming releases for the autumn season.
p2.ex2: She had three upcoming interviews scheduled to promote her new book.

p2.en: A success achieved by defeating an opponent or overcoming a challenge.
p2.example: Winning the Booker Prize was the greatest victory of her long literary career.
p2.ex1: The team celebrated their victory by dedicating the award to their late coach.
p2.ex2: After years of rejection, getting published felt like a personal victory.

p2.en: Involving physical force intended to hurt, injure, or kill; very forceful or intense.
p2.example: The film contained several violent scenes that led to an 18-certificate rating.
p2.ex1: Critics debated whether the violent content of the novel was necessary to its message.
p2.ex2: The director chose not to show violent scenes directly but implied them off-screen.

p2.en: To cause someone to feel so emotionally moved that they cry or nearly cry.
p2.example: The final scene of the documentary brought tears to everyone's eyes in the cinema.
p2.ex1: Her acceptance speech was so heartfelt that it brought tears to the eyes of everyone present.
p2.ex2: Reading that final chapter will bring tears to your eyes — it is absolutely beautiful.

p2.en: To see and talk to someone face to face, as opposed to communicating online or by phone.
p2.example: She had followed the author online for years before finally meeting her in person at a book fair.
p2.ex1: It was wonderful to finally meet the cast in person after watching the film so many times.
p2.ex2: He was nervous about meeting his literary idol in person at the awards ceremony.

p2.ru: уникальный опыт, событие раз в жизни
p2.en: An opportunity or experience that is so rare and special that it is unlikely to happen again.
p2.example: Attending the world premiere in Hollywood was a once-in-a-lifetime experience.
p2.ex1: Interviewing your favourite author is truly a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity.
p2.ex2: She described the backstage tour as a once-in-a-lifetime experience she would treasure forever.

p2.en: A brief or unofficial early look at something before it is officially released or shown.
p2.example: The director shared a sneak peek of the trailer online a month before the official release.
p2.ex1: Fans were excited when the author posted a sneak peek of the opening chapter on social media.
p2.ex2: The studio gave journalists a sneak peek of the film to generate early buzz.

p3.en: A book or text that is enjoyable and easy to read; something entertaining to read.
p3.example: The novel is a good read for anyone who enjoys fast-paced adventure stories.
p3.ex1: Her autobiography is an absolute good read that is almost impossible to put down.
p3.ex2: I would recommend it as a good read for a long journey or a relaxing weekend.

p3.en: Used to describe where or when the action of a book, film, or story takes place.
p3.example: The novel is set in 19th-century London during the height of the Victorian era.
p3.ex1: The film is set in a small coastal town where everyone knows everyone else's secrets.
p3.ex2: Most of her stories are set in her home country, which brings great authenticity to the writing.

p3.en: A detailed written account of someone's life, written by another person.
p3.example: The biography of the Nobel laureate revealed many surprising details about her early struggles.
p3.ex1: He spent three years researching and writing the biography of the pioneering scientist.
p3.ex2: Her biography became a bestseller and was later adapted into a major television series.

p3.en: The different categories or types of books, such as fiction, mystery, biography, or science fiction.
p3.example: The librarian organised all books by their book genres to make them easier to find.
p3.ex1: Understanding book genres helps readers quickly find the types of stories they enjoy most.
p3.ex2: Her favourite book genres include historical fiction and psychological thrillers.

p3.en: The quality of being willing to do things that are dangerous or difficult; courage.
p3.example: The protagonist's bravery in standing up to injustice is the heart of the entire novel.
p3.ex1: Her bravery in telling her story inspired millions of readers around the world.
p3.ex2: The biographer highlighted the bravery required to pursue such a revolutionary idea.

p3.en: Close to someone; offering support and companionship.
p3.example: Throughout every challenge the hero faced, his loyal companion remained by his side.
p3.ex1: She had her best friend by her side on the night her debut novel was published.
p3.ex2: Having a mentor by your side is invaluable when starting a career in literature.

p3.en: A person who has won first place in a competition; or someone who actively supports a cause.
p3.example: She was not only a literary champion but also a passionate champion of literacy for all children.
p3.ex1: He became champion of the national debate competition three years running.
p3.ex2: The character in the novel is a champion of the poor and the forgotten.

p3.en: A work of art or literature that is considered to be of the highest quality and lasting importance.
p3.example: To Kill a Mockingbird is widely regarded as a classic of 20th-century American literature.
p3.ex1: She spent the summer rereading the classics she had first encountered at school.
p3.ex2: A true classic transcends its time and continues to speak to new generations of readers.

p3.en: A single example of a book, magazine, or document produced as one of many.
p3.example: The first edition sold over a million copies in its opening week.
p3.ex1: She kept a signed copy of her favourite novel on her bedside table.
p3.ex2: Every student was given a copy of the required reading list at the start of term.

p3.en: The quality of continuing to try to do something even when it is difficult.
p3.example: Her determination to finish the novel despite personal hardship made her success all the more remarkable.
p3.ex1: With determination and patience, he eventually completed his first full-length manuscript.
p3.ex2: The biography showed that behind every great achievement lies years of quiet determination.

p3.en: Far away in space or time; or not closely connected; emotionally remote.
p3.example: The novel explores a distant future where technology has replaced all human relationships.
p3.ex1: She felt distant from the character and struggled to connect with the story emotionally.
p3.ex2: The story is set in a distant land that feels both magical and strangely familiar.

p3.en: Used to describe a book that is so gripping and enjoyable that you do not want to stop reading it.
p3.example: Her latest thriller is absolutely hard to put down — I read it in a single sitting.
p3.ex1: Once you reach the second chapter, this novel becomes hard to put down.
p3.ex2: The best page-turners are always the ones that are hard to put down no matter what time it is.

p3.en: A genre of fiction set in a historical period, often featuring real or fictional characters and events.
p3.example: The novel is a work of historical fiction set during the French Revolution.
p3.ex1: She discovered her love of history through the historical fiction novels she read as a teenager.
p3.ex2: Writing historical fiction requires extensive research to ensure accuracy.

p3.en: Having or showing creativity and the ability to think of new and interesting ideas.
p3.example: The author's imaginative use of language turned a simple story into something extraordinary.
p3.ex1: Children respond especially well to imaginative storytelling that sparks their curiosity.
p3.ex2: Her imaginative approach to world-building made the fantasy series utterly unique.

p3.en: Having or showing a high level of mental ability, understanding, or reasoning.
p3.example: The novel raises intelligent questions about identity, belonging, and the nature of truth.
p3.ex1: She crafted an intelligent script that challenged the audience to think deeply.
p3.ex2: Readers admired the intelligent structure of the plot, which rewarded careful attention.

p3.en: The creation of something that has never existed before; a new device, method, or process.
p3.example: The invention of the printing press made literature accessible to people across the world.
p3.ex1: Her latest novel imagines a world transformed by a single remarkable invention.
p3.ex2: He dedicated the book to his grandfather, whose invention had changed their family's life.

p3.en: Remaining faithful and supportive to a person, cause, or belief over a long period.
p3.example: The loyal readers of the series queued overnight for the release of the final book.
p3.ex1: The protagonist's loyal companion never abandoned him, even at the darkest moments.
p3.ex2: A loyal friendship is one of the most powerful themes in the entire novel.

p3.en: A very large and impressive house, typically belonging to a wealthy person.
p3.example: The mystery novel is set in an isolated Victorian mansion surrounded by fog and secrets.
p3.ex1: She described the old mansion so vividly that readers could almost smell the damp stone walls.
p3.ex2: The eccentric inventor lived alone in a crumbling mansion full of strange machines.

p3.en: An important assignment or goal that someone is committed to completing.
p3.example: The hero's mission was to recover the stolen manuscript before it fell into the wrong hands.
p3.ex1: She felt it was her personal mission to make literature available to every child in the country.
p3.ex2: His mission to document every endangered dialect resulted in a groundbreaking book.

p3.en: Something that is not fully understood or explained; also a genre of fiction involving a crime or secret to be solved.
p3.example: The novel is a gripping mystery centred around the disappearance of a famous writer.
p3.ex1: She had always loved mystery stories because of the pleasure of working out the solution.
p3.ex2: The mystery of who wrote the anonymous manuscript was never fully solved.

p3.en: Writing or literature based on real events, real people, and actual facts, rather than imagined stories.
p3.example: Non-fiction titles dominated the bestseller charts this year, reflecting a public hunger for truth.
p3.ex1: She preferred reading non-fiction because it connected her to the real world.
p3.ex2: The boundary between non-fiction and fiction is sometimes deliberately blurred by adventurous writers.

p3.en: A book that is so exciting and gripping that the reader wants to keep reading to find out what happens next.
p3.example: Her debut thriller was described by every critic as an absolute page-turner.
p3.ex1: A great page-turner combines suspense, vivid characters, and an irresistible plot.
p3.ex2: I started the page-turner at bedtime and finished it at four in the morning.

p3.en: Behaving or happening in a way that was expected; lacking surprise or originality.
p3.example: Reviewers felt the ending was predictable and wished the author had taken more risks.
p3.ex1: The plot became predictable after the first act, which disappointed many fans of the series.
p3.ex2: A truly great novel should never be predictable — it must surprise and challenge its readers.

p3.en: A person who works on a ship or who sails as a hobby or profession.
p3.example: The adventure novel follows a young sailor on a voyage across uncharted seas.
p3.ex1: The old sailor told extraordinary stories that inspired the author's first novel.
p3.ex2: Her character is a courageous sailor who discovers a hidden island in the middle of the Pacific.

p3.en: An artificial object placed in orbit around the Earth or another planet to collect information or for communication.
p3.example: The science fiction novel imagines a future where every human is monitored by satellite.
p3.ex1: The inventor dreamed of launching a satellite that could connect remote communities worldwide.
p3.ex2: Communication satellites have transformed the way stories and information are shared globally.

p3.en: A genre of fiction based on imagined future scientific or technological advances and their social consequences.
p3.example: The novel is a compelling work of science fiction that explores what it means to be human.
p3.ex1: She grew up reading science fiction and eventually wrote her own celebrated series in the genre.
p3.ex2: Science fiction often predicts technological developments that later become reality.

p3.en: To begin a journey by sea; to depart on a voyage.
p3.example: In the final chapter, the hero sets sail for an unknown island to find the lost treasure.
p3.ex1: The sailor set sail for the distant horizon with nothing but a compass and a dream.
p3.ex2: She set sail for a new life, leaving behind everything she had ever known.

p3.en: A feeling of excited uncertainty and anxiety about what will happen next, especially in a story.
p3.example: The author builds suspense brilliantly throughout the novel, keeping readers guessing until the very end.
p3.ex1: She kept the audience in suspense by not revealing the identity of the killer until the final page.
p3.ex2: Good suspense relies on withholding just enough information to keep the reader desperate to continue.

p3.en: The central topic or idea that a book, film, or artwork explores or is about.
p3.example: The central theme of the novel is the struggle between personal freedom and social duty.
p3.ex1: Love and loss are recurring themes throughout the author's body of work.
p3.ex2: The teacher asked students to identify the main theme of each chapter.

p3.en: Not affected by the passage of time; remaining relevant and important indefinitely.
p3.example: Shakespeare's plays are timeless because they explore emotions that every human being understands.
p3.ex1: The novel has a timeless quality that makes it as powerful today as when it was first published.
p3.ex2: True art is timeless — it speaks to people across centuries and cultures.

p3.en: The act of going from one place to another, especially over a long distance.
p3.example: Her love of travel inspired a memoir that blended personal experience with cultural observation.
p3.ex1: Travel writing is one of the oldest and most popular forms of non-fiction literature.
p3.ex2: The author believed that travel was the greatest education a writer could have.

p3.en: A collection of precious things such as gold or jewels; something highly valued.
p3.example: The adventure novel centres on the quest to find a legendary treasure buried centuries ago.
p3.ex1: The old map led the sailors to a remote island where the treasure was said to be hidden.
p3.ex2: For the protagonist, the real treasure was not gold but the friendships forged along the way.

p3.en: To discover something that was hidden or unknown; to reveal a fact or secret.
p3.example: The journalist spent years trying to uncover the truth behind the mysterious disappearance.
p3.ex1: Reading historical fiction can uncover forgotten aspects of our collective past.
p3.ex2: As the novel progresses, the detective slowly uncovers the identity of the culprit.

p3.en: Used to indicate competition or contrast between two things, people, or ideas.
p3.example: The essay explored the debate of fiction versus non-fiction as a tool for understanding reality.
p3.ex1: The battle of imagination versus reality lies at the heart of the story.
p3.ex2: Science fiction versus fantasy — both genres offer readers worlds beyond their own experience.

p3.en: Producing strong, clear images in the mind; very bright or intense; strikingly lifelike.
p3.example: Her vivid descriptions of the jungle made readers feel they were there alongside the characters.
p3.ex1: The author has a gift for creating vivid characters that stay with you long after the book is finished.
p3.ex2: His vivid imagination allowed him to build entire worlds from a single idea.

p1.en: To take something on as your own, such as a habit, policy, or child; to take a rescue animal into your home.
p1.example: The family decided to adopt a dog from the local animal shelter rather than buy one.
p1.ex1: Schools across the country have adopted new policies to combat cyberbullying.
p1.ex2: She adopted a more environmentally conscious lifestyle after learning about climate change.

p1.en: The act of adopting a child, animal, or policy; taking something on as one's own.
p1.example: The adoption of reusable bags instead of single-use plastic is a simple but powerful change.
p1.ex1: Pet adoption from animal shelters gives homeless animals a second chance at life.
p1.ex2: The adoption of stronger environmental policies is essential to combat climate change.

p1.en: A place where stray, abandoned, or rescued animals are housed and cared for until they find new homes.
p1.example: She volunteered every weekend at the animal shelter, feeding and walking the dogs.
p1.ex1: The campaign encouraged people to adopt pets from animal shelters rather than breeders.
p1.ex2: The animal shelter launched a hashtag campaign to find owners for all its animals.

p1.en: To help someone to do something, especially in a practical or professional way.
p1.example: Volunteers were trained to assist victims of flooding with first aid and emergency supplies.
p1.ex1: She used her media studies knowledge to assist the campaign with social media strategy.
p1.ex2: Neighbours came together to assist the family whose home had been destroyed by fire.

p1.en: Repeated aggressive behaviour intended to hurt, frighten, or control someone who is weaker.
p1.example: The school launched a campaign to raise awareness about the consequences of bullying.
p1.ex1: She used her platform to spread the word about the lasting damage caused by bullying.
p1.ex2: Bullying can take place online as well as face to face, which is why cyberbullying is such a concern.

p1.en: A plant smaller than a tree with many branches; also used informally to refer to wild, rural land.
p1.example: Volunteers spent the morning clearing litter from the bushes along the river bank.
p1.ex1: She pushed her way through the dense bush to reach the part of the forest that needed cleaning.
p1.ex2: The campaign focused on cleaning up neglected areas overgrown with weeds and bush.

p1.en: An organised series of activities or events intended to achieve a social, political, or environmental goal.
p1.example: They launched a campaign to reduce single-use plastic waste in their local community.
p1.ex1: The hashtag campaign spread the word about climate change to millions of people online.
p1.ex2: A successful campaign requires a clear message, strong organisation, and widespread support.

p1.en: To remove dirt, rubbish, or pollution from a place; to tidy or restore an area.
p1.example: Hundreds of volunteers gathered on Saturday to clean up the polluted beach.
p1.ex1: The community organised a monthly event to clean up the park near the school.
p1.ex2: After the flood, residents worked tirelessly to clean up the damage to their homes.

p1.en: Long-term shifts in global temperatures and weather patterns, largely driven by human activity.
p1.example: The students organised a march to demand stronger government action on climate change.
p1.ex1: Understanding the consequences of climate change is an important part of environmental education.
p1.ex2: Reducing single-use plastic is one practical step individuals can take to fight climate change.

p1.en: A result or effect of an action or condition, especially an unpleasant one.
p1.example: The long-term consequences of ignoring climate change will be felt by future generations.
p1.ex1: One serious consequence of cyberbullying is the lasting damage it causes to mental health.
p1.ex2: She helped students understand the real-world consequences of throwing rubbish in landfill sites.

p1.en: The use of digital technology to repeatedly harass, threaten, or humiliate someone.
p1.example: The campaign used social media itself to raise awareness about the dangers of cyberbullying.
p1.ex1: Schools are increasingly teaching students how to recognise and respond to cyberbullying.
p1.ex2: She made up her mind to report the cyberbullying she witnessed rather than ignore it.

p1.en: Relating to the natural world and the impact of human activity on it.
p1.example: She studied media studies to learn how to raise awareness of environmental issues effectively.
p1.ex1: Environmental campaigns have successfully persuaded many businesses to reduce single-use plastic.
p1.ex2: Every small environmental choice — like using reusable bags — adds up to make a real difference.

p1.en: To give food to a person or animal; to supply something that is needed to keep something going.
p1.example: Volunteers visited the animal shelter every morning to feed and care for the animals.
p1.ex1: She organised a weekly event to feed homeless people in her local community.
p1.ex2: Social media algorithms feed users content that keeps them engaged for longer.

p1.en: A word or phrase preceded by the # symbol, used on social media to label and group content by topic.
p1.example: The environmental organisation created a hashtag that went viral and reached millions of users.
p1.ex1: She used a powerful hashtag to spread the word about her animal shelter campaign.
p1.ex2: A well-chosen hashtag can turn a small local campaign into a nationwide conversation.

p1.en: A site where rubbish and waste materials are buried in the ground; a method of disposing of waste.
p1.example: Every piece of single-use plastic that is thrown away ends up in a landfill or the ocean.
p1.ex1: She made up her mind to reduce her waste after visiting a nearby landfill site.
p1.ex2: Communities are campaigning to close local landfill sites and invest in recycling instead.

p1.uz: qaror qilmoq, qat'iy qaror qabul qilmoq
p1.en: To reach a firm decision after considering the options; to decide.
p1.example: She finally made up her mind to join the environmental campaign after watching a documentary.
p1.ex1: He made up his mind to adopt a dog from the shelter rather than buy one from a breeder.
p1.ex2: Once you make up your mind to spread the word, the next step is to choose the right platform.

p1.en: The substance or matter from which things are made; also printed or digital information produced for a purpose.
p1.example: The campaign produced educational material to inform people about the dangers of single-use plastic.
p1.ex1: Reusable bags are made from materials designed to last for years rather than minutes.
p1.ex2: She gathered research material from a range of environmental organisations for her project.

p1.uz: media ta'limi, ommaviy axborot vositalari fani
p1.en: An academic subject that examines the role and influence of media, including television, social media, and journalism.
p1.example: Her media studies degree helped her run highly effective social media campaigns.
p1.ex1: Media studies students analysed how climate change is represented across different platforms.
p1.ex2: Understanding hashtags and audience behaviour is a core part of media studies today.

p1.en: Continuously and without stopping; for a long time without pausing.
p1.example: She talked on and on about the importance of reusable products until everyone was convinced.
p1.ex1: The volunteer went on and on about the benefits of adopting from animal shelters.
p1.ex2: The debate about single-use plastic went on and on for hours without reaching a conclusion.

p1.en: A person who possesses something; someone who has legal possession of a property, animal, or business.
p1.example: Responsible pet owners often choose to adopt from shelters rather than buy from breeders.
p1.ex1: The campaign urged every dog owner to clean up after their pet in public spaces.
p1.ex2: She became the proud owner of a rescued cat after visiting the animal shelter.

p1.en: To display or attach something in a public place; also to provide accommodation for someone.
p1.example: They put up posters around the school to spread the word about the anti-bullying campaign.
p1.ex1: Volunteers put up signs along the beach to remind visitors not to drop single-use plastic.
p1.ex2: She put up a friend who had nowhere to stay after the flood destroyed her flat.

p1.en: To study and investigate a subject carefully in order to discover new information or reach a new understanding.
p1.example: She spent months researching the effects of landfill pollution on nearby communities.
p1.ex1: Students were asked to research the environmental consequences of single-use plastic.
p1.ex2: He researched dozens of animal shelters before deciding which one to support.

p1.en: The state of being accountable for something; a duty or obligation to act correctly.
p1.example: She believed it was everyone's responsibility to reduce waste and protect the environment.
p1.ex1: The campaign reminded young people that taking responsibility for their actions online is essential.
p1.ex2: Looking after an adopted animal is a long-term responsibility that must be taken seriously.

p1.en: Designed or able to be used again and again rather than once and then thrown away.
p1.example: Switching to reusable water bottles and bags is one of the easiest ways to reduce plastic waste.
p1.ex1: The school launched a campaign encouraging students to bring reusable containers for lunch.
p1.ex2: Reusable products may cost more initially but save money and resources in the long term.

p1.en: Plastic items designed to be used once and then discarded, such as straws, bags, and bottles.
p1.example: Many countries have introduced laws to ban single-use plastic bags in supermarkets.
p1.ex1: She made up her mind to never buy single-use plastic after visiting the local landfill site.
p1.ex2: The campaign showed the devastating environmental consequences of single-use plastic on ocean life.

p1.en: To tell many people about something so that the information becomes widely known.
p1.example: She asked all her followers to spread the word about the beach clean-up event on Saturday.
p1.ex1: Using a hashtag is one of the most effective ways to spread the word on social media.
p1.ex2: They relied on volunteers to spread the word about the campaign through their own networks.

p2.en: A residential facility providing personal care and support for elderly or disabled people.
p2.example: She organised weekly visits to the local care home to read to the elderly residents.
p2.ex1: Volunteers from the community visited the care home to assist staff during the holiday period.
p2.ex2: The campaign raised funds to improve facilities at several care homes in the area.

p2.en: A group of people living in the same area or sharing common interests, values, or goals.
p2.example: The whole community came together to rebuild homes after the devastating flood.
p2.ex1: A strong community can turn small acts of kindness into powerful lasting change.
p2.ex2: She believed that real change starts at community level, not at national government level.

p2.en: To damage something so severely that it can no longer be used or no longer exists.
p2.example: The flood destroyed dozens of homes and left hundreds of families without shelter.
p2.ex1: Cyberbullying can destroy a person's confidence and mental health over time.
p2.ex2: Climate change has the power to destroy entire ecosystems if action is not taken now.

p2.en: Having no limit; continuing for a very long time without stopping; seeming to have no end.
p2.example: She felt the task of clearing up after the flood was endless, but the community kept going.
p2.ex1: The endless stream of negative news about climate change left many people feeling powerless.
p2.ex2: Volunteering at the care home gave her endless opportunities to help others and grow as a person.

p2.en: Basic emergency medical treatment given to an injured or ill person before professional help arrives.
p2.example: Every volunteer was trained in first aid before being sent to assist flood victims.
p2.ex1: Knowing first aid can make the difference between life and death in an emergency.
p2.ex2: The community organised free first aid classes so residents could be ready for any crisis.

p2.en: To cover or fill an area with water beyond its normal limits; to overwhelm with a large amount of something.
p2.example: Heavy rain flooded the streets and forced many families to leave their homes.
p2.ex1: The river flooded the surrounding farmland for the third time that year.
p2.ex2: Requests for help flooded into the emergency services within hours of the storm beginning.

p2.en: Not able to cause harm, injury, or damage; completely safe and without negative effects.
p2.example: What seems like harmless teasing online can quickly turn into serious cyberbullying.
p2.ex1: The chemicals used in the reusable packaging are completely harmless to the environment.
p2.ex2: A harmless joke is very different from bullying, but the line is often hard to define.

p2.en: Feeling or giving no hope; having no chance of success or improvement.
p2.example: She refused to feel hopeless about climate change and channelled her feelings into action.
p2.ex1: After the flood, many residents felt hopeless, but the community organisers kept spirits high.
p2.ex2: It may feel hopeless at first, but every campaign that has changed the world started small.

p2.en: Requiring help, support, or basic necessities; in a state of poverty or difficulty.
p2.example: The campaign raised money to provide reusable supplies for families in need after the flood.
p2.ex1: She volunteered at the care home because she wanted to support people in need.
p2.ex2: The community set up a fund to help those in need rebuild their lives after the disaster.

p2.en: A person responsible for planning and managing an event or activity.
p2.example: As lead organiser of the beach clean-up, she coordinated over a hundred volunteers.
p2.ex1: A good organiser makes sure every volunteer knows their task and feels valued.
p2.ex2: The organisers of the community campaign spread the word using a single well-chosen hashtag.

p2.en: The ability to do something or influence events; energy or force; political control.
p2.example: She reminded the group that ordinary people have the power to change their communities.
p2.ex1: The power of social media to spread the word about important causes is extraordinary.
p2.ex2: After the flood cut the power supply, the community relied on generators for days.

p2.en: Unable to take action or prevent something from happening; lacking strength or authority.
p2.example: Many people feel powerless in the face of climate change, but small actions do matter.
p2.ex1: She felt powerless watching the flood destroy everything the community had built.
p2.ex2: Victims of cyberbullying often feel powerless, which is why speaking up is so important.

p2.en: In a correct, appropriate, or satisfactory way; as expected or required.
p2.example: Volunteers were told to clean up properly after the event so the park was spotless.
p2.ex1: First aid must be carried out properly or it can do more harm than good.
p2.ex2: She made sure all the campaign material was properly researched and fact-checked.

p2.en: To build or construct something again after it has been damaged or destroyed.
p2.example: After the flood, the whole community united to rebuild homes and restore the area.
p2.ex1: It takes years to rebuild trust in a community after a serious bullying incident.
p2.ex2: She helped to rebuild the garden of the care home after the storm had flattened it.

p2.en: To do something again, usually because it was done incorrectly or needs improvement.
p2.example: She had to redo the campaign poster after realising she had misspelled the hashtag.
p2.ex1: He was asked to redo his research after his teacher pointed out several inaccuracies.
p2.ex2: Redo the task from the beginning if you are not happy with the result the first time.

p2.en: To take something away from where it is; to get rid of something.
p2.example: Volunteers worked hard to remove rubbish and debris left behind by the flood.
p2.ex1: The council agreed to remove the landfill site and replace it with a green park.
p2.ex2: She removed all single-use plastic from her kitchen as her first environmental action.

p2.en: To fix something that is broken, damaged, or not working properly.
p2.example: After the flood, skilled tradespeople volunteered to repair homes free of charge.
p2.ex1: She helped repair the fence that had been damaged during the storm.
p2.ex2: It is far better for the environment to repair a product than to throw it away and buy new.

p2.en: To arrange for something to happen at a different time from the one originally planned.
p2.example: The community clean-up had to be rescheduled due to heavy rain flooding the area.
p2.ex1: The organiser rescheduled the first aid training session to a date when more volunteers could attend.
p2.ex2: She rescheduled the care home visit when she heard that a resident was unwell.

p2.uz: qayta aytib bermoq, boshqalarga hikoya qilmoq
p2.en: To tell a story or account again, often to a different audience or in a different way.
p2.example: She was asked to retell the story of the flood for the school's environmental awareness magazine.
p2.ex1: Children at the care home were encouraged to retell memories from their lives.
p2.ex2: The campaign asked survivors to retell their experiences to help others understand the reality.

p2.en: To use something again after it has already been used, rather than throwing it away.
p2.example: The event encouraged participants to reuse containers and bags instead of reaching for single-use plastic.
p2.ex1: She found creative ways to reuse old materials instead of sending them to landfill.
p2.ex2: A simple step anyone can take is to reuse shopping bags every time they go to the supermarket.

p2.en: To write something again, especially to improve or correct it.
p2.example: She rewrote the campaign message three times until it was clear, powerful, and concise.
p2.ex1: He rewrote his research report after finding new evidence that changed his conclusions.
p2.ex2: A good organiser is willing to rewrite plans when circumstances change unexpectedly.

p2.en: A gesture, sound, or message that conveys information or a warning; also a mobile network or internet connection.
p2.example: The rescue team sent a signal to let volunteers know which areas had been cleared.
p2.ex1: There was no phone signal in the flooded area, making it impossible to call for help.
p2.ex2: Wearing reusable items sends a clear signal that you care about the environment.

p2.en: A piece of work that needs to be done, especially one that is assigned to a person or group.
p2.example: Each volunteer was given a specific task so the clean-up could be completed efficiently.
p2.ex1: Her task as campaign organiser was to spread the word using every available platform.
p2.ex2: Breaking a large goal into smaller tasks makes it far easier to make progress.

p2.en: Having no useful qualities; not able to achieve its purpose or produce a good result.
p2.example: A campaign is useless if the message is unclear and nobody understands what action to take.
p2.ex1: Without proper training, first aid equipment is practically useless in an emergency.
p2.ex2: She refused to feel useless and found a way to contribute despite having no experience.

p1.en: Completely and without any doubt; used to emphasise agreement or a strong statement.
p1.example: She was absolutely certain that taking a digital detox was the right decision for her wellbeing.
p1.ex1: He absolutely loved living in the countryside after years of city stress.
p1.ex2: Absolutely everyone agreed that the slow-paced lifestyle suited them far better.

p1.en: A strong dedication to something; the state of being bound to a course of action or to a person.
p1.example: Moving to the countryside required a serious commitment to changing her entire way of life.
p1.ex1: He showed great commitment to the project despite all the difficulties.
p1.ex2: A commitment to simplifying your lifestyle can lead to greater peace of mind.
