p1.en: A period during which someone refrains from using electronic devices such as smartphones and computers to reduce stress.
p1.example: She went on a week-long digital detox in the woods and felt completely refreshed.
p1.ex1: A digital detox helps people reconnect with the world around them rather than their screens.
p1.ex2: He noticed that even a short digital detox improved his concentration and sleep quality.

p1.en: Moving, changing, or happening very quickly; characterised by speed and intensity.
p1.example: After years of a fast-paced career in the city, she craved something slower and simpler.
p1.ex1: The fast-paced lifestyle of modern cities can be exciting but also exhausting.
p1.ex2: He struggled to keep up with the fast-paced demands of his new job.

p1.en: To become completely wet, usually from rain or water.
p1.example: She got completely soaked hiking through the woods after the unexpected rainstorm.
p1.ex1: They got soaked waiting for the bus because they had forgotten their umbrellas.
p1.ex2: He laughed when he got soaked but said it was the most fun he had had all year.

p1.en: The greater number or part of something; more than half of a group.
p1.example: The majority of people who tried a digital detox reported feeling calmer and more focused.
p1.ex1: The majority of his colleagues preferred working from home to commuting every day.
p1.ex2: A majority of city dwellers say they dream of moving to the countryside at some point.

p1.en: Not absolutely necessary; not vital or critical to a core function or need.
p1.example: During the digital detox, she deleted all non-essential apps from her phone.
p1.ex1: He decided to cut all non-essential spending in order to save for a move abroad.
p1.ex2: Simplifying life often means identifying what is truly important and removing the non-essential.

p1.en: To try to find or obtain something; to look for or pursue a goal or answer.
p1.example: More and more people are seeking a slower, more meaningful way of living.
p1.ex1: She sought advice from those who had already made the move to rural life.
p1.ex2: He sought quiet and solitude in the woods after months of relentless city noise.

p1.en: To make something less complicated or easier to understand or do.
p1.example: She decided to simplify her life by getting rid of possessions she no longer needed.
p1.ex1: Moving to a smaller house helped him simplify his daily routine significantly.
p1.ex2: The goal of a digital detox is to simplify your relationship with technology.

p1.en: Moving or progressing at a relaxed, unhurried speed; the opposite of fast-paced.
p1.example: She instantly fell in love with the slow-paced rhythm of life in the small village.
p1.ex1: A slow-paced lifestyle gives you time to appreciate the small moments.
p1.ex2: He found the slow-paced routine of rural life difficult at first but grew to treasure it.

p1.en: Things, objects, or possessions, especially when spoken about informally or in general terms.
p1.example: She realised she had accumulated far too much stuff that she never actually used.
p1.ex1: He put all his old stuff in boxes and donated most of it to charity.
p1.ex2: Moving forces you to confront just how much unnecessary stuff you have collected over the years.

p1.en: To have a habit or natural inclination to behave in a particular way; to be likely to do something.
p1.example: People who live in the countryside tend to report higher levels of life satisfaction.
p1.ex1: She tends to wake up earlier when she is away from the city noise.
p1.ex2: He tended to overwork before his digital detox changed his perspective on productivity.

p1.en: Not normal, typical, or in line with what is found in nature; forced or artificial.
p1.example: It felt unnatural at first to spend an entire day without checking her phone.
p1.ex1: He found the silence of the countryside unnatural after years of city living.
p1.ex2: There is something deeply unnatural about spending most of your waking hours staring at a screen.

p1.en: A small forest or area with many trees; less formal or dense than a full forest.
p1.example: She spent her mornings walking through the woods and found it deeply restorative.
p1.ex1: The children spent the whole afternoon exploring the woods behind the cottage.
p1.ex2: Living near the woods meant he could always clear his head with a quiet morning walk.

p1.en: Immediately; or at the same time as other things.
p1.example: She felt at once relieved and nervous when she finally switched off her phone.
p1.ex1: He tried to do too many things at once and ended up achieving very little.
p1.ex2: At once, she knew that leaving the city had been the right decision.

p1.en: To examine two things and note how they are similar or different.
p1.example: It is interesting to make a comparison between city living and life in the countryside.
p1.ex1: She asked students to make a comparison between fast-paced and slow-paced lifestyles.
p1.ex2: When making a comparison between the two options, the countryside clearly won.

p1.en: To be forced to do something because there is no other option available.
p1.example: She had no choice but to give up her flat in the city when the rent became unaffordable.
p1.ex1: He had no choice but to take the slower route after the main road was closed.
p1.ex2: With no savings left, she had no choice but to move back to her home town.

p1.en: To be completely unwilling or not planning to do something.
p1.example: She had no intention of returning to a fast-paced lifestyle after her year in the countryside.
p1.ex1: He made it clear he had no intention of giving up his digital detox after just one week.
p1.ex2: I have no intention of going back to the city — this slow-paced life suits me perfectly.

p1.en: Used to say that doing something will not help or produce a good result; it is pointless.
p1.example: It's no use complaining about city stress if you are not willing to make a change.
p1.ex1: It's no use checking your phone every five minutes during a digital detox.
p1.ex2: She sighed and said, 'It's no use — I simply cannot focus in this noisy environment.'

p1.en: Used to say that something is not surprising, given the circumstances.
p1.example: It's no wonder so many people are choosing to leave the city for a quieter life.
p1.ex1: It's no wonder she felt so much better after a week without social media.
p1.ex2: Given how stressful the job was, it's no wonder he eventually decided to leave.

p1.en: Used to say that a mistake or accident has not caused any serious problems.
p1.example: She knocked over her coffee on the first day in the new cottage — no harm done, thankfully.
p1.ex1: He forgot to lock the gate, but no harm done as the garden was perfectly safe.
p1.ex2: No harm done — the misunderstanding was quickly cleared up with a friendly conversation.

p1.en: Used to say that something is unnecessary; it does not need to be done.
p1.example: There's no need to check your emails every hour — they will still be there in the morning.
p1.ex1: There's no need to rush — we have plenty of time before the train leaves.
p1.ex2: She reassured him, 'There's no need to worry — everything is already sorted.'

p1.en: Used to say that doing something has no purpose or benefit; it is a waste of time or effort.
p1.example: There's no point in having a digital detox if you go back to your old habits the next day.
p1.ex1: There's no point in moving to the countryside if you bring all your city stress with you.
p1.ex2: He realised there was no point in keeping things that only added clutter to his life.

p1.en: Used to emphasise that action must be taken immediately because time is limited.
p1.example: There's no time to lose — she needed to book the cottage before someone else did.
p1.ex1: If you want to make real changes to your lifestyle, there's no time to lose.
p1.ex2: He said, 'There's no time to lose — pack your bags and let's go to the woods.'

p1.en: Used to say that a decision has been made and cannot be reversed; one must continue forward.
p1.example: Once she sold her city flat and moved to the village, she knew there was no turning back.
p1.ex1: He signed the contract and thought: there's no turning back now.
p1.ex2: After six months in the countryside, she realised there was truly no turning back.

p2.en: To ask someone urgently and humbly for something; or to ask for money from strangers.
p2.example: She begged her employer to let her work remotely from the countryside.
p2.ex1: He begged his children to give the rural lifestyle a fair chance before judging it.
p2.ex2: She would beg anyone who would listen to try at least one week of a slower pace of life.

p2.en: To travel regularly between one's home and place of work, usually a significant distance.
p2.example: After moving to the suburbs, he had to commute over an hour to reach the city centre.
p2.ex1: She used to commute by train but now works from a cosy home office in the countryside.
p2.ex2: Commuting every day for years was one of the main reasons she decided to move away.

p2.en: To ask for something firmly and with authority; to insist on having something.
p2.example: The journalist demanded to know why the council had approved the new development.
p2.ex1: She demanded a proper explanation before agreeing to any changes to her contract.
p2.ex2: Rural communities increasingly demand better transport links to nearby cities.

p2.en: To state that something is not true; or to refuse to give or allow something.
p2.example: Nobody can deny that city life offers opportunities that are harder to find in rural areas.
p2.ex1: He denied feeling homesick for the city but his friends could see it in his expression.
p2.ex2: She denied herself all non-essential technology for a month and felt remarkably better.

p2.en: The lively and energetic activity of a busy place, especially a city.
p2.example: After years of the hustle and bustle of the capital, she longed for silence and open space.
p2.ex1: He found the hustle and bustle of the market strangely comforting after months in the countryside.
p2.ex2: The hustle and bustle of city life can be thrilling when you are young and full of energy.

p2.en: The speed or intensity at which everyday life moves in a particular place or for a particular person.
p2.example: She chose the village specifically because of its calm and unhurried pace of life.
p2.ex1: The pace of life in the countryside is so different from what he had been used to.
p2.ex2: Many people move abroad simply in search of a more manageable pace of life.

p2.en: To allow something to happen or someone to do something, especially officially.
p2.example: The company eventually permitted her to work fully remotely from her rural home.
p2.ex1: Budget cuts did not permit the council to improve the local transport links.
p2.ex2: The weather permitted them to spend the entire weekend walking through the scenic hills.

p2.ru: выходить на пенсию, уходить на покой
p2.en: To stop working, usually because of age; to withdraw from one's occupation permanently.
p2.example: He decided to retire early and move to a scenic coastal village to enjoy a slower life.
p2.ex1: She plans to retire to the countryside once her children have finished school.
p2.ex2: Many people choose to retire to rural areas where property is more affordable.

p2.en: The period of one's life after leaving work permanently; the act of retiring.
p2.example: They spent years saving so that their retirement could be enjoyed in a spacious rural home.
p2.ex1: Her retirement in the countryside was everything she had dreamed of for decades.
p2.ex2: Retirement should be a reward for a lifetime of work — and this view inspired their move.

p2.en: Relating to the countryside rather than the town or city; characteristic of village life.
p2.example: She was drawn to rural areas because of the peace, fresh air, and sense of community.
p2.ex1: Rural areas often struggle with poor internet connectivity and limited job opportunities.
p2.ex2: Growing up in a rural area gave him a deep appreciation for nature and open spaces.

p2.en: Having or providing beautiful, picturesque natural views.
p2.example: The drive through the scenic valley was one of the most breathtaking experiences of her life.
p2.ex1: He chose the scenic route to work so he could enjoy the countryside every morning.
p2.ex2: The cottage sat on a hill with scenic views of rolling green fields in every direction.

p2.en: Having a lot of space; large and with room to move around comfortably.
p2.example: After years in a cramped city flat, she was overjoyed by her new spacious farmhouse.
p2.ex1: The spacious garden gave the children plenty of room to play and explore.
p2.ex2: Rural properties tend to be far more spacious than equivalent homes in the city.

p2.en: The time each evening when the sun goes below the horizon, producing colourful light in the sky.
p2.example: They sat on the porch every evening watching the spectacular sunset over the hills.
p2.ex1: She photographed every sunset for a month after moving to the countryside.
p2.ex2: Watching the sunset in silence became their favourite evening ritual.

p2.en: Having the qualities that are usual or expected for a particular person, place, or thing.
p2.example: A typical day in her new rural life began with a walk and ended without a single notification.
p2.ex1: It was a typical small village — one shop, one café, and everyone knew each other.
p2.ex2: The typical pace of life there was so different from what he had experienced in the city.

p2.en: Close enough to get to without much difficulty or effort.
p2.example: She loved that the seaside was within easy reach of her new countryside home.
p2.ex1: He chose the village because the city was still within easy reach by train.
p2.ex2: Having good schools within easy reach was one of their main criteria when choosing a location.

p2.en: A strong likelihood that something will happen.
p2.example: There is a good chance that more families will choose rural living over the coming decade.
p2.ex1: She felt there was a good chance the job offer would come through.
p2.ex2: With the right preparation, there is a good chance of making a successful move abroad.

p2.en: To allow someone to try again after a previous failure or mistake.
p2.example: She gave the rural lifestyle a second chance after her first difficult winter there.
p2.ex1: He asked the company to give him a second chance to prove himself in the new role.
p2.ex2: Sometimes all you need is a second chance to realise something is actually perfect for you.

p2.en: A small or unlikely possibility that something will happen.
p2.example: There was only a slim chance of finding good broadband in that remote part of the countryside.
p2.ex1: He admitted there was a slim chance of finding work in such a small village.
p2.ex2: Despite a slim chance of success, she applied for the dream job in the rural community.

p2.en: Used to ask politely if something is possible; perhaps or possibly.
p2.example: 'Do you, by any chance, know of any rural properties available to rent near here?'
p2.ex1: Are you, by any chance, the person who wrote the letter about moving to the countryside?
p2.ex2: She asked, 'By any chance, is there a shop within easy reach of the cottage?'

p2.en: Without planning; accidentally or unexpectedly.
p2.example: By chance, she met a woman on the train who had moved from the city to a rural village.
p2.ex1: He found his dream cottage by chance while driving through the countryside on holiday.
p2.ex2: It was entirely by chance that she discovered the perfect community for her new life.

p2.en: The likelihood or probability of something happening.
p2.example: The chances of finding affordable property in a scenic area increase if you look further from the city.
p2.ex1: What are the chances of getting a remote working contract in such a rural location?
p2.ex2: She researched the chances of successfully adapting to rural life before making her decision.

p2.en: To have the opportunity to do something.
p2.example: She finally got the chance to try the slow-paced lifestyle she had always dreamed of.
p2.ex1: If you ever get the chance to spend a week in the countryside, take it without hesitation.
p2.ex2: He got the chance to work remotely, which made moving away from the city possible.

p2.en: To eagerly and quickly accept an opportunity.
p2.example: When the company offered remote working, she jumped at the chance to move to the countryside.
p2.ex1: He jumped at the chance to retire early and spend more time with his family in the village.
p2.ex2: Any lover of nature would jump at the chance to live surrounded by scenic hills and woods.

p2.ru: не оставлять ничего на волю случая
p2.en: To plan everything very carefully so that nothing is left unprepared or uncertain.
p2.example: Before making the move, she left nothing to chance and researched every aspect of rural life.
p2.ex1: He left nothing to chance when choosing the right village for his retirement.
p2.ex2: Good preparation means leaving nothing to chance when starting a new life somewhere.

p2.en: To fail to take advantage of an opportunity when it presents itself.
p2.example: She almost missed the chance to buy the cottage because she hesitated for too long.
p2.ex1: Don't miss the chance to experience life outside the city — you might love it.
p2.ex2: He deeply regretted that he had missed the chance to retire to the countryside sooner.

p2.ru: ни малейшего шанса, и речи быть не может
p2.en: Used emphatically to say that something is completely impossible or will definitely not happen.
p2.example: 'Would you ever move back to the city?' she was asked. 'Not a chance,' she replied.
p2.ex1: Not a chance would he give up the spacious countryside life for a tiny city flat.
p2.ex2: After experiencing the sunset from her new home, she thought — not a chance I am leaving.

p2.en: To have no possibility of succeeding or surviving in a particular situation.
p2.example: Without proper planning, you do not stand a chance of making a successful move to a rural area.
p2.ex1: In such a remote location, a business without internet access would not stand a chance.
p2.ex2: She knew that without commitment, the new lifestyle would not stand a chance of lasting.

p2.en: To be very careful and avoid any risk, especially by preparing thoroughly.
p2.example: Not taking any chances, she spent months visiting rural areas before making her final decision.
p2.ex1: He decided not to take any chances and visited three different villages before choosing one.
p2.ex2: When it comes to such a major life change, it pays not to take any chances.

p3.en: Easy to reach, use, or understand; available to a wide range of people.
p3.example: Digital technology has made information accessible to billions of people around the world.
p3.ex1: The new app made healthcare advice accessible to people living in remote rural areas.
p3.ex2: She believed that high-quality education should be accessible to every child regardless of location.

p3.en: A development or improvement, especially in science, technology, or knowledge.
p3.example: The latest advances in medical technology have transformed the treatment of many diseases.
p3.ex1: Every advance in artificial intelligence raises new questions about the future of work.
p3.ex2: She dedicated her career to understanding how technological advances affect quality of life.

p3.en: A painting, drawing, or other work created as an artistic expression; illustrations in a book or media.
p3.example: Museums around the world have used technology to make their artwork accessible online.
p3.ex1: The artwork in the exhibition explored the tension between nature and modern technology.
p3.ex2: She spent hours creating digital artwork that blended traditional and contemporary styles.

p3.en: A routine task, especially one done regularly in and around the home; something tedious but necessary.
p3.example: Technology has made many household chores faster and far less time-consuming.
p3.ex1: She found that moving to the countryside added new chores she had never considered before.
p3.ex2: Even enjoyable activities can start to feel like a chore when done under stress every day.

p3.en: Consisting of many different and connected parts; not easy to understand or deal with.
p3.example: The relationship between technology and human wellbeing is complex and not easily reduced.
p3.ex1: Finding a balance between a fast-paced and slow-paced lifestyle is a complex challenge.
p3.ex2: The doctor explained that obesity is a complex condition with both physical and social causes.

p3.en: Causing strong disagreement or debate among people with different views.
p3.example: The idea that technology does more harm than good remains deeply controversial.
p3.ex1: She wrote a controversial article arguing that digital detoxes were a luxury, not a solution.
p3.ex2: The new health guidelines on screen time were controversial among parents and educators alike.

p3.en: Able to cause death; extremely dangerous or harmful.
p3.example: A sedentary lifestyle combined with poor diet can be as deadly as many serious diseases.
p3.ex1: Obesity is linked to a number of potentially deadly health conditions.
p3.ex2: Stress, when left unaddressed, can have deadly consequences for long-term health.

p3.en: An illness or medical condition that affects the body or mind in a harmful way.
p3.example: Technological advances have helped doctors detect and treat disease much earlier than before.
p3.ex1: Obesity is widely recognised as a contributing factor to several serious diseases.
p3.ex2: The isolation caused by too much screen time has been linked to mental disease in young people.

p3.en: A disadvantage or problem that makes something less attractive or effective.
p3.example: One major drawback of rural life is the limited access to healthcare and cultural facilities.
p3.ex1: The main drawback of a digital detox is feeling cut off from important information.
p3.ex2: Every lifestyle choice has its drawbacks — the key is to find one that suits you best.

p3.en: To provide enjoyment or amusement for someone; to keep someone occupied in a pleasant way.
p3.example: Streaming services now entertain billions of people every day across the world.
p3.ex1: She found it harder to entertain herself during the digital detox than she had expected.
p3.ex2: Good literature has the power to entertain, educate, and inspire at the same time.

p3.en: The state of being separated from others; a feeling of loneliness or being cut off from society.
p3.example: Excessive screen use can contribute to social isolation, particularly among young people.
p3.ex1: Moving to a remote rural area carries the risk of isolation if you do not build local connections.
p3.ex2: She found that the isolation of her first months in the countryside was unexpectedly difficult.

p3.en: Existing in great numbers; very many.
p3.example: There are numerous studies showing the benefits of reducing screen time for mental health.
p3.ex1: She gave numerous reasons for wanting to simplify her lifestyle.
p3.ex2: Numerous families have made the move from city to countryside in recent years.

p3.en: The condition of being significantly overweight in a way that poses a risk to health.
p3.example: Rising rates of obesity have been linked partly to sedentary, technology-driven lifestyles.
p3.ex1: She worked as a nutritionist helping people address the causes and risks of obesity.
p3.ex2: Obesity is a complex public health issue that cannot be solved by individual choices alone.

p3.en: Used to refer to a mutual action or feeling shared between two or more people.
p3.example: In close-knit rural communities, people tend to look after one another instinctively.
p3.ex1: Social media was designed to help people connect with one another, but it can also divide.
p3.ex2: They supported one another through every difficult stage of adapting to their new life.

p3.en: A person's past experience, education, family, and social origin.
p3.example: Her background in urban planning gave her a unique perspective on rural development.
p3.ex1: People from all different backgrounds are choosing to leave the city for a simpler life.
p3.ex2: Regardless of your background, adapting to a new lifestyle takes time and patience.

p3.en: To be greater or more important than something else; to exceed in value or significance.
p3.example: For most people who made the move, the benefits of rural life outweigh the drawbacks.
p3.ex1: She argued that the long-term health benefits of exercise outweigh any short-term discomfort.
p3.ex2: The advantages of a digital detox far outweigh the inconvenience of being offline for a week.

p3.en: Used to indicate a preference or alternative; instead of something.
p3.example: She chose to walk through the woods rather than stare at a screen after dinner.
p3.ex1: He decided to cook at home rather than order fast food, as part of his lifestyle change.
p3.ex2: Rather than complaining about city stress, she took action and moved to the countryside.

p3.en: The state of being free from tension and anxiety; rest and recreation.
p3.example: Gardening became her favourite form of relaxation after the move to the countryside.
p3.ex1: Doctors increasingly recommend outdoor activities as a form of relaxation and stress relief.
p3.ex2: Relaxation is not a luxury — it is essential for maintaining long-term health and productivity.

p3.en: Experiencing or affected by mental, emotional, or physical pressure.
p3.example: People who are constantly under stress are more likely to develop serious health problems.
p3.ex1: She found it impossible to think clearly when she was under stress in the city.
p3.ex2: Children who spend too much time online can find themselves under stress from social comparison.
